lessons.title: Putting Groups Together
takeaways: Putting together means counting both groups.
Every object gets one number.
The total is bigger than either group.

lessons.title: Adding with Fingers
takeaways: Fingers are a counting tool.
One group per hand.
Count every raised finger.

lessons.title: Adding with Drawings
takeaways: Drawings hold a group still.
Draw both groups.
Count every mark on the page.

lessons.title: Acting Out a Sum
takeaways: Acting out shows the change.
Joining makes the group grow.
Count on from the start.

lessons.title: Writing an Addition Sentence
takeaways: A sentence records the action.
Plus means joining.
Equals means the same amount.

lessons.title: Taking Some Away
takeaways: Taking away makes less.
Count what is left.
What is gone is a different number.

lessons.title: Subtracting with Drawings
takeaways: Crossing out shows leaving.
Count the plain marks.
Crossed marks are no longer in the group.

lessons.title: Acting Out a Take-Away
takeaways: Acting out shows the leaving.
The group shrinks.
Count who is still there.

lessons.title: Writing a Subtraction Sentence
takeaways: Minus records taking away.
The first number is the start.
The second number is what left.

lessons.title: How Many Are Left?
takeaways: "How many left" means what remains.
Count back one per object.
What is gone is a different number.

lessons.title: Add-To Stories
takeaways: Add-to stories start with a group.
More goes in.
The total is what is missing.

lessons.title: Take-From Stories
takeaways: Take-from stories remove part.
The group gets smaller.
What remains is missing.

lessons.title: Put-Together Stories
takeaways: Put-together stories have two parts.
Nothing joins or leaves.
Counting both names the whole.

lessons.title: Which One Is It?
takeaways: Decide what happened first.
Growing means add.
Shrinking means subtract.

lessons.title: Draw the Story
takeaways: Show the start.
Show the change.
Both together tell the story.

lessons.title: Sums to 5
takeaways: Known sums save counting.
Sums to 5 come back fast.
Practice builds recall.

lessons.title: Differences Within 5
takeaways: Differences within 5 are known facts.
Each is a sum's partner.
Taking one part leaves the other.

lessons.title: Plus One, Minus One
takeaways: Plus one is the next number.
Minus one is the number before.
These work for every number.

lessons.title: Zero Changes Nothing
takeaways: Zero means none.
Adding zero changes nothing.
Taking zero away changes nothing.

lessons.title: Speedy Fives
takeaways: Mixed facts stand alone.
Sums and differences within 5.
Recall, not counting.

lessons.title: More, Fewer, or the Same?
takeaways: More, fewer, or the same.
Pairing finds out which.
Leftovers name the bigger group.

lessons.title: Matching One to One
takeaways: One star takes one heart.
The side with leftovers is bigger.
The leftovers count the difference.

lessons.title: Which Group Is Bigger?
takeaways: Bigger means more members.
Size of the things never matters.
One extra is enough to win.

lessons.title: Which Group Is Smaller?
takeaways: Fewer means running out first.
The other side holds the extras.
One back in the song is one less.

lessons.title: Groups That Match Exactly
takeaways: Equal means the pairing comes out even.
Nothing stands alone on either side.
Shuffling cannot break a match.

lessons.title: Comparing Without Counting
takeaways: A glance works for big gaps.
Spreading fools the eye.
Close contests need counting.

lessons.title: Comparing by Counting
takeaways: Count both groups.
The later count names the bigger group.
The song does the comparing.

lessons.title: Which Number Is Greater?
takeaways: Numerals carry the song's order.
Later means greater.
8 beats 6 without any objects.

lessons.title: Which Number Is Less?
takeaways: Earlier in the song means less.
Less and greater state one fact.
Both are true together.

lessons.title: Same Number, Different Things
takeaways: A numeral names one amount.
It does not care what it counts.
Same numeral, same size of group.

lessons.title: Line Them Up in Order
takeaways: Counting order follows the song.
Smallest first, biggest last.
Each number sits after all lesser ones.

lessons.title: Greatest and Least
takeaways: The greatest ends the ordered line.
The least begins it.
Everything else lives between.

lessons.title: Twenty-One and Beyond
takeaways: Counting keeps its pattern past 20.
Each new ten counts like 1, 2, 3.
One more means the next number up.

lessons.title: The Next Ten
takeaways: Every ten ends in 9.
After 29 comes 30 — a new ten.
The counting pattern starts again.

lessons.title: Counting to Fifty
takeaways: The forties count like every other ten.
49 ends the forties; 50 starts the fifties.
The pattern repeats every ten.

lessons.title: Fifty to Seventy
takeaways: Fifty, sixty, seventy — the tens march on.
Inside each ten: 1 to 9, then a new ten.
69 then 70, just like 29 then 30.

lessons.title: Seventy to One Hundred
takeaways: Seventy, eighty, ninety — almost there.
89 then 90, just like every ten.
Next stop: one hundred.

lessons.title: All the Way to 100
takeaways: The count reaches 100.
100 is ten tens.
You can count all the way!

lessons.title: Ten, Twenty, Thirty
takeaways: Each tens-jump skips nine numbers.
Tens land on round numbers.

lessons.title: Tens All the Way to 100
takeaways: Ten tens make one hundred.
Big jumps, round landings.

lessons.title: Rows of Ten on the Chart
takeaways: Each chart row holds ten numbers.
Down one row = ten more.
The chart is counting, folded into rows.

lessons.title: Which Ten Comes Next?
takeaways: Every ten has a next ten.
One tens-hop finds it.
Adding one is not adding ten.

lessons.title: Counting Tens Backward
takeaways: Tens count down too: 50, 40, 30…
Each back-hop takes a whole ten.
Same jumps, other direction.

lessons.title: Start at Seven
takeaways: Counting can start anywhere.
Count on from where you are.
The pattern is the same.

lessons.title: Start in the Middle
takeaways: Start anywhere; count on.
The next number is always one more.
Middles are fine starting places.

lessons.title: Pick Up Where It Stops
takeaways: A stopped count is not lost.
Say the last number, then count on.
47, 48, 49 — carried on.

lessons.title: Counting On from Big Numbers
takeaways: Big numbers count on the same way.
87, then 88 — one more each time.
Even near 100 the rule holds.

lessons.title: What Comes Next on the Chart?
takeaways: The chart holds the count in rows.
Next square = next number.
Row ends wrap to the row below.

lessons.title: Missing Numbers on the Chart
takeaways: Blank squares still have numbers.
Read the row; the gap speaks.
Chart gaps are counting gaps.

lessons.title: Counting Backward from Twenty
takeaways: Counting walks backward too.
Each back-step is one less.
Backward undoes forward.

lessons.title: Count the Dots
takeaways: Touch and count: one number for each thing.
The last number said is how many there are.
Scattered or in a row — the count stays the same.

lessons.title: Numbers 0 to 10
takeaways: Each amount has a number symbol: 3 means three.
0 means none at all.
A full ten-frame is 10.

lessons.title: Count On
takeaways: Start at any number and count on.
Each hop is the next number.
Counting on beats starting over at 1.

lessons.title: More or Fewer
takeaways: Pair things up to compare groups.
Leftovers mean that group has more.
Matching exactly means equal.

lessons.title: Greater, Less, Equal
takeaways: Greater = later in the counting order.
Less = earlier in the counting order.
The same number twice is equal.

lessons.title: Order the Numbers
takeaways: Counting order: each number is one more.
Order by finding the smallest first.
Zero comes before all counting numbers.

lessons.title: Ten and Some More
takeaways: The name helps: four-teen is 4 and a ten.
Teens run from 11 up to 19.

lessons.title: Count to 20
takeaways: After 19 comes 20.
The counting pattern never stops at 10.
Hop by ones to travel between any two numbers.

lessons.title: Count by Tens
takeaways: Count by tens: 10, 20, 30 … 100.
Ten ten-hops reach 100.
The ones names hide inside the tens names.

lessons.title: Putting Together
takeaways: Join groups and count all: 2 and 3 make 5.
Count on from one group to add fast.
Adding zero changes nothing.

lessons.title: Taking Away
takeaways: Take away and count what is left.
Hop back on the number line to subtract.
Taking away all leaves 0; taking 0 changes nothing.

lessons.title: Break Apart Numbers
takeaways: A number splits into pairs of parts: 5 is 2 and 3, or 1 and 4.
Equal splits share evenly: 6 is 3 and 3.
Adding, taking away, splitting — you can do it all to 10!

lessons.title: Make Ten
takeaways: A ten frame is full at 10.
Every number has a ten partner: 6 and 4, 9 and 1, 5 and 5.
Find how many MORE make ten by filling the empty spots.

lessons.title: Touch and Count
takeaways: Touch one, say one.
Every toy gets exactly one number.
The touch keeps the pairing honest.

lessons.title: Don't Skip, Don't Repeat
takeaways: Skipping makes the count too small.
Repeating makes it too big.
Each toy is touched exactly once.

lessons.title: Counting in a Line
takeaways: Start at one end of the line.
Touch each thing in turn.
Counted things stay behind your finger.

lessons.title: Counting in a Circle
takeaways: A circle has no ends.
Remember the starting bead.
Stop just before reaching it again.

lessons.title: Counting Things You Can't Move
takeaways: Unmovable things get marks instead.
A tick means counted.
Clean means still waiting.

lessons.title: The Last Number Is the Answer
takeaways: The last number names the whole group.
That is what “how many” asks.
One count is enough.

lessons.title: How Many Now?
takeaways: A finished count keeps its answer.
Recount only when the group changes.
Adding means counting ON, not over.

lessons.title: It Doesn't Matter Where You Start
takeaways: Order is the counter's choice.
The amount never moves.
Each toy counted exactly once.

lessons.title: Count Again, Same Answer
takeaways: Spreading changes space, not amount.
Looking bigger is not being more.
Only adding or removing changes the count.

lessons.title: Scattered Things
takeaways: Scattered things need marks.
Marked means counted.
The clean ones still wait.

lessons.title: One More Makes the Next Number
takeaways: One more says the next number.
No recount needed.
Each number is one more than the last.

lessons.title: Growing by One
takeaways: Growing groups count ON.
Never start over.
One newcomer, one more number.

lessons.title: Which Group Has One More?
takeaways: One more than a group is the next number.
Pairing shows the single leftover.
The line shows them one hop apart.

lessons.title: Count Out That Many
takeaways: Counting out stops AT the number.
The pile's total is irrelevant.
One per number, then stop.

lessons.title: Quick Look: How Many?
takeaways: Small amounts have shapes.
The eye names them at once.
Counting can confirm afterwards.

lessons.title: Quick Look with Ten Frames
takeaways: A full row is five at a glance.
Read amounts as five-and-more.
The frame makes numbers into pictures.

lessons.title: What Can We Measure?
takeaways: Objects carry many measurable attributes.
Length, weight, capacity are different questions.
Each question has its own tool.

lessons.title: Long, Tall, and Short
takeaways: Long, tall, short — one attribute.
Tall is length standing up.
Turning changes the word, not the length.

lessons.title: Heavy and Light
takeaways: Heavy presses down, light barely presses.
The seesaw shows pressing as tilt.
Down, up, level — three answers.

lessons.title: Which Holds More?
takeaways: Capacity is the room inside.
Filling is the fair test.
Count scoops with one same scoop.

lessons.title: Comparing Two Lengths
takeaways: Side by side, one start line.
The farther end is longer.
Cube counts say by how much.

lessons.title: Comparing Two Weights
takeaways: One object per pan.
Sinking side is heavier.
Level means exactly equal.

lessons.title: Lining Up the Ends
takeaways: Head starts fake length.
Align the starting ends first.
Then the far ends tell the truth.

lessons.title: Taller Than, Shorter Than
takeaways: Taller means reaching higher.
The floor is a built-in start line.
Width plays no part.

lessons.title: Sorting by Color and Shape
takeaways: A sort asks one question of everything.
Answers build the groups.
Change the rule, change the groups.

lessons.title: Sorting by Size
takeaways: Big and small make a rule.
Declare where big begins.
Sorting asks yes-or-no, not how-many.

lessons.title: Counting Each Sort
takeaways: Count each sorted group.
Each group earns a number.
Counts turn piles into data.

lessons.title: Which Group Has Most?
takeaways: Greatest count means most.
Least count means fewest.
Sort, count, compare — the whole chain.

lessons.title: Writing 1, 2, 3
takeaways: A numeral promises an amount.
3 names three, always.
One practised path per mark.

lessons.title: Writing 4, 5, 6
takeaways: 4, 5, 6 — new shapes, same promises.
6 wears its loop low.
Orientation is part of the mark.

lessons.title: Writing 7, 8, 9
takeaways: 7, 8, 9 close the single marks.
Nine is the last one-mark amount.
Backwards marks get misread.

lessons.title: Zero and Ten
takeaways: 0 promises an empty group.
10 reports one ten, no extras.
Two marks, one number.

lessons.title: Match the Numeral to the Group
takeaways: Matching runs both directions.
Group to numeral, numeral to group.
Exact — never roughly.

lessons.title: Write How Many
takeaways: Count first, write second.
The numeral copies the last word.
Never write a guess.

lessons.title: Writing the Teens
takeaways: Teen numerals take two marks.
The front 1 is a full ten.
The second digit counts extras.

lessons.title: Eleven and Twelve Are Tricky
takeaways: Eleven and twelve hide their ten in the name.
The numeral shows it anyway.
Trust the leading 1.

lessons.title: Thirteen Through Nineteen
takeaways: 13 to 19: the ones digit climbs.
The front 1 stands still.
One writing recipe covers them all.

lessons.title: Writing Twenty
takeaways: Twenty closes the teens.
2 tens, 0 extras.
The 0 keeps the ones place open.

lessons.title: Write How Many: Teens
takeaways: Claim the ten, count the extras.
Write 1, then the extras' digit.
Count-on equals ones digit.

lessons.title: Show That Many
takeaways: A numeral can be an order.
Build until the count says its name.
Then stop exactly.

lessons.title: Draw That Many
takeaways: Drawing follows the same order.
Count each circle as it lands.
The numeral stops the pencil.

lessons.title: Numeral, Word, Picture
takeaways: One amount, three costumes.
Numeral, word, picture agree.
Translation is the skill.

lessons.title: Name the Shapes
takeaways: Circle: round. Triangle: 3 sides.
Square: 4 equal sides. Rectangle: long and short.
Hexagon: 6 sides, like honeycomb.

lessons.title: Shapes Any Way Up
takeaways: A tipped square is still a square.
Size never changes a shape's name.
Sides and corners decide — nothing else.

lessons.title: Where Is It?
takeaways: Above = over. Below = under.
Beside = next to.
In front of and behind are opposites.

lessons.title: Shapes We Can Hold
takeaways: Ball = sphere. Dice = cube.
Can = cylinder. Party hat = cone.
Solids hide all around your home.

lessons.title: Roll, Stack, Slide
takeaways: Spheres roll every way; cubes never roll.
Cylinders roll on their side AND stack on their ends.
Cones roll in circles around their point.

lessons.title: Build with Shapes
takeaways: Two triangles make a square; two squares make a rectangle.
Drawings hide shapes: a house is a square plus a triangle.
Building with shapes is math you can touch.

lessons.title: Longer or Shorter
takeaways: Line up starting ends before comparing.
Sticks out = longer; ends first = shorter.
Taller is longer, straight up.

lessons.title: Heavier, Lighter, Holds More
takeaways: Seesaw down = heavier; up = lighter; level = equal.
Big does not always mean heavy.
Buckets hold more than cups; spoons hold less than bowls.

lessons.title: Sort and Count
takeaways: Sort by a rule: color, kind, or size.
Count each group to compare them.
Sorting never changes the total.

lessons.title: Above, Below, Beside
takeaways: Position words need a landmark.
Above, below, beside compare.
The landmark makes the word true.

lessons.title: In Front, Behind, Next To
takeaways: In front, behind, next to compare.
Opposites come in pairs.
Swap the landmark, flip the word.

lessons.title: Describing Where Shapes Are
takeaways: Describing position: word plus landmark.
One thing, many true words.
Each landmark grants its own.

lessons.title: Corners and Sides
takeaways: Sides are straight edges.
Corners are where sides meet.
Their counts name the shape.

lessons.title: Counting Corners
takeaways: Touch each corner once.
Triangle three, square four.
Size and pose never change the count.

lessons.title: Counting Sides
takeaways: Run the outline edge by edge.
Turn at each corner.
Stop when you arrive home.

lessons.title: Same Shape, Different Size
takeaways: Size is a costume.
Sides and corners are the shape.
Tiny and giant squares share one name.

lessons.title: How Are These Alike?
takeaways: Alike hides in the counts.
Ask both shapes the same questions.
Square and rectangle both answer four.

lessons.title: How Are These Different?
takeaways: Different lives in the counts too.
Three against four splits the names.
Color never decides.

lessons.title: Flat Shapes vs. Solid Shapes
takeaways: Flat lies on paper.
Solid takes up space.
Solids wear flat faces — and flat faces stack.

lessons.title: Drawing a Shape
takeaways: Drawing makes the rules real.
Straight sides, true corners.
Close the outline — then it is born.

lessons.title: Building a Shape from Sticks
takeaways: One stick, one side.
One meeting, one corner.
The sticks expose the shape's rules.

lessons.title: Two Triangles Make a Square
takeaways: Shapes compose edge to edge.
Two triangles make a square.
More squares, twos counting up.

lessons.title: Making a Bigger Shape
takeaways: Four small triangles, one bigger square.
Six squares fold into a cube.
Composing runs as far as pieces last.

lessons.title: Ten and One More
takeaways: Eleven is ten and one more.
The ten stays finished.
One extra rides on top.

lessons.title: Ten and Two More
takeaways: Twelve is ten and two.
Count on from ten: 11, 12.
Never recount the finished ten.

lessons.title: Building Teens on a Ten Frame
takeaways: The full frame is the ten.
Outside dots are the ones.
Read ten at a glance, count only extras.

lessons.title: Eleven, Twelve, Thirteen
takeaways: Eleven, twelve, thirteen hide their tens.
The numeral shows it plainly.

lessons.title: Fourteen Through Sixteen
takeaways: -teen means ten.
The word's front counts the ones.
Fourteen: four past ten.

lessons.title: Seventeen Through Nineteen
takeaways: The pattern holds to 19.
Nineteen is ten and nine.
One more makes a second ten.

lessons.title: Breaking a Teen into Ten and Some
takeaways: Any teen breaks into ten and ones.
The numeral stores the split.
Adding the parts re-makes the whole.

lessons.title: Writing Teen Equations
takeaways: 15 = 10 + 5 writes the split.
Equals means same amount.
Whole on one side, parts on the other.

lessons.title: How Many Left Over?
takeaways: Leftovers past the frame are the ones.
The frame sorts the teen for you.
17: ten inside, 7 outside.

lessons.title: Teens on the Number Line
takeaways: Teens live between 10 and 20.
The ones count steps past ten.
Line and frame tell one story.

lessons.title: Which Teen Is It?
takeaways: Count the extras, say “ten and”.
Picture, name, numeral — one path.
Both digits have jobs.

lessons.title: Teen Numbers All Around
takeaways: Teens hide in trays and packs.
Spot the ten, count the extras.
The habit lasts a lifetime.

lessons.title: Counting On from a Number
takeaways: To add, start at a number and count on — don't start from 1.
Each hop is one more.
Counting on works even past 10.

lessons.title: Count On 1, 2, 3
takeaways: +1, +2, +3 are quick counting-on hops.
Adding 0 keeps the number the same.
Some small adds land right on 10.

lessons.title: Start with the Bigger Number
takeaways: Either order gives the same sum: 3 + 8 = 8 + 3.
Start at the bigger number so you hop fewer times.
Fewer hops means fewer mistakes.

lessons.title: Partners of Ten
takeaways: Partners of ten add to exactly 10.
Knowing partners makes bigger adds fast.

lessons.title: Split to Make Ten
takeaways: Split the second number to fill the first up to ten.
Add the leftover to ten to get a teen number.

lessons.title: Adding by Making Ten
takeaways: Fill the bigger number up to ten first.
Split the smaller number to do it.
Add the leftover to ten for the answer.

lessons.title: Make Ten: You've Got It
takeaways: Fill the bigger number to ten, then add the leftover.
Teen numbers are one ten and some ones.
Making ten turns hard sums into easy ones.

lessons.title: Take Away
takeaways: Subtract (−) means take away.
Hop back on the number line to subtract.
Taking away makes the number smaller.

lessons.title: Counting Back
takeaways: Count back to subtract.
Don't count the start number as a hop.
The last hop is your answer.

lessons.title: Finding the Difference
takeaways: Subtraction can mean 'how many more'.
Count up from the smaller number to the bigger.
The number of hops is the difference.

lessons.title: Subtraction Facts
takeaways: Every subtraction has a partner addition.
Use the adds you know to subtract fast.

lessons.title: Fact Families
takeaways: Three numbers make four facts.
Two adds (flipped) and two subtractions.
Knowing one fact gives you the other three.

lessons.title: The Equal Sign Means Same As
takeaways: = means 'same as', not 'answer next'.
Both sides of = are the same amount.
The amount can come before the = too.

lessons.title: Find the Unknown
takeaways: An unknown is a missing number in an equation.
Think of the fact family to find it.
For a missing whole, add the part back.

lessons.title: Add To & Take From
takeaways: Joining groups means add.
Taking away means subtract.
Read the story to choose + or −.

lessons.title: Put Together & Take Apart
takeaways: Two parts add to the whole.
Whole minus one part gives the other.
A bar model shows the parts and whole.

lessons.title: Compare: How Many More
takeaways: Comparing finds the difference — subtract.
'How many more' does NOT always mean add.
Count up or subtract to find the gap.

lessons.title: Three Addends in a Row
takeaways: Three groups join into one total.
Add a pair first.
Then join the third addend.

lessons.title: Find the Ten First
takeaways: Look for a ten-partner pair.
Group those two first.
Ten plus the rest is easy.

lessons.title: Doubles First
takeaways: Equal addends make a double.
Start with the double.
Then join the third addend.

lessons.title: Any Order Works
takeaways: Any grouping is allowed.
The total never changes.
Choose the easiest pair.

lessons.title: Grouping to Make It Easy
takeaways: Read the addends before adding.
Ten-partners first, then doubles.
Otherwise left to right is fine.

lessons.title: Three-Addend Stories
takeaways: Every collection is an addend.
Write the equation first.
Then group the easiest pair.

lessons.title: Which Two Go Together?
takeaways: Choose the pair deliberately.
Ten-partners are the best first choice.
Be able to say why.

lessons.title: Three Numbers Past Ten
takeaways: Three addends often pass ten.
Build the ten first.
Ten-and-some is easy to name.

lessons.title: Missing Third Addend
takeaways: Build the part you can.
The gap to the total is the missing addend.
Add it back to check.

lessons.title: Adding Three, Your Way
takeaways: Three tools: ten, double, or in order.
The numbers tell you which fits.
Every valid strategy protects the total.

lessons.title: Adding a One-Digit Number
takeaways: Start at the bigger number.
Count on the small number.
Counting on works for any two-digit number.

lessons.title: When the Ones Fill a Ten
takeaways: Split to make a ten first.
Ten ones bundle into one ten.
The leftover is added after the ten is made.

lessons.title: Adding a Multiple of Ten
takeaways: Adding a ten moves the tens digit up by one.
The ones digit never changes.
This works for any starting number.

lessons.title: Tens Plus Tens
takeaways: Tens plus tens is like ones plus ones, scaled up.
Add the tens digits.
The ones digit stays zero.

lessons.title: Ten More, Ten Less in Your Head
takeaways: Ten more or less changes only the tens digit.
No counting by ones is needed.
This can be done in your head.

lessons.title: Using the Hundred Chart to Add
takeaways: The hundred chart shows tens as rows.
Down one row adds ten.
This matches the mental ten-more strategy.

lessons.title: Adding on a Number Line
takeaways: A forward hop is addition.
The landing point is the sum.
The number line makes count-on visible.

lessons.title: Breaking a Number to Add
takeaways: Breaking a number apart does not change its value.
One split makes ten first.
The rest is added after the ten is made.

lessons.title: Subtracting Multiples of Ten
takeaways: Subtracting a ten moves the tens digit down by one.
The ones digit never changes.
This mirrors adding a ten.

lessons.title: Subtracting on the Hundred Chart
takeaways: The hundred chart shows subtracting ten as a move up a row.
This mirrors adding ten as a move down.
Rows are tens; columns are ones.

lessons.title: Explaining Why It Works
takeaways: A strategy must agree with counting by ones.
Checking confirms a method is trustworthy.
Explaining why is part of doing the math.

lessons.title: Addition Stories Within 100
takeaways: Find the two known parts.
Add them to find the whole.
The whole is bigger than either part.

lessons.title: Subtraction Stories Within 100
takeaways: Find the starting total and the amount removed.
Subtract to find what remains.
What remains is smaller than the start.

lessons.title: Choose Your Method
takeaways: Match the strategy to the problem.
Small amounts suit counting on.
Crossing a ten suits making ten first.

lessons.title: What Makes It That Shape
takeaways: Sides and corners define a shape.
Count each exactly once.
That count names the shape.

lessons.title: Color and Size Don't Count
takeaways: Colour, size and turning are non-defining.
They can change freely.
Sides and corners cannot.

lessons.title: Sorting by Defining Attributes
takeaways: Sort by defining attributes.
Then groups are truly alike.
Colour sorts mix shapes together.

lessons.title: Two Shapes Make a New One
takeaways: Two shapes join along a matching edge.
The shared edge goes inside.
Count the new outline only.

lessons.title: Making a Rectangle
takeaways: Two squares make a rectangle.
The shared edge hides inside.
The outline has four sides.

lessons.title: Making a Hexagon
takeaways: Six triangles make a hexagon.
More than two pieces can compose.
Only outer edges count.

lessons.title: Filling an Outline
takeaways: Cover the outline completely.
No gaps, no overlaps.
Several fillings can be correct.

lessons.title: Building with Solids
takeaways: Solids take up space.
Flat shapes lie on the page.
Solids have faces and edges.

lessons.title: Taking a Shape Apart
takeaways: Shapes can be cut into smaller shapes.
Straight cuts give straight edges.
The pieces rebuild the whole.

lessons.title: New Shapes from Old
takeaways: Build new shapes from old.
Take them apart again.
Name a shape by its own attributes.

lessons.title: Keep Counting Past 20
takeaways: Counting keeps its pattern past 20.
Each ten counts like 1, 2, 3.
One more means the next number up.

lessons.title: Crossing to a New Ten
takeaways: At every 9, the ones roll back to 0.
The ten ticks up by one.

lessons.title: Counting to Fifty
takeaways: The count order holds all the way up.
Fill gaps by counting on.
New tens (40, 50) never break the pattern.

lessons.title: Rows of Ten
takeaways: Each row is ten numbers.
Rows end in 0: 10, 20, 30…
The next row starts the next ten.

lessons.title: Find a Number
takeaways: The tens digit names the row.
The ones digit is the spot across.
Across a row counts up by one.

lessons.title: Down a Row is Ten More
takeaways: Down a row = ten more.
Up a row = ten less.
A column shares the ones digit.

lessons.title: Tens and Ones Make a Numeral
takeaways: A two-digit number is tens then ones.
The tens digit is worth ten each.
A 0 can hold the ones place.

lessons.title: The Tricky Teens
takeaways: A teen is 1 ten plus some ones.
'-teen' means a ten is hiding.
13 and 31 are flips — watch the order.

lessons.title: Past One Hundred
takeaways: Ten tens make 100.
Past 100, count on: 100 and 13 is 113.
120 is 12 tens — the chart's top.

lessons.title: Skip-Counting by Tens
takeaways: Each ten-hop adds ten.
The ones digit stays; the tens grow.
You can start from any number.

lessons.title: Counting a Pile
takeaways: Group a pile into tens plus leftover ones.
First digit = tens, second = ones.
More tens means a bigger number.

lessons.title: Tens and Ones to 120
takeaways: Ten tens make one hundred.
Tens keep going past 100.
Big numbers still have tens and ones.

lessons.title: One More, One Less
takeaways: One more = the next number.
One less = the number before.
Sometimes a ten rolls over.

lessons.title: Ten More, Ten Less
takeaways: Ten more/less changes the tens digit.
The ones digit stays the same.
Don't confuse it with one more/less.

lessons.title: Mixing Jumps
takeaways: Ten jumps move the tens; one jumps move the ones.
Do each jump in order.
Up for more, down for less.

lessons.title: Asking a Question
takeaways: Data begins with a question.
Good questions give one sortable choice.
Choices become categories to count.

lessons.title: Sorting into Categories
takeaways: Sorting puts matches together.
The rule decides the groups.
Sorted groups are ready to count.

lessons.title: Making a Tally
takeaways: Each mark counts one.
The fifth mark crosses its group.
Five-groups make counts fast to read.

lessons.title: Reading a Tally Chart
takeaways: Count crossed groups by fives.
Count singles on by ones.
A crossed group always holds five.

lessons.title: Building a Picture Graph
takeaways: One picture stands for one.
A row's pictures are its count.
Longer rows mean bigger counts.

lessons.title: Reading a Picture Graph
takeaways: Reading a row is counting it.
Touch each picture once.
Miscounts change the story.

lessons.title: Building a Bar Graph
takeaways: One bar per category.
The bar's top touches its count.
Taller bar, bigger count.

lessons.title: Reading a Bar Graph
takeaways: Follow the top to the scale.
The touched gridline is the count.
The scale counts for you.

lessons.title: How Many in All?
takeaways: “In all” adds every category.
Every vote counts exactly once.
Skipping a category loses votes.

lessons.title: How Many More?
takeaways: “How many more” is a difference.
Subtract the smaller from the larger.
The gap between bar tops shows it.

lessons.title: Which Category Has Most?
takeaways: Most means the biggest count.
Fewest means the smallest.
Position never decides — counts do.

lessons.title: Telling the Story of the Data
takeaways: Data tells a checkable story.
True sentences match the counts.
The counts are the judges.

lessons.title: What the Equal Sign Means
takeaways: The equal sign claims same value.
Value each side to test the claim.
Sides can look different and still match.

lessons.title: True or False?
takeaways: Equations can be true or false.
Value each side, then compare.
Matching values make it true.

lessons.title: Both Sides the Same
takeaways: Both sides can hold work.
Value the complete side first.
Fill the blank to match that value.

lessons.title: Numbers on the Right
takeaways: The total can be written first.
The equal sign compares values only.
Complete the working side to match.

lessons.title: Sums on Both Sides
takeaways: Sums can stand on both sides.
The equal sign is a balance.
True means one shared value.

lessons.title: Unknown at the End
takeaways: The end-unknown is the total.
Join the known parts to find it.
A letter can name the hiding place.

lessons.title: Unknown in the Middle
takeaways: The middle-unknown is a missing part.
Total minus known part finds it.
Adding it back checks it.

lessons.title: Unknown at the Start
takeaways: Start-unknowns are missing parts too.
Total minus known part — always.
Rebuild the total to check.

lessons.title: Subtraction Unknowns
takeaways: Subtraction hides unknowns too.
The removed amount is a gap.
Remainder plus removed rebuilds the start.

lessons.title: Using a Fact Family to Solve
takeaways: Unknowns live inside fact families.
Name the family's three numbers.
The right family member is the answer.

lessons.title: Checking Your Answer
takeaways: Substitute the answer back in.
Value both sides.
Matching sides prove it right.

lessons.title: Writing Your Own True Equation
takeaways: Writing an equation is making a claim.
The equals sign must be earned.
Verify both sides before keeping it.

lessons.title: Comparing Two Objects
takeaways: Line up one end first.
Then the far end decides.
Position is not length.

lessons.title: Ordering Three Objects
takeaways: Compare two at a time.
Repeat to build the order.
Shortest to longest.

lessons.title: Comparing Without Moving
takeaways: A third object can compare two.
Compare each to the same go-between.
The results settle the pair.

lessons.title: Using a Third Object
takeaways: A beats B, B beats C, so A beats C.
The chain never reverses.
That is why go-betweens work.

lessons.title: Laying Units End to End
takeaways: Start at the object's edge.
Lay same-size units end to end.
The count is the length.

lessons.title: No Gaps, No Overlaps
takeaways: No gaps, no overlaps.
Gaps undercount; overlaps overcount.
Exact touching makes the count true.

lessons.title: Counting the Units
takeaways: Count one per unit placed.
The total is the length.
Counts make lengths comparable.

lessons.title: Measuring with Cubes
takeaways: Cubes are identical units.
Identical size makes counting meaningful.
They touch cleanly end to end.

lessons.title: Measuring with Paper Clips
takeaways: Any identical object can be a unit.
Different units give different counts.
Each count names its own unit.

lessons.title: Same Object, Different Units
takeaways: Bigger units give smaller counts.
The object never changes.
Always say which unit was used.

lessons.title: Swapping the Addends
takeaways: Addends can swap.
The total stays the same.
Start at the bigger number to count less.

lessons.title: Why Swapping Is Safe
takeaways: Addition joins groups.
Order does not change the pile.
The swap rule works for every pair of numbers.

lessons.title: Counting On from the Bigger
takeaways: Start at the bigger number.
Count on the smaller number.
The last count is the total.

lessons.title: Counting On Three or Less
takeaways: Counting on fits add-ons of 3 or less.
Few hops, few mistakes.
Bigger add-ons will want other strategies.

lessons.title: Counting Back to Subtract
takeaways: Count back to subtract small amounts.
One hop per counter removed.
The landing is what remains.

lessons.title: Doubles You Know
takeaways: A double joins two equal groups.
Doubles are always even.
Knowing doubles makes nearby sums fast.

lessons.title: Doubles Plus One
takeaways: Near-doubles hide a known double.
Double the smaller addend.
Then add exactly one.

lessons.title: Doubles Minus One
takeaways: The bigger double overshoots by one.
Double, then subtract one.
Either neighboring double can anchor a near-double.

lessons.title: Making Ten to Add
takeaways: Complete the ten first.
Add the leftover to ten.
Ten-and-some is easy to name.

lessons.title: Making Ten to Subtract
takeaways: Stop at ten first.
Then take away the rest.
A related addition fact checks the answer.

lessons.title: Using a Known Fact
takeaways: Three numbers make a fact family.
One known fact unlocks the others.
Whole minus one part is the other part.

lessons.title: Equivalent Sums
takeaways: Different sums can share one total.
Moving counters keeps the total steady.
Balance the sides to match.

lessons.title: Which Strategy Fits?
takeaways: Read the numbers first.
Small add-ons: count on. Crossing ten: make ten.
Near-equal addends: use a double.

lessons.title: Explaining Your Strategy
takeaways: A strategy protects the total.
Explaining it names what stays the same.
The why makes the strategy trustworthy.

lessons.title: What Makes a Shape Flat
takeaways: A shape's sides and corners are the same number.
Triangle 3, square/rectangle 4, pentagon 5, hexagon 6.
A circle has no straight sides and no corners.

lessons.title: Flat or Solid?
takeaways: Flat shapes (triangle, hexagon) are 2D.
Solids (cube, cone, cylinder) are 3D.
Cubes are all flat faces; cones and cylinders mix flat and curved.

lessons.title: Counting a Solid's Parts
takeaways: A cube and a rectangular prism both have 6 faces, 12 edges, 8 vertices.
Faces are surfaces, edges are lines, vertices are points.
A curved solid (cone, cylinder) isn't made only of flat faces.

lessons.title: Splitting a Shape in Half
takeaways: Halves means splitting into 2 equal parts.
Each equal part is called a half.
Unequal parts are never halves, no matter the number.

lessons.title: Splitting a Shape into Fourths
takeaways: Fourths means splitting into 4 equal parts.
"Quarter" and "fourth" name the same size part.
All 4 pieces must match in size.

lessons.title: Fourths Make Halves
takeaways: A fourth is smaller than a half.
2 fourths together make 1 half.
4 fourths (or 2 halves) make the whole.

lessons.title: Which Is Longer?
takeaways: More units of length means longer.
Fewer units means shorter.
Only compare counts measured in the same unit.

lessons.title: How Many More?
takeaways: Subtract to find how many more units one object is.
Always take the smaller count away from the bigger.
This works with any matching unit — paperclips, cubes, or blocks.

lessons.title: Longest and Shortest
takeaways: Compare every count before deciding.
The biggest count is the longest object.
The smallest count is the shortest object.

lessons.title: Telling Time on the Hour
takeaways: The short hand shows the hour.
Minute hand at 12 means ":00".
Read the hour hand's number, then add ":00".

lessons.title: Telling Time at Half Past
takeaways: Minute hand at 6 means ":30".
The hour hand sits between two numbers at half past.
Use the smaller (already-passed) number for the hour.

lessons.title: On the Hour or Half Past?
takeaways: Minute hand at 12: read ":00".
Minute hand at 6: read ":30" using the passed hour.
Short hand always tells the hour.

lessons.title: Ten Ones Make a Ten
takeaways: 1 ten = 10 ones.
To turn tens into ones, count by tens.
To find tens, count the groups of ten.

lessons.title: Tens and Ones in a Number
takeaways: In a two-digit number, left = tens, right = ones.
Tens and ones build the number: 4 tens 6 ones = 46.
A 0 in the ones place means no extra ones.

lessons.title: Reading Base-Ten Blocks
takeaways: Each rod is a ten; each cube is a one.
Count the rods, then the cubes.
No cubes means a 0 in the ones place.

lessons.title: Breaking a Number Apart
takeaways: 46 = 40 + 6 (tens value plus ones).
A tens digit is worth the digit × 10.
Add the parts back to get the number.

lessons.title: Reading Expanded Form
takeaways: The tens part is a multiple of ten.
Add the values, don't just join the digits.

lessons.title: Which Digit Is Worth More?
takeaways: The same digit is worth more in the tens place.
In 33, the left 3 is 30 and the right 3 is 3.
Place value is why 40 is bigger than 4.

lessons.title: Ten More, Ten Less
takeaways: +10 moves the tens digit up by 1.
−10 moves the tens digit down by 1.
The ones digit never changes.

lessons.title: Adding Tens
takeaways: Adding 20, 30, 40 … adds that many tens.
The tens digits add like small numbers.
The ones digit stays the same.

lessons.title: Subtracting Tens
takeaways: Subtracting 20, 30 … removes that many tens.
The tens digit drops; the ones stay.
Counting down by tens gives the same answer.

lessons.title: Which Has More Tens?
takeaways: Look at the tens digit first.
More tens wins, even with smaller ones.
The sign opens toward the bigger number.

lessons.title: Same Tens, Check the Ones
takeaways: Equal tens? Compare the ones.
Same tens and same ones means the numbers are equal.
Use = only when every digit matches.

lessons.title: Comparing Any Two Numbers
takeaways: Different tens? More tens wins.
Same tens? More ones wins.
Same tens and ones? The numbers are equal.

lessons.title: Doubles
takeaways: A double is the same number twice.
Doubles always land on even numbers.
Halving a double gives the number back.

lessons.title: Near Doubles
takeaways: Neighbors = double the smaller, add 1.
Near doubles land on odd numbers.
Doubles + near doubles cover many facts.

lessons.title: Choose Your Strategy
takeaways: Doubles and near doubles are instant.
Make ten for big-plus-medium facts.
Count on for tiny adds.

lessons.title: Adding Tens
takeaways: 3 tens + 4 tens = 7 tens.
The ones digit stays 0.
Ten tens make 100.

lessons.title: Add Ones to a Two-Digit Number
takeaways: Ones add to the ones digit.
The tens digit doesn't move.

lessons.title: Adding Two-Digit Numbers
takeaways: Split into tens and ones.
Add tens with tens, ones with ones.
Join the two sums back.

lessons.title: Trade Ten Ones
takeaways: Ones at 10+ trade ten for a rod.
The traded rod joins the tens.
Check the ones first to spot a trade.

lessons.title: Subtracting Tens
takeaways: 7 tens − 3 tens = 4 tens.
The ones digit stays 0.
Think the small fact, then say tens.

lessons.title: Take Ones Away
takeaways: Ones subtract from the ones digit.
The tens digit doesn't move.

lessons.title: Subtracting Two-Digit Numbers
takeaways: Split into tens and ones.
Take tens from tens, ones from ones.
Join what's left.

lessons.title: Break a Ten
takeaways: Short ones? Break a rod into 10 ones.
The broken rod is spent — one less ten.
Never flip to small-from-big.

lessons.title: Two-Step Stories
takeaways: Do the steps in the order they happen.
Arrivals add; departures subtract.
The middle number feeds the second step.

lessons.title: Stories that Trade
takeaways: A step may trade (adding) or break (subtracting).
Do each step fully before the next.
Watch whether each event adds or removes.

lessons.title: Choose the Two Steps
takeaways: Gain words add; lose words subtract.
'How many more' compares — subtract.
Do the two steps in story order.

lessons.title: Odd & Even
takeaways: Even = pairs up with none left over.
Odd = one left over.
Shortcut: check the last digit.

lessons.title: Adding Odds & Evens
takeaways: Same parity adds to even; different adds to odd.
Odd + odd = even (leftovers pair up).
Every double is even.

lessons.title: Adding Hundreds
takeaways: Hundreds add like ones.
The place holds the size.
Zeros keep the empty places.

lessons.title: Adding Without Trading
takeaways: Add place by place.
Ones, then tens, then hundreds.
No trade when every column fits.

lessons.title: Trading Ones for a Ten
takeaways: Ten ones bundle into a ten.
Carry it left.
The total never changes.

lessons.title: Trading Tens for a Hundred
takeaways: Ten tens make a hundred.
Carry moves left.
Every place obeys the same rule.

lessons.title: Two Trades at Once
takeaways: Two trades, one problem.
Ones bundle first.
Each carry feeds the next column.

lessons.title: Subtracting Without Trading
takeaways: Subtract place by place.
Each column pays its own.
No trade when the top digits suffice.

lessons.title: Breaking a Ten
takeaways: Break a ten into ten ones.
One fewer ten remains.
Never flip the digits instead.

lessons.title: Breaking a Hundred
takeaways: Break a hundred into ten tens.
One fewer hundred remains.
Then subtract as usual.

lessons.title: Subtracting Across a Zero
takeaways: A zero relays the trade.
Hundred to tens, ten to ones.
Two breaks, then subtract.

lessons.title: Ten More, Ten Less Mentally
takeaways: Ten more, ten less: one digit.
The tens digit slides.
No written work needed.

lessons.title: Hundred More, Hundred Less Mentally
takeaways: Hundred more, hundred less: the front digit.
Tens and ones ride along.
Say it, don't write it.

lessons.title: Jumping on an Open Number Line
takeaways: Jumps make adding visible.
Big jumps first.
The last landing is the answer.

lessons.title: Why Trading Works
takeaways: Ten of one unit equal one of the next.
Non-standard forms are legal.
Trading tidies, never changes.

lessons.title: Explaining a Strategy
takeaways: Name the move and the reason.
'Because they are equal.'
Every trade earns a sentence.

lessons.title: Three-Digit Stories
takeaways: Stories hide equations.
Joining adds, remaining subtracts.
Write it, then solve it.

lessons.title: Choosing a Method
takeaways: Numbers point at methods.
Friendly: mental. Messy: columns.
Estimate either way.

lessons.title: Pairing Things Up
takeaways: Pair into twos.
Leftover means odd.
No leftover means even.

lessons.title: Odd or Even?
takeaways: The ones digit decides.
Tens pair automatically.
0,2,4,6,8 end even numbers.

lessons.title: Doubles Make Evens
takeaways: A double is two equal groups.
Twins pair across.
Doubles are always even.

lessons.title: Writing an Even as a Double
takeaways: Even numbers split equally.
The double names the halves.
Equal groups are the requirement.

lessons.title: Rows and Columns
takeaways: Rows run across.
Columns run up and down.
Each counter lives in one of each.

lessons.title: Counting an Array by Rows
takeaways: Add one row at a time.
The step is the row size.
The last step is the total.

lessons.title: Counting an Array by Columns
takeaways: Columns count the array too.
Both paths must agree.
Disagreement means a miscount.

lessons.title: Writing the Repeated Sum
takeaways: Array to sum: addend is the row size.
One addend per row.
Reading back rebuilds the array.

lessons.title: Same Total, Different Array
takeaways: One total, many shapes.
Rearranging never changes count.
Choose the easy slicing.

lessons.title: Arrays in the World
takeaways: The world is full of arrays.
Spot, name, write, stage.
Row-by-row totals anything.

lessons.title: Measuring a Whole Group
takeaways: One unit for all.
Mark to mark is the length.
Shared units make comparisons honest.

lessons.title: Recording Measurements
takeaways: Keep every measurement.
Repeats are real data.
Records feed the graphs.

lessons.title: Building a Line Plot
takeaways: One x per measurement.
Stacks sit on their values.
Repeats build height.

lessons.title: Reading a Line Plot
takeaways: Labels name, x's count.
Read one stack at a time.
The stack is the answer.

lessons.title: Most Common Measurement
takeaways: The tallest stack wins.
Read the value beneath it.
Count and value are different crowns.

lessons.title: Building a Picture Graph
takeaways: One row per category.
The key sets each picture's worth.
Building is faithful counting.

lessons.title: Reading a Picture Graph
takeaways: Count the row, apply the key.
Longer rows hold more.
Gaps answer 'how many more'.

lessons.title: Building a Bar Graph
takeaways: One bar per category.
Tops rest exactly on counts.
Gridlines keep bars honest.

lessons.title: Reading a Bar Graph
takeaways: Follow tops to the scale.
Taller means more.
Height gaps are count gaps.

lessons.title: Put-Together Questions
takeaways: Read, then add.
The graph supplies addends.
Together collects every count.

lessons.title: Take-Apart and Compare Questions
takeaways: 'More' means the gap.
Smaller from larger.
The overhang is visible subtraction.

lessons.title: Which Graph Should I Use?
takeaways: The data picks the display.
Lengths take line plots.
Categories take bars and pictures.

lessons.title: Doubles from Memory
takeaways: A double adds a number to itself.
Doubles are recalled, not counted.

lessons.title: Near Doubles
takeaways: A near double is a double plus one.
Adjust a known fact instead of recounting.

lessons.title: Making Ten
takeaways: Make ten first, then add the rest.
Split the second number into two parts.

lessons.title: Ten Plus Something
takeaways: Ten plus ones keeps the ten whole.
Teen numbers are a ten and some ones.

lessons.title: Sums to 12
takeaways: Every sum has a strategy.
Reach for the fact, not the count.

lessons.title: Sums to 16
takeaways: Big addends still make ten first.
The leftover part names the ones.

lessons.title: Sums to 20
takeaways: The largest facts are mostly doubles.
Doubles carry the top of the table.

lessons.title: Subtracting from Ten
takeaways: Ten has two parts.
Knowing the pairs makes subtraction instant.

lessons.title: Subtracting Across Ten
takeaways: Stop at ten on the way down.
Two easy steps beat one hard one.

lessons.title: Think Addition to Subtract
takeaways: Subtraction is addition backwards.
Ask what joins the part to the total.

lessons.title: Fact Families to 20
takeaways: Two parts and a total make a family.
One family holds four facts.

lessons.title: Missing Numbers
takeaways: A missing part is a subtraction.
The total decides what fits.

lessons.title: Speed Round: Addition
takeaways: Fluency is recall, not fast counting.
Strategies were the scaffolding.

lessons.title: Speed Round: Subtraction
takeaways: Subtraction facts follow their partners.
Families make both directions automatic.

lessons.title: Adding Three Two-Digit Numbers
takeaways: Add two at a time.
Bank the running total.
The last addend joins it.

lessons.title: Adding Four Two-Digit Numbers
takeaways: Four addends, three joins.
The rhythm repeats.
The running total carries you.

lessons.title: Look for Tens First
takeaways: Scan the ones first.
Pair the ten-makers.
Bank the clean ten.

lessons.title: Adding the Tens, Then the Ones
takeaways: Split every addend by place.
Add tens, add ones.
Rejoin the two piles.

lessons.title: Grouping Friendly Pairs
takeaways: Scan before adding.
Ones that complete each other.
A found pair is free work.

lessons.title: Keeping Track of the Total
takeaways: The running total is the cargo.
Narrate every join.
A safe pause needs only the total.

lessons.title: Four-Addend Stories
takeaways: Name the addends first.
Stage the sum as always.
Add contents, not containers.

lessons.title: Checking a Long Sum
takeaways: Check by re-adding differently.
Matching paths mean confidence.
Disagreement means recount now.

lessons.title: How Much Longer?
takeaways: Align the starts.
The overhang is the difference.
Longer minus shorter.

lessons.title: Comparing Two Measurements
takeaways: Ranking needs every number.
Middle values are traps.
Extremes take the titles.

lessons.title: Finding the Difference in Length
takeaways: The end mark is not the length.
Subtract the start mark.
The span between is the answer.

lessons.title: Adding Two Lengths
takeaways: End to end adds.
The far end reads the sum.
Joining order is free.

lessons.title: Total Distance
takeaways: Totals collect every leg.
Stage and bank.
No leg twice, none skipped.

lessons.title: Missing Length
takeaways: The parts rebuild the whole.
Whole minus known part.
Re-join to check.

lessons.title: Length Stories with Drawings
takeaways: One bar per quantity.
The picture asks the question.
Gaps subtract, stacks add.

lessons.title: Using a Number Line for Length
takeaways: The line is an endless ruler.
Lengths are jumps.
Joins chain, gaps subtract.

lessons.title: Two-Step Length Problems
takeaways: Two steps, one running total.
Direction per step.
The total bridges the moves.

lessons.title: Does the Answer Make Sense?
takeaways: Test answers against the story.
Totals outgrow parts.
Gaps fit inside the longer.

lessons.title: Reading a Ruler
takeaways: Length = end mark − start mark.
Small objects: inches. Big distances: feet.
Starting at 0 makes the end mark the length directly.

lessons.title: Measuring with Different Starting Points
takeaways: Length = end mark − start mark, always.
Reading only the end mark is a common mistake when the start isn't 0.
Match the unit to the size of what you're measuring.

lessons.title: Choosing the Right Unit
takeaways: Small objects: inches. Big spaces: feet.
The right unit gives friendly, sensible numbers.
Reading a ruler is always end mark minus start mark.

lessons.title: Estimating Before You Measure
takeaways: Estimate before measuring, as a smart guess.
Being off by 1 or 2 inches is fine.
A far-off number is not a good estimate.

lessons.title: Which Is Longer?
takeaways: More inches means longer; fewer means shorter.
Subtract to find exactly how many inches more.
This works the same way you already learned, now with standard units.

lessons.title: Ordering Three Lengths
takeaways: Compare every measurement before deciding.
The biggest number is the longest object.
The smallest number is the shortest object.

lessons.title: What Are Coins Worth?
takeaways: Penny 1¢, nickel 5¢, dime 10¢, quarter 25¢.
Coin size doesn't tell you its value.
Add every coin's value to find the total.

lessons.title: Counting Mixed Coins
takeaways: Start with the biggest coins and skip-count.
Add each coin type's total value in order.
The same amount can be made with different mixes of coins.

lessons.title: How Many Coins Make That?
takeaways: Number of coins = total cents ÷ one coin's value.
This works for any coin type, when it divides evenly.
A dollar is 100 cents — 4 quarters, 10 dimes, or 20 nickels.

lessons.title: Skip-Counting by 5s on the Clock
takeaways: Each clock number is 5 minutes apart.
Minutes = clock number × 5.
12 means 0 minutes; 6 means 30 minutes.

lessons.title: Reading Five-Minute Times
takeaways: Check the minute hand at 12 first — that's still ":00".
Otherwise, skip-count the minute hand's position by 5s.
Pair that minute count with the hour hand's (passed) number.

lessons.title: Practicing Five-Minute Times
takeaways: Minutes = minute hand's clock number × 5.
12 means ":00"; every other position skip-counts the same way.
The short hand always gives the hour.

lessons.title: Reading a Picture Graph
takeaways: Each picture equals 1 — count directly, no multiplying.
More pictures always means a bigger total.
Zero pictures means zero votes.

lessons.title: Reading a Bar Graph
takeaways: Each gridline equals 1 — read the height directly.
A taller bar means a bigger amount.
No multiplying needed at this scale.

lessons.title: Reading a Line Plot and Comparing Data
takeaways: Count the X's above a number for its data-point total.
Subtract to find how many more one amount is than another.
The same reading and comparing skills work across picture graphs, bar graphs, and line plots.

lessons.title: Numbers on a Line
takeaways: Every number has a home.
Bigger lives to the right.
Position is value.

lessons.title: Equally Spaced Marks
takeaways: Marks keep equal gaps.
Equal amounts, equal room.
Spacing is the line's promise.

lessons.title: Finding a Number Between
takeaways: Labels skip; the line doesn't.
Every gap is full of numbers.
Halfway in a tens-gap ends in 5.

lessons.title: Jumping Forward to Add
takeaways: Addition walks right.
Start, jump, land.
The landing is the sum.

lessons.title: Jumping Backward to Subtract
takeaways: Subtraction walks left.
Start big, jump back.
Land on the difference.

lessons.title: Big Jumps and Small Jumps
takeaways: Jumps have sizes.
Tens first, ones last.
Plans must land exactly.

lessons.title: Showing a Sum on the Line
takeaways: The drawing tells the sum's story.
Start, jumps, landing.
Picture and equation agree.

lessons.title: Showing a Difference on the Line
takeaways: Two drawings of a difference.
Walk back, or measure the gap.
Both land together.

lessons.title: Which Jump Is Missing?
takeaways: The missing jump is the gap.
Landing minus start.
Re-jump to check.

lessons.title: Number Line Stories
takeaways: Stories move along lines.
Forward adds, backward subtracts.
'Apart' measures a gap.

lessons.title: Hundreds Join the Party
takeaways: Hundreds, tens, and ones are the three spots in a 3-digit number.
The same digit is worth different amounts in different spots.
A zero spot still counts — it can't be skipped.

lessons.title: Trading Up and Down
takeaways: Trading up: 10 of a spot becomes 1 of the next spot over.
A 3-digit number's hundreds digit maxes out at 9.
Building a number combines hundreds, tens, and ones in order.

lessons.title: Any Number, Any Spot
takeaways: A digit's worth depends entirely on its spot.
Building a number combines hundreds, tens, and ones in order.
Zero spots always count — never skip them.

lessons.title: Skip-Counting by Tens and Hundreds
takeaways: Skip-counting by 10s adds 10 each jump; by 100s adds 100 each jump.
When a spot rolls over (9 to 0), the next spot over grows by 1.
The rules never change, even near 1000.

lessons.title: Skip-Counting by Fives
takeaways: Skip-counting by 5s adds 5 each jump.
The result always ends in 0 or 5.
The process works the same near a rollover as anywhere else.

lessons.title: Counting Forward from Any Start
takeaways: Count forward N times means adding the skip amount N times.
The starting number can be anything, not just a round number.
The process crosses hundred-rollovers the same way it works anywhere else.

lessons.title: Reading and Writing 3-Digit Numbers
takeaways: Word form: hundreds word, then tens-ones.
Empty spots aren't said out loud.
You can convert either direction: number to words, or words to number.

lessons.title: Comparing Numbers with Symbols
takeaways: Check hundreds first; if tied, check tens; if still tied, check ones.
A bigger digit later can't outweigh a smaller digit earlier.
If every spot matches, the numbers are equal.

lessons.title: Ordering 3-Digit Numbers
takeaways: Order a list by comparing pairs, spot by spot.
Word form and standard form both describe the same number.
The same left-to-right comparison strategy works for any pair.

lessons.title: Adding by Place, Then Combining
takeaways: Combine hundreds, tens, and ones each on their own.
A spot with 10 or more trades into the next spot over.
A trade can cascade through more than one spot.

lessons.title: Subtracting by Place, with Trading
takeaways: Subtract hundreds, tens, and ones each on their own.
When a spot is too small, trade 1 of the next spot over into 10 of the smaller spot.
A trade-down can cascade through more than one spot, even across an empty spot.

lessons.title: Adding and Subtracting in Real Situations
takeaways: Translate the story into an addition or subtraction problem first.
Decompose into hundreds, tens, ones, and work each spot.
Trade whenever a spot overflows (adding) or comes up short (subtracting).

lessons.title: Bigger Shape Families
takeaways: Heptagon = 7 sides and corners.
Octagon = 8 sides and corners.
You can name a shape from its side count, and vice versa.

lessons.title: Meet the Pyramid
takeaways: A square pyramid: 1 square base + 4 triangle faces.
8 edges: 4 around the base, 4 to the point.
5 vertices: 4 base corners + 1 top point.

lessons.title: Naming Any Shape
takeaways: Triangle (3) through octagon (8) — the full family.
Heptagon and octagon are easy to mix up — check the exact count.
A square pyramid comes to a point; prisms have flat tops.

lessons.title: Counting a Grid of Squares
takeaways: A grid has rows going across and columns going up and down.
Count every unit square, not just the row and column counts.
More rows or columns always means more squares.

lessons.title: Bigger Grids
takeaways: Bigger grids mean more squares, but the same counting idea.
Rows and columns can trade places and give the same total.
Count every square in the grid, however big it is.

lessons.title: Grids in Everyday Objects
takeaways: Chocolate bars, windows, checkerboards, tiles — all grids of squares.
Count every square in every row, no matter the object.
The counting rule never changes, only the size of the grid.

lessons.title: Splitting into Thirds
takeaways: Thirds means splitting into 3 equal parts.
The 3 pieces must be truly equal in size.
Any shape can be split into thirds, in different ways.

lessons.title: Naming a Third
takeaways: 3 equal parts are called thirds.
2 is halves, 3 is thirds, 4 is fourths.
3 thirds put back together make the whole.

lessons.title: Comparing Halves, Thirds, and Fourths
takeaways: Halves are the biggest of the three shares.
Fourths are the smallest.
Thirds sit in between — bigger than fourths, smaller than halves.

lessons.title: Adding Three-Digit Numbers
takeaways: Line the places up.
Add each column on its own.
No overflow means no trade.

lessons.title: Two Regroupings
takeaways: Over nine? Bundle and carry.
The carry lands in the next column.
Trading repackages, never removes.

lessons.title: Subtracting Three-Digit Numbers
takeaways: Subtract column by column.
Ones first, working left.
Big enough on top means no trade.

lessons.title: Regrouping Twice to Subtract
takeaways: Short column? Trade, never flip.
Ten ones for one ten.
The lending column drops by one.

lessons.title: Across Two Zeros
takeaways: Zero cannot lend until it borrows.
The trade passes through.
A passed-through zero keeps nine.

lessons.title: Adding on an Open Number Line
takeaways: Jump hundreds, then tens, then ones.
Big jumps first.
The line and the column must agree.

lessons.title: Compensation Strategy
takeaways: Round to a friendly number.
Repay exactly what you borrowed.
Compensation changes work, not answers.

lessons.title: Checking by Adding Back
takeaways: Addition undoes subtraction.
Answer plus subtrahend rebuilds the start.
Agreement is evidence.

lessons.title: Three-Digit Stories
takeaways: Read for the action.
Spending down, raising up.
Two-step stories need both moves.

lessons.title: Which Strategy Is Fastest?
takeaways: All roads reach one answer.
Friendly numbers invite compensation.
Choosing the road is fluency.

lessons.title: Dividing by 2
takeaways: Dividing by 2 halves.
Halving undoes doubling.

lessons.title: Dividing by 3
takeaways: ÷3 makes three equal shares.
It undoes a ×3 fact.

lessons.title: Dividing by 4 and 5
takeaways: ÷4 halves twice.
÷5 undoes the ×5 facts.
Check by multiplying back.

lessons.title: Dividing by 6 and 7
takeaways: ÷6 and ÷7 undo the hard tables.
Same fact, read backwards.

lessons.title: Dividing by 8 and 9
takeaways: ÷8 and ÷9 finish the tables.
Find the matching product.

lessons.title: Dividing by 10
takeaways: ÷10 shifts digits right.
Seven tens become seven.

lessons.title: Think Multiplication
takeaways: Turn division into multiplication.
Every fact has a twin.

lessons.title: Missing Factor, Missing Quotient
takeaways: The missing number can be anywhere.
Divisor and quotient are the factors.

lessons.title: Dividing by 1 and Itself
takeaways: ÷1 leaves a number unchanged.
A number ÷ itself is 1.

lessons.title: Why You Can't Divide by Zero
takeaways: Division by zero is undefined.
Zero divided by a number is 0.
The zero's position decides.

lessons.title: Mixed Division Facts
takeaways: Any divisor, any order.
Rhythm is gone; recall remains.

lessons.title: Multiply or Divide?
takeaways: Missing total: multiply.
Missing share: divide.
Read what the problem gives you.

lessons.title: Cutting into Equal Parts
takeaways: Fair cuts earn names; unequal pieces are just chunks.
The piece COUNT gives the name: 4 equal pieces → fourths.
Count pieces, not cuts — pieces always beat straight cuts by one.

lessons.title: Unit Fractions: One Piece
takeaways: 1/b is one piece of a fair b-cut — the unit fraction.
The bottom number records the cut; the 1 says you hold one piece.
Finer cuts make smaller units — 1/8 is tiny next to 1/2.

lessons.title: Counting Pieces: a/b
takeaways: The top counts the pieces you take; a/b = a copies of 1/b.
Read it as a recipe: bottom cuts, top takes.
A picture earns a fraction name only if the cut is fair AND both numbers match it.

lessons.title: Top Number, Bottom Number
takeaways: Denominator (bottom) = the cut — it names the piece kind and sets piece size.
Numerator (top) = the count — how many pieces you take.
Zero can sit on top (take nothing) but never on the bottom (a cut must make pieces).

lessons.title: Cutting the Line
takeaways: The 0→1 stretch is a whole; equal jumps are its fair pieces.
Inside marks = jumps − 1 — the fencepost trick.
Equal jumps pin each fraction name to one exact spot.

lessons.title: Locating 1/b
takeaways: 1/b = one jump from 0 on a b-jump trip.
The bottom number sets the jump SIZE — it is never the landing mark.
Bigger bottoms make shorter jumps: 1/8 lands closer to 0 than 1/3.

lessons.title: Locating a/b
takeaways: a/b = a jumps of size 1/b — the top is your jump count.
Counting up the line says the names: 1/4, 2/4, 3/4, 4/4 = 1.
Same jump size? The jump count alone sets who's farther along.

lessons.title: Fractions Past One
takeaways: Top bigger than bottom? Keep jumping past 1 — 5/4 is a whole plus a fourth.
n/n always lands exactly on 1; every b jumps banks another whole.
To place a big fraction, find the whole-number landings first, then count the extras.

lessons.title: Same Point, Different Names
takeaways: Equivalent = the exact same point, the exact same amount.
Finer cuts never move a point — they only add names for it.
More pieces isn't more amount when the pieces are smaller.

lessons.title: Seeing 2/4 = 1/2
takeaways: Cutting finer renames an amount — it never resizes it.
Fair trade = every piece cut the same way, so both counts grow together.
Test any trade on the bar or the line, never by digit patterns.

lessons.title: Whole Numbers in Disguise
takeaways: n/n always lands on 1 — all the pieces rebuild the whole.
Count wholes in groups: b jumps per whole, so 12/4 banks three wholes.
The fraction bar reads as sharing: 6/3 is 6 shared by 3.

lessons.title: Same Bottom, Compare Tops
takeaways: Same bottoms = same piece size, so the tops settle it by counting.
On the line: same jump size, more jumps lands farther.
The shortcut is safe ONLY because the pieces match.

lessons.title: Same Top, Compare Bottoms
takeaways: Same tops = same count, so PIECE SIZE decides — the smaller bottom wins.
On the bottom, bigger means more cuts and smaller pieces — instinct runs backwards there.
Counting pieces only works when the pieces match (rule one's fine print).

lessons.title: Why 1/3 Beats 1/4
takeaways: Same whole + more sharers = smaller shares, every time.
Unit fractions climb down as bottoms climb up: 1/2 > 1/3 > 1/4 > …
When in doubt, make it concrete — centimeters don't argue.

lessons.title: Only If the Wholes Match
takeaways: Ask 'of what?' first — no verdict without matching wholes.
Same bottoms: count the tops. Same tops: the smaller bottom wins.
Fair cuts, honest names, one shared whole — that's the entire fraction game.

lessons.title: Equal Parts, Unequal Parts
takeaways: Fractions need EQUAL pieces.
The name states the piece count.
Unequal pieces have no fraction name.

lessons.title: Naming the Unit Fraction
takeaways: One piece is a unit fraction.
The bottom names piece size.
More pieces, smaller each.

lessons.title: Building a/b from 1/b
takeaways: Fractions are built from unit pieces.
Collecting raises only the count.
The denominator holds still.

lessons.title: Fractions of a Set
takeaways: A set can be the whole.
Equal groups earn fraction names.
One group of n is 1/n.

lessons.title: Fractions on a Ruler
takeaways: A ruler stretches the whole into a line.
Count jumps from zero.
Every mark has a fraction name.

lessons.title: Marking Thirds on a Line
takeaways: Cut 0 to 1 into equal jumps.
Count spaces, not marks.
Thirds means three jumps.

lessons.title: Marking Sixths and Eighths
takeaways: More jumps, shorter jumps.
Bigger bottom means smaller pieces.
The journey stays the same.

lessons.title: Finding Equivalents with a Strip
takeaways: Different names, same amount.
Scale top and bottom together.
Renaming never changes the value.

lessons.title: Equivalents on the Number Line
takeaways: Equivalents share one point.
Same landing means equal.
The line proves equality.

lessons.title: Whole Numbers as Fractions
takeaways: Whole numbers can be written as fractions.
Group by the denominator.
Each full group is one whole.

lessons.title: Fractions Equal to One
takeaways: Matching top and bottom equals one.
You hold every piece.
Cut fineness does not matter.

lessons.title: Comparing with the Same Whole
takeaways: Comparison needs one shared whole.
Equal pieces make counting fair.
Different wholes prove nothing.

lessons.title: Ordering Three Fractions
takeaways: Same denominator: order the counts.
Same numerator: bigger bottom is smaller.
One whole throughout.

lessons.title: Fraction Stories
takeaways: The cut goes on the bottom.
The count goes on top.
Read the story for both.

lessons.title: Reading the Clock
takeaways: Short hand names the hour; long hand counts the minutes — read short first.
Minute marks count by fives: the 8-mark is 40, never 8.
The hour hand drifts with the minutes — halfway through the hour, halfway to the next number.

lessons.title: Minutes Before and After
takeaways: PAST counts forward from the old hour; TO counts back from the next.
Minutes-to = 60 − minutes-past.
A quarter-hour is 15 minutes; the landmarks are :15, :30, :45.

lessons.title: Elapsed Time on a Number Line
takeaways: Elapsed time = jumps on a timeline; land on the hour border first.
Never add or subtract minute labels across an hour — there is no :75.
Multi-task stories chain the hops: finish one task's clock before starting the next.

lessons.title: How Heavy? Grams and Kilograms
takeaways: Grams for light things, kilograms for heavy — keep the number friendly.
Kilo = 1,000: 1 kg = 1,000 g, the thousand-badge.
Match units before you compare or add.

lessons.title: How Much? Liters
takeaways: Liters measure how MUCH liquid — capacity, the space it fills.
Pourable isn't liters: flour pours but is weighed in grams.
Fill adds, drain/leak subtracts — track the tank in order.

lessons.title: Measure-and-Solve Stories
takeaways: Read the phrase, pick the operation, keep the unit attached.
Two-step stories chain the moves in order.
Guard with a size-check first — and match units before computing.

lessons.title: Pictographs with a Key
takeaways: Read the key first — it's the multiplier for every symbol.
Real count = symbols × key value.
A half-symbol is worth half the key, not a whole one.

lessons.title: Scaled Bar Graphs
takeaways: Read the scale first — grid steps can be worth 2, 5, or 10.
A bar between two lines lands halfway — an in-between number.
Tallest bar = most; a bigger scale fits bigger data.

lessons.title: Asking the Graph Questions
takeaways: Match the question word: more → subtract, in all → add, most → tallest bar.
Bars count categories; heights count amounts — don't swap them.
Multi-step questions total each group first, then compare.

lessons.title: Line Plots with Halves and Quarters
takeaways: A line plot stacks one X per measurement above a number line.
The line is marked in halves and quarters — the fraction line at work.
Tallest stack = most common; add all X's for the total; ends give the range.

lessons.title: Covering with Squares
takeaways: Area = unit squares that cover a shape, no gaps or overlaps.
Its unit is SQUARE units (cm²), not plain length units.
Squares are the measuring tool because they tile perfectly.

lessons.title: Rows × Columns = Area
takeaways: Equal rows of squares → area = rows × columns.
The flip holds: rows × cols = cols × rows, same carpet.
Area fills the inside (multiply); perimeter walks the edge (add).

lessons.title: The Break-Apart Rectangle
takeaways: Break one side into two; each piece keeps the other side; add the areas.
6 × 7 = 6×5 + 6×2 — the rectangle shows why multiplication breaks apart.
A split is honest only if the pieces rebuild the full side.

lessons.title: Odd Shapes: Add the Pieces
takeaways: Odd shapes cut into rectangles — find each area, add.
A whole with a piece removed? Subtract the bite instead.
Match the method to the shape: building up adds, cutting out subtracts.

lessons.title: Walking the Fence
takeaways: Perimeter = the distance all the way around — add every side.
Rectangle: two lengths + two widths, or double (length + width).
Square: 4 × side. Perimeter is the edge; area is the inside.

lessons.title: The Missing Side
takeaways: Missing side = perimeter minus the sides you know.
Rectangle: peel both known sides, then split the rest between the equal pair.
Square: side = perimeter ÷ 4.

lessons.title: Same Area, Different Fence
takeaways: Area (inside) and perimeter (edge) move independently — one never fixes the other.
For a fixed fence, a squarer shape holds the most area.
Always ask which one a problem wants: cover the inside, or walk the edge?

lessons.title: The ×2 Facts
takeaways: Multiplying by 2 doubles.
Every ×2 fact is an addition double.

lessons.title: The ×3 Facts
takeaways: ×3 means three equal groups.
Skip-count 3, 6, 9, 12.
Each row adds one more group.

lessons.title: The ×4 Facts
takeaways: ×4 is doubling twice.
Know the ×2 fact, double it.
Four equal rows.

lessons.title: The ×5 Facts
takeaways: ×5 skip-counts by fives.
Products end in 5 or 0.
The pattern checks; it does not answer.

lessons.title: The ×6 Facts
takeaways: ×10 makes tens.
Digits shift one place left.
The zero marks the empty ones place.

lessons.title: The ×7 Facts
takeaways: A square multiplies a number by itself.
Rows equal columns.

lessons.title: The ×8 Facts
takeaways: ×6 doubles ×3.
Derive from a fact you know.

lessons.title: The ×9 Facts
takeaways: ×7 has no shortcut pattern.
Derive from a near fact.

lessons.title: The ×10 Facts
takeaways: ×8 doubles ×4.
Double twice from ×2.

lessons.title: Squares: 3×3, 4×4, 5×5
takeaways: ×9 is ×10 minus one group.
One fewer group, not one fewer.

lessons.title: The Facts That Stick
takeaways: Some facts have no pattern.
Memorize the sticky handful.

lessons.title: Using a Fact You Know
takeaways: Build unknown facts from known ones.
One more group adds the group size.

lessons.title: Mixed Facts to 5×5
takeaways: Mixed practice tests recall.
Order hides no clues.
Facts must come on sight.

lessons.title: Mixed Facts to 9×9
takeaways: Any pair, any order.
Fluent means immediate.
Counting is understanding, not yet fluency.

lessons.title: Finding a Fact Fast
takeaways: Recall beats rushing.
Practise the slow facts.
Automatic facts need no drilling.

lessons.title: Missing Factor
takeaways: A missing factor is a division.
Divide the product by the known factor.

lessons.title: Fact Families in Multiplication
takeaways: Three numbers, four facts.
Multiplication and division share a family.

lessons.title: The Whole Table
takeaways: The table is 2×2 through 10×10.
Most facts are now recall.
Name the few that still resist.

lessons.title: Groups of: What Multiplication Means
takeaways: Multiplication counts equal groups fast.
3 × 4 means 3 groups of 4 — the same as 4 + 4 + 4.
Groups must be equal, or × doesn't apply.

lessons.title: Arrays: Rows and Columns
takeaways: An array lines up equal groups in straight rows.
Rows × in-each-row = the total.
Count the rows and just one row — then multiply.

lessons.title: Skip Counting: Multiplication Out Loud
takeaways: Skip counting adds the same hop every time.
The Nth number you say equals N × the hop size.
Landing number and number of hops answer different questions.

lessons.title: Hops on the Number Line
takeaways: A number line shows multiplication as equal hops from 0.
Hops × hop length = landing spot.
Know any two of the three parts and the picture gives you the third.

lessons.title: Turn It Around: Flipping Facts
takeaways: Flipping the two numbers never changes the total — the array only turns sideways.
Flip to whichever direction is easier to count.
Order changes the story (6 packs of 4 ≠ 4 packs of 6) but never the total.

lessons.title: Fair Shares
takeaways: Division deals a total out into equal shares.
Total ÷ sharers = each share — the total always comes first.
Check a share with its family fact: sharers × share = total.

lessons.title: How Many Groups?
takeaways: Grouping division counts how many equal groups fit in a total.
It works like repeated subtraction: take the group size away until you reach 0.
Same division, two stories — the story tells you whether the answer counts groups or a share.

lessons.title: Division Is a Missing Factor
takeaways: Every division is a multiplication with a blank: a ÷ b asks b × ___ = a.
No fact handy? Skip count to the total and count your hops.
One times fact you know unlocks the divisions hiding inside it.

lessons.title: Fact Families
takeaways: Three numbers make a family: two multiplications and two divisions, one array.
Every times fact you know unlocks its two divisions for free.
Doubles families (like 5, 5, 25) collapse to just two facts.

lessons.title: The Strange Ones: ×1, ×0, ÷1
takeaways: ×1 and ÷1 keep the number exactly as it is.
Anything × 0 is 0 — in either order, no matter how big.
Don't let +0 and +1 habits leak into × problems.

lessons.title: Doubles: the ×2 Machine
takeaways: ×2 = the number plus itself — an addition you already know.
Double big numbers by splitting, doubling the parts, and rejoining.
Doubles chain: doubling again and again builds new facts fast.

lessons.title: Fives and Tens
takeaways: ×10 shifts the number left — ones become tens, 0 holds the ones place.
×5 is half of ×10, and its answers always end in 0 or 5.
The clock counts fives: clock number × 5 = minutes.

lessons.title: Double-Double: ×4 and ×8
takeaways: ×4 = double twice; ×8 = double three times.
Count your doublings — each one moves you to a new fact.
Doubling a known answer (like 9 × 2) unlocks the next fact free.

lessons.title: The Nines Pattern
takeaways: Nines answers: digits add to 9, tens digit one less than the multiplier.
The reason: 9 × n = 10 × n − n — a ten-fact giving one group back.
Patterns are checkers — use them to catch your own slips.

lessons.title: Split It: the Break-Apart Trick for 6, 7, 8
takeaways: Split a hard factor into friendly pieces; the other factor rides in every piece.
The pieces must rebuild the number you cut — check by adding them.
Splits subtract too: the nines trick is 10 × n minus one group.

lessons.title: Which Operation?
takeaways: Equal groups → × or ÷; one-time joins or removals → + or −.
Total known and being split → ÷; total unknown and being built → ×.
Structure beats keywords — "each" lives in both × and ÷ stories.

lessons.title: What's Unknown: Group Size or Group Count?
takeaways: Every equal-groups story fits: groups × size = total.
Point at the empty slot before computing.
Missing total → multiply; missing size or count → divide.

lessons.title: Letters Stand for Numbers
takeaways: A letter is a name tag on the empty slot — nothing more.
Catch its number with the fact family.
Always substitute back in: a true sentence proves the catch.

lessons.title: Two-Step Problems
takeaways: Plan first: step one's answer is step two's starting pile.
Say the new pile out loud before acting on it.
One expression can carry the whole chain: build, then change.

lessons.title: Does the Answer Make Sense?
takeaways: Size test: shares shrink below the pile; products grow past one group.
Estimate with friendly numbers to fence in the true answer.
Rebuild to verify: groups × size + leftover must equal the total.

lessons.title: Patterns in the Addition Table
takeaways: The diagonal holds the doubles; the table mirrors across it because order never changes a sum.
Parity rules predict sums with zero computing: matching parities make even, mixed makes odd.
Walking the table works like arithmetic: right/up grows by 1, left/down shrinks by 1.
