lessons.title: Patterns in the Multiplication Table
takeaways: The diagonal holds the squares; the grid mirrors across it via the flip.
Rows own each other: 8s double the 4s, 10s take every other 5.
One step down a column adds one more group — the grid is skip counting, drawn.

lessons.title: Even × Odd: What Happens?
takeaways: Any even factor forces an even product; only odd × odd makes odd.
The rule reverses: an odd product proves both factors were odd.
Odd rows beat odd-even-odd-even; even rows are even throughout.

lessons.title: Multiples on the Hundred Chart
takeaways: A multiple is a times-table landing, and the list never ends.
Chart shapes reveal structure: row-length multiples make columns; one-less makes staircases.
Two counts can share landings — the first shared one solves real scheduling puzzles.

lessons.title: Hundreds, Tens, Ones
takeaways: The spot decides the worth: the same digit means 6, 60, or 600 by position.
Zero is a placeholder — it holds spots open so other digits keep their worth.
Adding or removing blocks moves exactly one spot's digit by one.

lessons.title: Build and Break Numbers
takeaways: Expanded form: each digit becomes a piece worth its spot.
Empty spots leave no piece — but inside the number, their zero still holds the place.
Pieces let you change one spot at a time — mental math's favorite trick.

lessons.title: Which Is Bigger?
takeaways: Walk the spots left to right; the first difference decides everything.
Each spot outweighs all the spots to its right combined — that's why the walk works.
Building small means parking small digits in expensive spots.

lessons.title: Ten of These Is One of Those
takeaways: 10-for-1 trades go up (bundle) and down (break) between neighboring spots.
Trades change packaging, never value — count it both ways to prove it.
Carrying and borrowing are just these trades wearing school clothes.

lessons.title: The Closer Ten
takeaways: Every number lives between two ten-neighbors; rounding names the closer one.
Ones digit 1–4 → down; 6–9 → up. It's step-counting in one glance.
Rounding doesn't change a number — it nicknames it for fast math.

lessons.title: The Closer Hundred
takeaways: Every number lives between two hundred-neighbors; the hundreds digit names the street.
The tens digit decides which end is closer — the ones digit never overrules it.
Rounding both players first makes big additions one-glance easy.

lessons.title: The Halfway Rule
takeaways: A tie happens only at the exact middle — equal steps to both neighbors.
The standard rule: halfway rounds UP, every time, on every street.
It's a convention — its power comes from everyone using the same one.

lessons.title: Estimating in Stories
takeaways: For 'about' questions: round the players first, then compute once.
Estimates guard exact work — they catch big blunders and honestly miss small slips.
Safe-direction rounding (against yourself) can settle yes/no questions with certainty.

lessons.title: Friendly-Number Jumps
takeaways: Jump through friendly numbers — reach the next round landing first.
Overshoot and repay: +99 is +100 then −1.
The hops must spend exactly what you're adding — count what each hop costs.

lessons.title: Regrouping You Can See
takeaways: A spot holds at most 9; a bigger sum trades ten of itself one spot up.
The carry mark is a trade receipt — always count it with the next spot.
Trades chain: an overflow in the tens sends a hundred upstairs the same way.

lessons.title: Subtracting Across a Zero
takeaways: A short spot trades down: one ten becomes ten ones (value unchanged).
Across a zero, chain it: hundred → tens first, then ten → ones.
Never flip to smaller-from-larger — short spots trade, they don't surrender.

lessons.title: Check It with an Estimate
takeaways: Every exact answer gets a guard: round, compute friendly, compare.
Impossible sizes (a difference bigger than its start) need no rounding at all.
Safe-direction rounding turns estimates into certainty for yes/no questions.

lessons.title: 4 × 60 Is 4 × 6 Tens
takeaways: Say the tens number in units: 60 = 6 tens.
Run the one-digit fact, then read the answer in tens.
The shift writes it out: 24 tens = 240.

lessons.title: The Zero Pattern
takeaways: Zeros on the answer are unit badges: 24 hundreds must end in two zeros.
A fact's own zero (5 × 4 = 20) belongs to the count, not the badge: 5 × 40 = 200.
Tens counts size answers instantly — over or under a fence, no full computing.

lessons.title: Tens in Stories
takeaways: Spot the tens unit, run the small fact, read the badge.
Two-step stories: build the pile, say it out loud, then change it.
The guard checks every final answer — the habit that never retires.

lessons.title: What Makes a Shape a Shape?
takeaways: Defining attributes (sides, corners, closed) are a shape's entry rules.
Color, size, and tilt are costumes — they never change the shape.
To name a shape, check only its rules.

lessons.title: The Quadrilateral Family
takeaways: Quadrilateral is the umbrella: any closed 4-sided shape.
Rectangle = square corners; rhombus = equal sides; square = both; trapezoid = one parallel pair.
Branch names add rules, but every branch is still a quadrilateral.

lessons.title: Squares Are Rectangles?!
takeaways: A square passes the rectangle's rule, so every square is a rectangle.
Not every rectangle is a square — inclusion runs strict-into-loose, one way only.
More rules = stricter club = smaller box nested inside the looser one.

lessons.title: Sorting by Rules
takeaways: A sorting rule is a yes/no question asked of every shape.
A shape can pass several rules; shapes passing two overlapping rules sit in the shared middle.
For a compound rule, a shape must pass EVERY part.

lessons.title: The Misfits
takeaways: A misfit breaks exactly one rule — and that break reveals the rule.
'Almost' never counts: one broken rule drops a shape from the club.
Non-examples define a shape as sharply as examples do.

lessons.title: Splitting Shapes Fairly
takeaways: Equal parts means equal SIZE — counting pieces isn't enough.
Pieces can differ in shape as long as their areas match.
More equal parts of one whole means smaller pieces.

lessons.title: Naming the Parts
takeaways: Split into n equal parts → each part is 1/n; m parts shaded is m/n.
Bottom counts the total equal parts; top counts the ones you mean.
All parts shaded (n/n) is the whole, equal to 1.

lessons.title: Finding the Hidden Question
takeaways: Two-step problems hide a question.
The hidden quantity is unstated.
Answer it before the final step.

lessons.title: Add Then Multiply
takeaways: A changed group count comes first.
Then multiply the groups.
Parentheses record the order.

lessons.title: Multiply Then Subtract
takeaways: Build the total from equal groups.
Then remove once, from the whole.
'Each' changes where the step lands.

lessons.title: Divide Then Add
takeaways: Share into equal groups first.
Then add what joins.
Where it joins changes the equation.

lessons.title: Two Steps with a Letter
takeaways: Letters name unknown quantities.
A letter is a placeholder.
Undo the steps to find it.

lessons.title: Writing the Equation
takeaways: Equations record the order.
Parentheses hold the first step.
Same numbers can mean different stories.

lessons.title: Drawing a Bar Model
takeaways: Bar models picture the steps.
Equal parts build the total.
Where the mark sits sets the order.

lessons.title: Estimating First
takeaways: Estimate before computing.
Round, then run the same steps.
The estimate is a guard, not an answer.

lessons.title: Checking with Rounding
takeaways: Compare exact to estimate.
Close means plausible.
Estimates catch the big errors.

lessons.title: Spotting an Unreasonable Answer
takeaways: Ask what the story allows.
Removing cannot raise a count.
Impossible answers need no arithmetic.

lessons.title: Extra Information
takeaways: Not every number is needed.
Read for the question.
Extra information is a decoy.

lessons.title: Writing Your Own Two-Step Problem
takeaways: Start from the equation.
The hidden step must be genuinely hidden.
The story must force the order.

lessons.title: Splitting One into Ten
takeaways: One whole splits into 10 equal tenths.
The tenths count sits right after the decimal point.
0.3 means 3 of 10 equal parts.

lessons.title: Writing a Tenth
takeaways: The tenths digit counts shaded columns.
0.5 and 0.9 follow one pattern.
A count of tenths is less than one whole.

lessons.title: Tenths on a Number Line
takeaways: The strip runs from 0 to 1.
Each tenth is one step of ten.
0.4 stops one step short of halfway.

lessons.title: Tenths as Fractions
takeaways: 0.7 and 7/10 name the same amount.
The fraction shows the split; the decimal hides it.
Tenths always means 10 equal parts.

lessons.title: Splitting a Tenth into Ten
takeaways: Splitting each tenth by ten makes 100 hundredths.
A full column is a tenth — ten hundredths.
The grid shows both sizes at once.

lessons.title: Writing a Hundredth
takeaways: Hundredths counts end two places after the point.
A zero can hold the tenths place: 0.09.
0.9 and 0.09 are very different amounts.

lessons.title: Hundredths on a Grid
takeaways: Full columns carry the tenths digit.
Single cells carry the hundredths digit.
The decimal's digits are the grid recipe.

lessons.title: Tenths to Hundredths
takeaways: Each tenth is worth 10 hundredths.
0.4 = 40/100 — same shading, new name.
Renaming lets tenths and hundredths meet.

lessons.title: Adding Tenths and Hundredths
takeaways: Rename tenths as hundredths before adding.
0.2 + 0.05 is 20 + 5 hundredths: 0.25.
Digits only add when they share a place.

lessons.title: Reading a Decimal Aloud
takeaways: Read a decimal by its last place.
0.62 is sixty-two hundredths.
A leading zero holds a place, silently.

lessons.title: Decimal Place Names
takeaways: First place after the point: tenths.
Second place: hundredths.
Each digit's place sets its worth.

lessons.title: Fraction to Decimal
takeaways: The denominator names the place.
The numerator fills that place.
62/100 = 0.62 with no arithmetic.

lessons.title: Decimal to Fraction
takeaways: Hundredths decimals are fractions over 100.
0.43 = 43/100 — digit order matters.
Decimal and fraction are two views of one shading.

lessons.title: Comparing Two Decimals
takeaways: Compare tenths digits first.
Hundredths only break ties.
Digit count is not size: 0.5 > 0.35.

lessons.title: The Trailing Zero
takeaways: A trailing zero adds no value.
0.60 = 0.6 — sixty hundredths is six tenths.
A zero BEFORE a digit still matters: 0.07 ≠ 0.7.

lessons.title: Ordering Decimals
takeaways: Order by tenths digits first.
Hundredths break the ties.
Short names can beat long ones.

lessons.title: Decimals and Money
takeaways: A dollar is 100 cents.
Dimes fill the tenths place, pennies the hundredths.
$0.37 is 37 hundredths of a dollar.

lessons.title: Decimals in Measurement
takeaways: One meter is 100 centimeters.
Each centimeter is a hundredth of a meter.
42 cm = 0.42 m — the grid's renaming, measured.

lessons.title: A Fraction Added Again and Again
takeaways: Repeated addition collects equal groups.
Only the piece count grows.
The denominator holds still.

lessons.title: Writing It as Multiplication
takeaways: The whole number counts groups.
Multiply the numerator only.
The denominator names piece size.

lessons.title: Multiples of a Unit Fraction
takeaways: A unit fraction is one piece.
Multiples collect those pieces.
The count becomes the numerator.

lessons.title: n × a/b
takeaways: n × a/b multiplies the count only.
The piece size never changes.
One rule covers every case.

lessons.title: On the Number Line
takeaways: Each group is one jump.
Jumps are all the same length.
The landing point is the product.

lessons.title: Using an Area Model
takeaways: Rows stack the groups.
The pieces never shrink.
Count every shaded piece.

lessons.title: Products Greater Than One
takeaways: A whole holds b of its b-pieces.
More pieces means more than one whole.
Fractions are not capped at one.

lessons.title: Writing the Answer as a Mixed Number
takeaways: Group pieces into wholes.
Leftovers stay a fraction.
Renaming never changes the value.

lessons.title: Word Problems: Equal Groups
takeaways: Stories name a group size and count.
The size is the fraction.
Equal groups multiply.

lessons.title: Word Problems: Recipes
takeaways: Recipes scale by whole numbers.
Multiply the numerator.
Rename as a mixed number to measure.

lessons.title: Word Problems: Distance
takeaways: Distance repeats a fractional length.
The structure matches every equal-group story.
Rename the answer to read it.

lessons.title: Estimating a Fraction Product
takeaways: Compare each group to one whole.
Then scale by the count.
Pieces are not wholes.

lessons.title: Same Amount, New Cut
takeaways: Equivalent fractions still mean the exact same amount, cut differently — the G3 model never stops being true.
Every equivalent pair hides one shared multiplier connecting its top and bottom.
Finding that multiplier from the bottoms lets you predict the top, without drawing.

lessons.title: The ×n/×n Rule, Derived
takeaways: Slicing every piece of a fraction into n smaller pieces multiplies BOTH the shaded count and the total count by n.
That's the ×n/×n rule — not an arbitrary shortcut, but exactly what re-cutting does.
The rule reverses too: dividing both numbers by n un-slices back to a simpler fraction.

lessons.title: Using the Rule (and Reversing It)
takeaways: ÷n/÷n simplifies a fraction the exact same way ×n/×n grows one — same rule, opposite direction.
The greatest common factor gets you to simplest form in one step.
A fraction is in simplest form when its top and bottom share no factor besides 1.

lessons.title: Halfway Benchmarks
takeaways: A fraction is more than 1/2 when the numerator beats half the denominator.
The doubling trick avoids decimals: double the numerator, compare to the denominator.
This works with any denominator, odd or even, without ever finding a common one.

lessons.title: Comparing Without a Common Denominator
takeaways: If one fraction is below 1/2 and the other above, the comparison is settled instantly.
If both land on the same side of 1/2, the halfway trick alone isn't enough — use a finer method.
Recognizing which case you're in is the real skill.

lessons.title: Ordering with Benchmarks
takeaways: Sort roughly by zone first: near 0, near 1/2, or near 1.
Fractions on opposite sides of 1/2 are already ordered by the coarse sort alone.
Same-side ties need a finer method — cross-multiplication finishes the job.

lessons.title: Adding Like Fractions
takeaways: Adding like fractions adds only the numerators.
The denominator names the piece size, which never changes.
Adding the denominators too is the classic trap — the pieces don't shrink when you combine them.

lessons.title: Subtracting Like Fractions
takeaways: Subtracting like fractions subtracts only the numerators.
The denominator stays fixed — subtracting it too is the classic trap.
After subtracting, check whether the result simplifies using the greatest common factor.

lessons.title: Word Problems with Like Fractions
takeaways: Combining language means add; leftover/remaining language means subtract.
If a sum's numerator equals or passes its denominator, the amount reaches or passes one whole.
Multi-step stories just chain the same rule — add or subtract, one piece at a time.

lessons.title: Improper to Mixed
takeaways: Convert an improper fraction by dividing the numerator by the denominator.
The quotient becomes the whole number; the remainder becomes the new numerator.
The new numerator keeps the ORIGINAL denominator — a remainder of 0 means an exact whole number.

lessons.title: Mixed to Improper
takeaways: Multiply the whole number by the denominator to count the whole pieces.
Add the numerator for the extra pieces.
Keep the same denominator throughout — it's the only piece size in play.

lessons.title: Adding & Subtracting Mixed Numbers
takeaways: Combine whole numbers and fraction parts separately.
Adding: if the fraction parts pass a whole, carry the extra into the whole-number part.
Subtracting: if the fraction part is too small, borrow a whole and convert it into that many pieces.

lessons.title: Repeated Addition of Fractions
takeaways: Whole × fraction means adding that fraction to itself, whole times.
The shortcut: multiply the numerator by the whole number; the denominator never changes.
The result can pass one whole — convert it to a mixed number the same way as before.

lessons.title: The Shortcut and Word Problems
takeaways: Whole × fraction multiplies just the numerator; the denominator never changes.
Word problems translate directly: count × amount-each.
An improper product converts to a mixed number — and simplifies, if it can — for a sensible real answer.

lessons.title: Naming the Basics
takeaways: A point is an exact location with no size.
Lines have zero endpoints; rays have one; line segments have two.
Counting endpoints is the fast way to identify which term fits.

lessons.title: Two Rays Make an Angle
takeaways: Two rays sharing a starting point form an angle; that shared point is the vertex.
The rays themselves are the angle's sides.
A three-letter angle name always puts the vertex in the middle.

lessons.title: Reading Geometric Figures
takeaways: A complex figure is just points, rays, angles, and segments layered together.
The vertex-sharing rule finds an angle's vertex even in a busy figure.
Several rays from one point hide MULTIPLE angles — count every pair.

lessons.title: Lines That Never Meet
takeaways: Parallel lines stay the same distance apart forever and never cross.
Matching arrow marks in a diagram show which lines are parallel to each other.
A shrinking gap between two lines means they aren't parallel — they'll eventually meet.

lessons.title: Lines That Cross Exactly Right
takeaways: Perpendicular lines cross at exactly 90° — the same right-angle benchmark from Course 9.
A small square symbol marks a perpendicular crossing in diagrams.
89° or 91° isn't 'close enough' — only an exact 90° crossing counts.

lessons.title: Spotting Both in Figures
takeaways: A rectangle's opposite sides are parallel; its adjacent sides are perpendicular.
In a grid, every same-direction pair is parallel; every cross-direction pair is perpendicular.
Some lines, like a rectangle's diagonal, are neither parallel nor perpendicular to a given side.

lessons.title: Classifying Triangles
takeaways: A triangle's largest angle decides its family: acute, right, or obtuse.
Every triangle can have at most one angle of 90° or more.
The same acute/right/obtuse vocabulary from single angles now classifies whole shapes.

lessons.title: A Triangle's Angles Always Sum to 180°
takeaways: Every triangle's three angles add up to exactly 180°, no exceptions.
Given two angles, subtract their sum from 180 to find the third.
This connects directly to angles on a straight line, which also total 180°.

lessons.title: Classifying Quadrilaterals
takeaways: A rectangle's entry rule requires all four angles to be exactly 90°.
A quadrilateral can have 0, 1, 2, or 4 right angles — never exactly 3, since the fourth is then forced.
Failing one club's entry rule never disqualifies a shape from being a quadrilateral at all.

lessons.title: What Symmetry Means
takeaways: A line of symmetry is a fold line where both halves land on top of each other exactly.
Not every line through a shape works — only specific, well-placed ones.
Shapes with no matching sides or angles can have zero lines of symmetry.

lessons.title: Finding Every Line of Symmetry
takeaways: A regular shape has as many symmetry lines as it has sides.
Non-regular shapes can have fewer — a rectangle has only 2, an isosceles triangle only 1.
A shape with no matching sides anywhere has zero lines of symmetry.

lessons.title: Symmetry All Around
takeaways: Letters can have vertical symmetry, horizontal symmetry, both, or none — check with the fold test.
Rotational symmetry (spinning) and line symmetry (folding) are different ideas — don't mix them up.
The regular-shape pattern (sides = symmetry lines) applies everywhere, from road signs to windows.

lessons.title: Metric Prefixes as Badges
takeaways: Kilo means ×1000 of the base unit, no matter what's being measured.
Centi means 100 of the small unit make one base unit.
The same badge system works for mass, length, and volume alike.

lessons.title: Converting Length
takeaways: Multiply to convert bigger units into smaller ones; divide to go the other way.
Some conversions combine two badges in one hop — meter to millimeter is always ×1,000.
Convert everything to the same unit before adding or comparing.

lessons.title: Converting Mass & Volume
takeaways: The kilo badge works identically for mass (g/kg) and volume (mL/L): ×1,000.
Choose the unit that keeps the number reasonable — not absurdly huge or a tiny fraction.
Convert to matching units before adding or subtracting different-unit amounts.

lessons.title: The Area Formula
takeaways: Area = length × width — the formula replaces counting unit squares one by one.
For bigger rectangles, break apart one side into tens and ones, just like in Course 6.
Area answers 'how much surface,' like carpet or paint.

lessons.title: The Perimeter Formula
takeaways: Perimeter = 2 × (length + width) — walking every side, formalized.
Area and perimeter move independently — matching one never guarantees matching the other.
Perimeter answers 'how much distance around,' like fencing or framing.

lessons.title: Formulas in Word Problems
takeaways: Covering verbs (tile, paint, carpet, sod) signal area.
Edge verbs (fence, frame, border, trim) signal perimeter.
Bigger numbers still break apart the same way, whichever formula applies.

lessons.title: What a Degree Measures
takeaways: A full turn is 360°; half of that is a straight angle, 180°.
Half of a straight angle is a right angle, 90°.
Half of a right angle is 45° — the same halving move as fractions, one level deeper.

lessons.title: Measuring with a Protractor
takeaways: A clock face splits 360° into 12 equal 30° hours.
Count the hour-jumps between two positions, then multiply by 30.
A real protractor does the same counting, just in single-degree units instead of 30° jumps.

lessons.title: Classifying Angles
takeaways: Acute is under 90°; right is exactly 90°; obtuse is between 90° and 180°; straight is exactly 180°.
The 90° and 180° boundaries are exact — one degree flips the family.
Every angle belongs to exactly one of the four families.

lessons.title: Angles That Combine
takeaways: Adjacent angles combine by adding their measures.
The combined angle can be any size — it doesn't need to land on a benchmark.
Three or more adjacent angles still just add, one after another.

lessons.title: Finding a Missing Angle
takeaways: Angles on a straight line always total 180° — subtract the known part to find what's missing.
A right angle split into parts always totals 90° instead.
With three or more angles, add the knowns first, then subtract from the benchmark.

lessons.title: Benchmark Angles
takeaways: A full turn around a single point always totals 360°.
Right angle (90°), straight line (180°), and full turn (360°) form one benchmark toolkit.
With several angles, add every known one first, then subtract from the right total.

lessons.title: Measuring to the Nearest Fraction
takeaways: An eighths-ruler has a tick at every 1/8 inch, up to 8/8 (one whole).
Reading a measurement means counting tick marks to the nearest one.
Simplify the reading afterward, using the same greatest-common-factor skill as always.

lessons.title: Building a Line Plot
takeaways: A line plot stacks a mark above each measurement's tick — repeats stack higher.
The total data count adds up every stack's height.
The tallest stack shows the most common measurement, no matter its size.

lessons.title: Reading Line Plot Questions
takeaways: 'How many' questions count stack heights directly.
Difference and combined-length questions reuse fraction subtraction and addition.
Reading a line plot ties every measurement and fraction skill together in one place.

lessons.title: Bigger Unit, Smaller Number
takeaways: Converting changes the number, not the amount.
Smaller units give larger numbers.
The object never changes.

lessons.title: Building a Conversion Table
takeaways: A table records one constant factor.
Every row obeys it.
Any row can be predicted.

lessons.title: Converting Length
takeaways: Down a unit: multiply.
Up a unit: divide.
Decide direction before computing.

lessons.title: Converting Mass and Weight
takeaways: Mass converts by the same rule.
Only the factor changes.
Structure carries across families.

lessons.title: Converting Liquid Volume
takeaways: Volume converts by the same rule.
Liters hold 1,000 millilitres.
Only the factor is new.

lessons.title: Converting Time
takeaways: Time uses 60, not 10.
The method is unchanged.
Direction and factor settle it.

lessons.title: Distance Problems
takeaways: Build the total from equal parts.
Adjust once at the end.
Order changes the meaning.

lessons.title: Time Interval Problems
takeaways: Build the total in one unit.
Convert once, at the end.
Fewer conversions, fewer slips.

lessons.title: Money Problems
takeaways: Money follows the same structure.
Equal groups build the total.
The discount comes off once.

lessons.title: Problems with Fractions of a Unit
takeaways: Measurements land between whole units.
Four quarters rebuild one unit.
Smaller pieces, bigger count.

lessons.title: Multi-Step Measurement
takeaways: Build, adjust, then convert.
One conversion at the end.
Order keeps the numbers simple.

lessons.title: Diagrams for Measurement Problems
takeaways: Diagrams show equal parts and removals.
Where the mark sits sets the order.
Draw the plan before computing.

lessons.title: Multiplying by 10, 100, 1000
takeaways: Basic facts scale by tens.
Zeros come from the factors.
Never invent or drop a zero.

lessons.title: Partial Products with an Area Model
takeaways: Split a factor by place.
Multiply each piece.
Add every region back.

lessons.title: Four-Digit by One-Digit
takeaways: Every place gets multiplied.
Columns hold one digit each.
The algorithm is the area model, compressed.

lessons.title: Regrouping in Multiplication
takeaways: Products over nine carry.
The carry joins the next column.
A stranded carry loses exactly its value.

lessons.title: Two-Digit by Two-Digit: Area Model
takeaways: Both factors split into places.
Four regions, not two.
Every region is real area.

lessons.title: Two-Digit by Two-Digit: Partial Products
takeaways: Four partial products, four lines.
Keep the places straight.
Then add them all.

lessons.title: Estimating a Product
takeaways: Round both factors.
Multiply the friendly numbers.
The estimate guards the place value.

lessons.title: Checking a Product
takeaways: Compare exact to estimate.
Close means plausible.
An order of magnitude out is a place-value slip.

lessons.title: Dividing with Place Value
takeaways: Division starts at the largest place.
That place sets the quotient's first digit.
Then work rightward.

lessons.title: Partial Quotients
takeaways: Remove convenient chunks.
Add the chunks for the quotient.
Order never changes the total.

lessons.title: Three-Digit by One-Digit
takeaways: Divide each place in turn.
Leftovers move down a place.
Nothing is discarded.

lessons.title: Four-Digit by One-Digit
takeaways: Longer dividends, identical method.
Estimate to check the digit count.
March left to right.

lessons.title: Remainders in Division
takeaways: The remainder is what is left over.
It is always under the divisor.
Otherwise another group fits.

lessons.title: What to Do with the Remainder
takeaways: The remainder's meaning depends on the question.
Full groups, leftover, or rounded up.
Read what the story wants.

lessons.title: Estimating a Quotient
takeaways: Round the dividend to a friendly multiple.
Divide the friendly numbers.
The estimate fixes the digit count.

lessons.title: Checking a Quotient
takeaways: Multiplication undoes division.
Quotient times divisor rebuilds the dividend.
With a remainder, add it back too.

lessons.title: Times as Many
takeaways: 'n times as many' = n whole copies of the other pile — multiply.
Unwinding a times-as-many comparison is division (the fact family).
'Times' copies the whole bar; 'more' only tacks on a piece.

lessons.title: Comparison Stories
takeaways: Big pile = copy count × small pile — write it before solving.
Unknown big → multiply; unknown small or unknown count → divide.
Rebuild to check: count × small should equal the big pile.

lessons.title: More or Times?
takeaways: 'More/fewer' shifts by a fixed piece; 'times/twice' copies the whole pile.
When unsure, draw the two bars — a tacked-on piece vs stacked copies.
Mixed stories give each comparison word its own operation.

lessons.title: Factor Pairs
takeaways: A factor divides evenly — it makes a clean rectangle with no leftover tiles.
Hunt factors in pairs, climbing from 1; stop when the pair meets or crosses.
Each rectangle is one factor pair (n×m and m×n are the same rectangle).

lessons.title: Multiples on the Trail
takeaways: A multiple is a skip-count landing — no remainder when you divide.
Factors build a number (small); multiples are what it lands on (big) — same fact, two ends.
A common multiple is a spot two skip-counts share; the smallest is the LCM.

lessons.title: Prime and Composite
takeaways: Prime = exactly two factors (1 and itself) = only a 1×n rectangle.
Composite = more than two factors = more than one rectangle.
1 is neither — it has just one factor, too few for either.

lessons.title: Tens Times
takeaways: n × (a ten) = the small fact (n × a) counted as tens.
Multiplying by 10 opens the ones slot — written as one 0.
The zero is the tens-place badge, not glue between digits.

lessons.title: Break the Big Number
takeaways: Split the big number into tens + ones; multiply each by the digit.
Two rectangles, then add — the area model of a multiplication.
Forgetting the ones piece leaves the answer short.

lessons.title: Two-Digit Times Two-Digit
takeaways: Two two-digit numbers each split into tens + ones → four rectangles.
Multiply tens×tens, tens×ones, ones×tens, ones×ones, then add all four.
The tiny ones×ones piece is the easiest to forget — always include it.

lessons.title: Sharing with Leftovers
takeaways: A remainder is what's left after the biggest whole number of full groups.
A remainder must always be smaller than the divisor.
A too-big remainder means one more full group still fits — bump the quotient and recompute.

lessons.title: Big Division
takeaways: Split the dividend into a friendly piece plus the rest, then divide each.
Add the quotients; keep any remainder from the last piece.
The same splitting trick that multiplies now divides — just run in reverse.

lessons.title: What the Leftover Means
takeaways: Round UP when the leftover still needs a whole extra unit.
Round DOWN when the leftover can't fill one more full group.
Split as a fraction (remainder over divisor) when the leftover can be physically shared.

lessons.title: Number Patterns
takeaways: Additive rules add/subtract the same amount; multiplicative rules multiply/divide by the same amount.
Find the rule with the gap (subtract) or the ratio (divide) between consecutive terms.
A pattern can carry a hidden feature beyond its rule, like every term being even.

lessons.title: Multi-Step Stories
takeaways: Break a multi-step problem into small pieces, solved in the story's own order.
Earlier skills — comparisons, area-model multiplication, remainders — often hide inside one bigger problem.
When items can't be split, keep only the whole quotient and set the remainder aside.

lessons.title: Two Operations, One Story
takeaways: Multi-step stories hide a total.
Build it before adjusting.
The adjustment hits the whole, once.

lessons.title: Three Operations
takeaways: Chain the steps in story order.
Each acts on the running total.
Name every intermediate quantity.

lessons.title: Multiplicative Comparison Stories
takeaways: 'Times as many' is a factor.
'More than' is a gap.
Divide for one, subtract for the other.

lessons.title: Problems with Remainders
takeaways: A remainder is not the whole answer.
The story decides its meaning.
Partial groups often round up.

lessons.title: Writing Equations with a Letter
takeaways: Letters name unknown quantities.
The equation records the plan.
Undo the operation to solve it.

lessons.title: Estimating to Check
takeaways: Estimate before computing.
Round but keep the operations.
The estimate guards place value.

lessons.title: Rounding to Assess Reasonableness
takeaways: Note which way you rounded.
Rounding a factor up raises the product.
A leaning estimate catches more.

lessons.title: Explaining Your Plan
takeaways: Name what each step produces.
Named quantities can be checked.
A plan turns errors into findable steps.

lessons.title: Finding All Factor Pairs
takeaways: A factor pair builds a rectangle.
Search upward from 1.
Stop when the pairs repeat.

lessons.title: Is It a Factor?
takeaways: A factor divides with no remainder.
Divide to test a candidate.
Remainder means not a factor.

lessons.title: Listing Multiples
takeaways: Multiples are the landings when counting by a number.
Every number has endless multiples.
Factors are finite, multiples are not.

lessons.title: Is It a Multiple?
takeaways: Test a multiple by dividing.
Factor and multiple are one relationship.
Read it from either end.

lessons.title: Prime or Composite?
takeaways: A prime has exactly two factors.
A composite has more.
One is neither.

lessons.title: The Sieve
takeaways: The sieve eliminates composites.
Only primes are sieve numbers.
Survivors are the primes.

lessons.title: Number Patterns from a Rule
takeaways: A rule generates every term.
Check the first step, confirm on the second.
Growing gaps mean multiplying.

lessons.title: Shape Patterns from a Rule
takeaways: Shape patterns follow arithmetic rules.
A constant step makes every term a multiple.
The rule reaches any step directly.

lessons.title: Features Not in the Rule
takeaways: Patterns show features the rule never states.
Those features are consequences.
Look beyond the instruction.

lessons.title: Extending and Explaining
takeaways: The rule reaches any term.
The next number reaches one.
Explaining beats listing.

lessons.title: Climbing the Ladder
takeaways: Every place value is 10 times the place to its right — the same rule at every rung.
Past thousands, the names continue: ten-thousand, hundred-thousand, million.
Six ×10 rungs separate ones from millions — which is why a million has six zeros.

lessons.title: Ten Times Bigger, Ten Times Smaller
takeaways: ×10 shifts every digit one rung up; a new zero fills the ones-spot.
÷10 shifts every digit one rung down, removing the last zero.
Repeated shifts climb multiple rungs — two ×10s reach two rungs higher.

lessons.title: Naming Six-Digit Places
takeaways: A digit's real value is the digit times its place (5 in the thousands place is worth 5,000).
Big numbers group into three-digit periods, separated by commas.
Expanded form breaks a number into its place-value pieces, which sum back to the original.

lessons.title: Standard, Word, and Expanded Form
takeaways: Standard, word, and expanded form all name the exact same number.
Expanded form skips zero-digit places — they contribute nothing to the sum.
Converting between forms always comes back to each digit's place value.

lessons.title: Reading Big Numbers Aloud
takeaways: Read the thousands-period digits, say 'thousand,' then read the last three digits.
A zero digit in the middle of either period stays silent — it isn't spoken as its own word.
The exact place of the last spoken digit changes everything — nine isn't ninety, forty isn't four hundred.

lessons.title: Comma Periods
takeaways: Commas mark groups of exactly 3 digits, counting from the right.
The rightmost group is always 3 digits; the leftmost group can be 1, 2, or 3.
The number of commas equals the number of gaps between 3-digit groups.

lessons.title: Rounding to Any Place
takeaways: Always check the digit exactly one place to the right of your rounding target.
5 or more rounds up; less than 5 rounds down; exactly 5 follows the honest convention of rounding up.
A round-up can carry through every digit — even rolling all the way into a new million.

lessons.title: Rounding Word Problems
takeaways: Rounding each number before adding is fast, but it can drift from the true rounded total.
For an accurate estimate, add the exact numbers first, then round once.
The two methods can disagree — sometimes by a full rung.

lessons.title: Front-End Estimation
takeaways: Front-end estimation keeps only the leading digit and zeros everything after it — no up-or-down decision needed.
It always truncates down, unlike true rounding, which can go either way.
It's the fastest estimate, but the roughest — save it for split-second decisions.

lessons.title: Adding with Regrouping
takeaways: A column sum of 10 or more trades 10 of that place for 1 of the next place up.
A carry always joins the very next column to the left.
Carries can cascade — one trade can trigger another, and another.

lessons.title: Subtracting with Regrouping
takeaways: When a top digit is smaller than what you're subtracting, break 1 from the next place over into 10 of this place.
A break is spent — it's never repaid, even later in the same problem.
Breaks can cascade — one break can trigger another, and another.

lessons.title: Subtracting Across Zeros
takeaways: If the digit you'd break is zero, reach one place further — and keep reaching until you find a nonzero digit.
Every zero the chain passes through becomes a 9, not a 0 and not a 10.
The chain can be as long as it needs to be — one zero, two zeros, or four.

lessons.title: Comparing Big Numbers
takeaways: Count digits first — more digits (almost) always wins.
When digit counts match, compare place by place from the LEFT, stopping at the first difference.
A bigger digit further right never overrides an earlier difference.

lessons.title: Ordering Big Numbers
takeaways: Ordering repeats comparison: sort by digit count first, then break ties place by place.
Greatest-to-least uses the identical rule, just read in reverse.
Close numbers sharing many leading digits still separate cleanly once you reach their first difference.

lessons.title: The Coordinate Plane
takeaways: An ordered pair (x, y) means x right, then y up from the origin (0, 0).
Order matters: (2, 5) and (5, 2) are different points.
Sharing an x stacks points vertically; sharing a y lines them up sideways.

lessons.title: Plotting Points
takeaways: Plot (x, y) by walking right to x, then up to y.
Along a shared row or column, distance = the difference of the numbers that change.
Count spaces between points, never the dots themselves.

lessons.title: Graphs That Tell Stories
takeaways: Real-world graphs name their axes; a point pairs one x-meaning with one y-meaning.
Distance along one street is the difference of the numbers that change.
Reading a point answers a question: find the x, read the height.

lessons.title: Two Patterns at Once
takeaways: Run two rules step by step and pair the terms from the same step.
Compare across each pair — a relationship appears (here: doubling).
The relationship is a shortcut: jump to any pair without listing terms.

lessons.title: Pairs on the Plane
takeaways: Pairs from two rules plot as points: first rule gives x, second gives y.
Steady rules repeat one move, so the points line up straight.
Extend by stepping the rules — or jump with the pair relationship.

lessons.title: Attributes Carry Down
takeaways: If every member of a category has an attribute, every subcategory member inherits it.
The arrow points down only — subcategory attributes don't climb (5-by-2 rectangle!).
Chains work: attributes ride down through several levels at once.

lessons.title: The Quadrilateral Family
takeaways: Quadrilateral → parallelogram → rectangle / rhombus → square; each level adds one attribute.
A square is both a rectangle and a rhombus — it has both additions.
Our trapezoid has exactly one parallel pair, so it sits outside the parallelogram branch.

lessons.title: The Triangle Family
takeaways: Sides: scalene / isosceles (at least two equal) / equilateral; angles: acute / right / obtuse.
Every triangle wears one label from each system — like right isosceles.
Equilateral is always isosceles, and never right: its angles are locked at 60°.

lessons.title: Sorting by Properties
takeaways: Most specific name = as far down the tree as the clues force, never further.
A shape's name promises its whole ancestry of properties.
Cross-cutting property rules gather shapes across different families.

lessons.title: True in the Hierarchy
takeaways: Always: down the tree, guaranteed by the name's promises.
Sometimes: prove it with one example AND one counterexample.
Never: find the blocker — one fact that kills every example.

lessons.title: Adding Decimals with a Model
takeaways: A decimal continues place value.
Tenths and hundredths name piece sizes.
Same-size pieces combine by counting.

lessons.title: Lining Up the Decimal Point
takeaways: Line up the decimal points.
Matching places add.
The point aligns every column at once.

lessons.title: Adding with Different Lengths
takeaways: Pad with trailing zeros.
A trailing zero changes nothing.
It fills the column for working.

lessons.title: Subtracting Decimals
takeaways: Subtraction uses the same alignment.
Trade a tenth for ten hundredths.
Never flip a short column.

lessons.title: Subtracting with Padding
takeaways: Pad before subtracting.
The zero creates a place to borrow into.
The value is unchanged.

lessons.title: Multiplying a Decimal by a Whole Number
takeaways: Multiply in the smallest place.
Then place the point.
Digits from multiplying, point from places.

lessons.title: Estimating a Decimal Product
takeaways: Round to a friendly whole number.
The estimate guards the point.
Right digits can still be wrong.

lessons.title: Multiplying Two Decimals
takeaways: Multiply the digits.
Add the decimal places.
Below one, the product shrinks.

lessons.title: Where Does the Point Go?
takeaways: Count the places in both factors.
Their sum is the product's places.
Digits and point are separate results.

lessons.title: Dividing a Decimal by a Whole Number
takeaways: Divide in the smallest place.
Then place the point.
Sharing shrinks each part.

lessons.title: Dividing by a Decimal
takeaways: Scale both numbers alike.
The quotient is unchanged.
A whole divisor is easier to work with.

lessons.title: Moving the Point to Divide
takeaways: The divisor sets the shift.
Move both numbers equally.
Unequal shifts change the answer.

lessons.title: Checking a Decimal Answer
takeaways: Check the size first.
Right digits can sit in the wrong place.
Estimating catches misplaced points.

lessons.title: Money Problems
takeaways: Money is decimals with named places.
A penny is one hundredth.
Compute in cents, then place the point.

lessons.title: Measurement Problems
takeaways: A centimeter is a hundredth of a meter.
Converting up shrinks the number.
The point records the shrink.

lessons.title: Multi-Step Decimal Problems
takeaways: Compute in the smallest place.
Place the point once, at the end.
Estimate before, check after.

lessons.title: Why Order Matters
takeaways: Without a rule, the same expression could give different answers — so we agree on an order.
Multiplication and division come before addition and subtraction.
Think of × and ÷ as binding tighter: they take their turn first.

lessons.title: Grouping Symbols First
takeaways: Grouping symbols (parentheses) are done before anything else.
They let you force an addition or subtraction ahead of a multiply or divide.
After the grouping, finish with the normal rule: ×÷ before +−.

lessons.title: Writing & Reading Expressions
takeaways: Translate words to expressions by finding which step happens first — that step gets the parentheses.
Word order changes the grouping: 'double 4, then add 5' ≠ 'add 4 and 5, then double.'
You can read an expression's structure ('three times the sum') without computing it.

lessons.title: Partial Products Recap
takeaways: Partial products split a number into its places, multiply each, and add the pieces.
This is the area model as arithmetic — and the foundation the standard algorithm hides.

lessons.title: The Standard Algorithm
takeaways: The standard algorithm is partial products written compactly, ones first then tens.
When a step's product passes 9, write the ones digit and carry the tens digit.
Add the carry into the next column — forgetting it is the most common error.

lessons.title: Multi-Digit × Multi-Digit
takeaways: Multiply the top number by each digit of the bottom number — one row each.
The tens-digit row is ten times bigger, so it starts with a placeholder 0 in the ones place.
Add the rows to get the product: 23 × 45 = 115 + 920 = 1035.

lessons.title: Estimating the Quotient
takeaways: Round the divisor to the nearest ten and pick a nearby dividend that divides evenly.
The estimate gives the rough size of the quotient.
Use it as a check: a full answer far from the estimate signals a mistake.

lessons.title: Long Division, Two-Digit Divisor
takeaways: Use your estimate to pick each quotient digit, largest that fits without going over.
Multiply, subtract to find the leftover, then bring down the next digit.
Sometimes there's a remainder left at the end — more on that next.

lessons.title: Interpreting Remainders
takeaways: Round up when everyone or everything must fit (buses, tables, vans).
Drop the remainder when only complete groups count (full packs).
The remainder itself is the answer when the question asks what's left over.

lessons.title: Line Up the Points
takeaways: Line up the decimal points — never the right ends — so each place matches.
Pad with trailing zeros to equal length before adding or subtracting.
Bring the point straight down; carry and borrow just as with whole numbers.

lessons.title: Padding & Regrouping
takeaways: Pad the shorter number with trailing zeros so every place lines up.
Each borrow lowers the next place by one — track that across multiple borrows.
Subtracting from a whole number chains the borrow across the zeros.

lessons.title: Decimal Sums in Context
takeaways: Total / combined / altogether means add; change / difference / how much left means subtract.
Line up points and pad, exactly as in bare calculations.
Two-step problems total first, then subtract — answer the question actually asked.

lessons.title: Counting Decimal Places
takeaways: Multiply the factors as whole numbers, ignoring the points at first.
Count the total decimal places in both factors; the answer gets that many.
Place the point by the count before dropping any trailing zeros.

lessons.title: Multiplying Decimals
takeaways: Multiply as whole numbers, then place the total decimal places from both factors.
A quick estimate (round each factor) confirms the point is in the right spot.
If your answer is ten times off the estimate, the point is misplaced.

lessons.title: Dividing Decimals
takeaways: Dividing by a whole number: divide normally and bring the point straight up.
Dividing by a decimal: shift both numbers until the divisor is whole, then divide.
Shifting both the same amount keeps the answer unchanged.

lessons.title: Tenths: The First Rung Below One
takeaways: Splitting one whole into 10 equal parts makes tenths; one tenth is written 0.1.
The single digit after the decimal point is the tenths digit — and the numerator over 10.
The ×10 ladder still rules: 0.1 × 10 = 1, and 1 ÷ 10 = 0.1.

lessons.title: Hundredths and Thousandths
takeaways: A hundredth is one of 100 equal parts (0.01, two places); a thousandth is one of 1000 (0.001, three places).
Each rung down splits the one above into 10: 10 hundredths make a tenth, 10 thousandths make a hundredth.
The zeros in a fraction's denominator match the number of decimal places.

lessons.title: ×10 and ÷10 as Ladder Moves
takeaways: ×10 slides a digit one rung left (ten times bigger); ÷10 one rung right (ten times smaller).
The decimal point is a landmark, not a wall — the same moves cross it unchanged.
Chaining moves just counts rungs: two ×10 is two rungs left, three ÷10 is three rungs right.

lessons.title: Place Names After the Point
takeaways: The places after the point are tenths, hundredths, thousandths — first, second, third.
A digit's place name is its piece size; the digit counts how many pieces.
Read a single-place decimal by its place: 0.6 is 'six tenths'.

lessons.title: Expanded Form with Decimals
takeaways: Expanded form splits a decimal into one piece per place: 0.375 = 3/10 + 7/100 + 5/1000.
It works in both directions — split apart, or add the pieces back to rebuild the decimal.
An empty place still needs a 0 to hold the other digits in position.

lessons.title: Words to Decimals and Back
takeaways: Say a decimal by reading its digits as a number, then naming the last (smallest) place.
Words back to a decimal: fill up to the named last place, using placeholder zeros as needed.
In a mixed number, the word 'and' marks the decimal point.

lessons.title: Lining Up the Places
takeaways: Line up the decimal points and compare place by place, starting at tenths.
The first place where digits differ decides — later places don't matter.
More digits does not mean bigger: 0.7 is greater than 0.68.

lessons.title: The Trailing-Zero Trap
takeaways: Trailing zeros on the right end don't change value: 0.5 = 0.50 = 0.500.
Pad decimals to equal length, then compare like whole numbers.
A zero right after the point is different — it shrinks the value (0.5 ≠ 0.05).

lessons.title: Ordering a Set of Decimals
takeaways: Pad every decimal to the same number of places with trailing zeros.
Then compare and order them exactly like whole numbers.
This handles mixed-length sets (0.3 vs 0.301) without any guesswork.

lessons.title: Rounding to a Whole
takeaways: To round to the nearest whole, check the tenths digit: 5 or more rounds up, 4 or less rounds down.
An exact half (tenths digit 5) rounds up by agreed convention.
The rest of the digits after the tenths don't change the decision.

lessons.title: Rounding to Any Decimal Place
takeaways: To round to any place, look at the digit one place to its right — the decider.
5 or more rounds the target place up; 4 or less leaves it.
Nearest tenth checks hundredths; nearest hundredth checks thousandths.

lessons.title: Rounding in Context
takeaways: Word problems tell you the target place: nearest dollar (ones), nearest dime or tenth, nearest hundredth.
Whatever the target, the decider is the digit one place to its right.
5 or more rounds up, 4 or less stays — the same rule in every context.

lessons.title: Order of Operations
takeaways: An expression names one value.
Multiplication binds before addition.
Left to right settles equal ranks.

lessons.title: Parentheses First
takeaways: Brackets override the ranking.
They make the enclosed part one quantity.
They change the value named.

lessons.title: Brackets and Braces
takeaways: Groupings nest.
They resolve inside out.
Nothing outside starts first.

lessons.title: Evaluating a Long Expression
takeaways: Apply the rules in turn.
Groupings, ranks, then left to right.
The expression names one value.

lessons.title: Writing an Expression from Words
takeaways: Words carry an order.
Brackets record that order.
Dropping them changes the meaning.

lessons.title: Reading an Expression Aloud
takeaways: Reading aloud must keep the grouping.
Name the bracket as one quantity.
Otherwise the listener rebuilds another expression.

lessons.title: Comparing Expressions Without Computing
takeaways: Some comparisons need no arithmetic.
Treat the bracket as one object.
Structural claims hold for any value.

lessons.title: Two Rules at Once
takeaways: Two rules can run together.
Matching terms have a fixed relationship.
Here it is a ratio, not a difference.

lessons.title: Making Ordered Pairs
takeaways: Pair the terms step by step.
A's term goes first.
The order names which rule produced it.

lessons.title: Graphing the Pattern
takeaways: Plot A across and B up.
Constant rules give a straight path.
The relationship becomes visible.

lessons.title: Finding the Relationship
takeaways: Divide the second coordinate by the first.
That reveals the factor.
It holds for every pair.

lessons.title: Explaining Why the Pattern Holds
takeaways: Examples show a pattern.
Structure explains why it must hold.
That is the difference between noticing and knowing.

lessons.title: Sharing That Doesn't Come Out Even
takeaways: Sharing continues past whole numbers.
The leftover is cut, not abandoned.
Each share can be under one.

lessons.title: a ÷ b = a/b
takeaways: a ÷ b equals a/b.
The dividend goes on top.
The bar means division exactly.

lessons.title: Interpreting the Quotient
takeaways: A quotient has two readings.
Cuttable leftovers become fractions.
Uncuttable ones stay remainders.

lessons.title: Sharing Problems
takeaways: Read for the amount and the shares.
Amount on top, shares beneath.
The fraction writes itself.

lessons.title: Dividing a Unit Fraction by a Whole Number
takeaways: Sharing a fraction cuts it further.
The denominator grows.
Each piece gets smaller.

lessons.title: Dividing a Whole Number by a Unit Fraction
takeaways: Dividing by a fraction counts how many fit.
Small pieces mean a large count.
A divisor under one enlarges.

lessons.title: Using a Visual Model
takeaways: A model shows which question is asked.
Sharing and fitting differ.
The picture keeps them apart.

lessons.title: On the Number Line
takeaways: The line shows the pieces fitting.
Smaller jumps, more of them.
The count exceeds the dividend.

lessons.title: Checking with Multiplication
takeaways: Multiplication undoes division.
Quotient times divisor rebuilds the start.
It works in both directions.

lessons.title: Which Is It?
takeaways: Ask what the answer counts.
Pieces means dividing by a size.
Shares means dividing by a number.

lessons.title: Division Word Problems
takeaways: Name the whole and the piece.
Decide which is unknown.
That picks the operation.

lessons.title: Estimating a Quotient
takeaways: Ask how many fit in one whole.
Then scale by the wholes.
A divisor under one enlarges.

lessons.title: Finding a Common Denominator
takeaways: A common denominator is a number both denominators divide into; the least is the LCD.
Find it by listing multiples until they first match.
Rewrite each fraction by multiplying top and bottom by the same factor.

lessons.title: Adding Unlike Fractions
takeaways: Rewrite the fractions over a common denominator first.
Add the numerators and keep the common denominator — never add the denominators.
Simplify the final answer whenever top and bottom share a factor.

lessons.title: Subtracting Unlike Fractions
takeaways: Rewrite both fractions over a common denominator before subtracting.
Subtract the numerators and keep the denominator — never subtract the bottoms.
Simplify the final answer whenever you can.

lessons.title: Groups of a Fraction
takeaways: A whole times a fraction is that many groups of the fraction.
Multiply the whole number by the numerator; keep the denominator.
Then simplify, or convert an improper fraction to a mixed number.

lessons.title: A Fraction of a Number
takeaways: A fraction of a number splits it into equal parts and takes some of them.
Divide by the denominator, then multiply by the numerator.
'Of' means multiply: a fraction of a number equals that fraction times the number.

lessons.title: The Area Model
takeaways: A fraction times a fraction is the overlap in a grid: cells = denominators multiplied, shaded = numerators multiplied.
The product is smaller than both factors — a part of a part.
Numerators multiply, denominators multiply — never add across.

lessons.title: Multiply Across
takeaways: Multiply the numerators together and the denominators together.
This is the area-model grid without drawing it: shaded = tops multiplied, total = bottoms multiplied.
Simplify the product when top and bottom share a factor.

lessons.title: Simplify the Product
takeaways: After multiplying across, reduce the product by its greatest common factor.
You can cancel common factors before multiplying to keep the numbers small.
Both paths — reduce-after and cancel-before — reach the same simplified answer.

lessons.title: Bigger, Smaller, or Same?
takeaways: Multiplying by a fraction under 1 (top < bottom) shrinks the number.
Multiplying by a fraction over 1 (top > bottom) grows it.
A fraction equal to 1 (top = bottom) leaves it unchanged — no computing needed.

lessons.title: Scaling Without Computing
takeaways: A product is one factor scaled by the other — read its size off the scaler.
Scaler under 1 → product smaller than the factor; over 1 → bigger; exactly 1 → equal.
Compare or order products by their scalers, without computing.

lessons.title: Wholes into Unit Fractions
takeaways: Dividing a whole by a unit fraction counts how many pieces fit.
To divide by 1/n, multiply the whole by n (the denominator).
The result is bigger than the whole — smaller pieces means more of them.

lessons.title: Unit Fractions into Wholes
takeaways: Dividing a unit fraction by a whole cuts the piece into that many smaller pieces.
To divide 1/n by a whole number w, multiply the denominator: 1/(n × w).
The result is smaller than the fraction — the opposite of dividing a whole by a unit fraction.

lessons.title: Division in Context
takeaways: Sharing one piece among people: the piece ÷ the people — each share gets smaller.
Counting how many servings fit in a whole: the whole ÷ the serving — the count is bigger.
Read the situation to choose which division it is, then compute.

lessons.title: Estimating with Compatible Numbers
takeaways: Estimate before dividing.
Compatible numbers divide cleanly.
The estimate sizes the quotient.

lessons.title: Dividing by a Multiple of Ten
takeaways: Multiples of ten split in two.
Divide by the digit, then by ten.
Place value does the work.

lessons.title: Partial Quotients
takeaways: Partial quotients uses convenient batches.
Batches need not be equal.
The quotient is their total.

lessons.title: The Standard Algorithm
takeaways: The standard algorithm fixes batches by place value.
It counts the same groups.
A digit one column out is wrong tenfold.

lessons.title: Adjusting a Too-Big Guess
takeaways: Trial digits are guesses.
An overshoot means lower the digit.
No step leaves a negative remainder.

lessons.title: Checking and Interpreting
takeaways: Multiply back and add the remainder.
It must rebuild the dividend.
A remainder must stay under the divisor.

lessons.title: Why You Need the Same Pieces
takeaways: Fractions add by counting pieces.
The pieces must be the same size.
Adding across ignores size.

lessons.title: Finding a Common Denominator
takeaways: A common denominator is a shared piece size.
Renaming re-cuts, never resizes.
Scale both parts alike.

lessons.title: The Least Common Denominator
takeaways: Any common multiple works.
The least keeps numbers smallest.
Larger choices need more simplifying.

lessons.title: Renaming Both Fractions
takeaways: Rename both fractions.
Each needs its own factor.
Both land on the shared size.

lessons.title: Adding Unlike Fractions
takeaways: Matching pieces add by counting.
The denominator holds still.
Only the numerator changes.

lessons.title: Subtracting Unlike Fractions
takeaways: Subtraction needs matching pieces too.
Rename first, then remove.
The denominator holds still.

lessons.title: Adding Mixed Numbers
takeaways: Add wholes and parts separately.
Reassemble at the end.
Carry when the parts pass one.

lessons.title: Subtracting Mixed Numbers
takeaways: Convert to improper fractions to avoid trading.
Each whole is b pieces.
Then subtract the counts.

lessons.title: Regrouping to Subtract
takeaways: Trade a whole when the top part is short.
One whole is b pieces.
The amount never changes.

lessons.title: Simplifying the Answer
takeaways: Simplify by dividing both parts.
Use the greatest common factor.
The value never changes.

lessons.title: Benchmark Estimation
takeaways: Round each fraction to a benchmark.
Estimate before renaming.
It catches adding across instantly.

lessons.title: Is the Answer Reasonable?
takeaways: A sum exceeds each of its parts.
Two proper fractions stay under two.
Comparison rejects wrong answers fast.

lessons.title: Fraction Word Problems
takeaways: Read for the quantities and the direction.
Find the shared piece size.
Then count the pieces.

lessons.title: Multi-Step Fraction Problems
takeaways: Rename once, to a size all share.
Run the steps in story order.
Simplify at the end.

lessons.title: Converting Metric Units
takeaways: Metric units step by 10s: km→m and kg→g and L→mL are ×1000; m→cm is ×100.
Bigger unit to smaller: multiply. Smaller to bigger: divide.
The quantity stays the same — only the counting unit changes.

lessons.title: Converting Customary Units
takeaways: Customary factors: 1 ft = 12 in, 1 yd = 3 ft, 1 lb = 16 oz, 1 gal = 4 qt.
Bigger unit to smaller: multiply. Smaller to bigger: divide.
Use the right factor for each pair of units.

lessons.title: Multi-Step Conversions
takeaways: Multi-step conversions chain two rungs through a middle unit — write it down.
Chained factors multiply (yd→in is ×3 then ×12, i.e. ×36), never add.
Most mistakes are a skipped rung: check that you finished the whole chain.

lessons.title: Reading a Line Plot
takeaways: Each X is one measurement; the stack height is how many share that length.
Most common = tallest stack; total = all X's added.
Range = longest − shortest length on the plot.

lessons.title: Using Line Plot Data
takeaways: Total length = each value times its stack count, added over a common denominator.
Difference = longest − shortest; equal share = total ÷ number of items.
Every line-plot question is fraction arithmetic on the data.

lessons.title: What Volume Means
takeaways: Volume is the amount of space a solid fills, counted in unit cubes.
One unit cube = 1 cubic unit; the number of cubes is the volume.
Real sizes add a cubic label: cm³, in³, or m³.

lessons.title: Counting Cubes
takeaways: A box's volume = cubes in one layer × the number of layers.
That shortcut is length × width × height.
Slice from any direction and the count comes out the same.

lessons.title: Layers of Cubes
takeaways: The base layer's cube count equals the area of the base.
Volume = base area × number of layers (the height).
Area covers the floor; height repeats it upward.

lessons.title: V = l × w × h
takeaways: V = l × w × h: multiply a box's three edge lengths.
Centimeter edges give cm³; the volume counts unit cubes.
Multiply in any order — pick the easiest pairing.

lessons.title: V = B × h
takeaways: V = B × h: base area times height.
It's V = l × w × h with the base pair grouped as B.
Given B, multiply straight away; otherwise compute B = l × w first.

lessons.title: Adding Volumes
takeaways: Volume is additive: non-overlapping pieces' volumes add.
Find each box with l × w × h, then add — never multiply the volumes.
Every unit cube gets counted exactly once.

lessons.title: Splitting Solids
takeaways: Odd solids split into boxes: find each l × w × h, then add.
Any legal cut gives the same total — every cube counts once.
Never use the box a solid merely fits inside; empty notches aren't volume.

lessons.title: Counting Unit Cubes
takeaways: Volume counts unit cubes.
Each cube fills one unit of space.
The formula is a shortcut for the count.

lessons.title: Layers and Height
takeaways: A prism stacks identical layers.
The height multiplies the base.
Adding would count only a handful of cubes.

lessons.title: Using V = l × w × h
takeaways: V = l × w × h.
l × w builds one layer.
h stacks the layers.

lessons.title: Using V = B × h
takeaways: V = B × h works for any prism.
B is the base's area.
It agrees with l × w × h.

lessons.title: Finding a Missing Dimension
takeaways: A missing dimension divides out.
Height counts base-layers.
Multiplying back checks it.

lessons.title: Composite Solids
takeaways: Build the simple solid first.
Subtract what was cut away.
A notch always lowers the count.

lessons.title: Volume Word Problems
takeaways: Read the base and the height from the words.
Base area is only one layer.
The depth stacks it.

lessons.title: Comparing Two Solids
takeaways: Compute both volumes to compare.
Different shapes can hold equal volume.
The cube count settles it.

lessons.title: The Triangle's Half
takeaways: Triangle area = 1/2 × base × height — always half of the enclosing rectangle.
Height is the PERPENDICULAR distance from base to apex, never a slanted side.
Work backwards from area to find a missing base or height by undoing the ×1/2 first.

lessons.title: Parallelograms and Trapezoids
takeaways: Parallelogram area = base × height — no halving, it's rectangle-equivalent.
Trapezoid area = 1/2 × (base1 + base2) × height — average the bases, then apply the triangle rule.
Every formula traces back to decomposing the shape into triangles or rectangles.

lessons.title: Choosing the Right Formula
takeaways: Same base and height give different areas for a triangle, parallelogram, and trapezoid — always identify the shape first.
A trapezoid's area sits between a triangle's and a parallelogram's, since it blends both bases.
Composite shapes often combine addition and subtraction of simpler shape areas.

lessons.title: Decomposing L-Shapes
takeaways: Split an L-shape into two rectangles and ADD their areas.
Or take the bounding box and SUBTRACT the missing corner — same answer either way.
Using both methods on the same shape is a built-in check on your work.

lessons.title: Composite Figures with Triangles
takeaways: Composite figures mix different shapes — apply each piece's OWN formula.
An attached piece ADDS to the total; a cut-away piece SUBTRACTS.
Never apply a triangle's ×1/2 to a rectangle piece, or skip it on a triangle piece.

lessons.title: Multi-Step Composite Problems
takeaways: Multi-piece figures scale the same rule: identify each piece's shape, compute separately.
Addition can be grouped any way without changing the total.
Track which pieces ADD (attached) and which SUBTRACT (cut away) before combining.

lessons.title: Finding Side Lengths from Coordinates
takeaways: A horizontal side: same y, subtract the x-values. A vertical side: same x, subtract the y-values.
Length is always a positive distance, even crossing zero into negatives.
A rectangle's missing corner shares one coordinate with each neighboring corner.

lessons.title: Area of Polygons on the Grid
takeaways: Find each side length from coordinate differences, then apply the shape's own area formula.
A right triangle with horizontal and vertical legs uses those legs directly in 1/2 × leg1 × leg2.
Complete a missing vertex first if a rectangle isn't fully given.

lessons.title: Coordinate Plane Capstone
takeaways: Read every side from coordinate differences before applying any area formula.
Identify each piece's shape (rectangle, triangle) to pick its formula correctly.
Combine composite pieces with the right sign — attached adds, cut-away subtracts.

lessons.title: Unfolding a Rectangular Prism
takeaways: Surface area = total area of all six faces; the net makes them all visible at once.
The formula 2(lw + lh + wh) packages the three matching pairs.
Surface area (square units) and volume (cubic units) are different measurements — don't swap them.

lessons.title: Surface Area with Triangular Faces
takeaways: A triangular prism has 2 triangle ends + 3 rectangular wrap-around faces.
Each face keeps its own formula — triangles halve, rectangles don't.
Count your faces (should be 5) before trusting a total.

lessons.title: Surface Area Word Problems
takeaways: Wrapping/painting/covering questions are surface area; filling questions are volume.
Count exactly the faces the situation includes — rooms skip floors, tents skip the ground.
Equal volumes can have different surface areas; flatter shapes expose more.

lessons.title: Volume and the Formula
takeaways: V = length × width × height — the formula is stacked layer-counting.
Volume is cubic units (inside); surface area is square units (outside).
Doubling one dimension doubles the volume.

lessons.title: Volume with Fractional Edges
takeaways: V = l × w × h works unchanged with fractional edges — smaller cubes pack the fractional parts.
Convert mixed numbers to improper fractions BEFORE multiplying.
Dropping the fraction (3½ → 3) is the classic slip — the packing argument shows why it's wrong.

lessons.title: Volume in the Real World
takeaways: Real volume problems: convert mixed numbers, multiply three dimensions, answer in cubic units.
"How many fit" divides total volume by per-item volume.
You now command area, composite figures, coordinates, surface area, and volume — 2D through 3D.

lessons.title: Questions That Expect Variety
takeaways: A statistical question anticipates variability — many differing answers.
Asking about a GROUP (not one case) is what usually invites the variety.
Fixed facts and single-person questions aren't statistical, whatever the topic.

lessons.title: Data as Answers
takeaways: A data set is the collection of answers to ONE statistical question.
One value per unit of observation — repeats count separately.
Fix WHAT you ask and WHO you ask before collecting.

lessons.title: From Question to Data
takeaways: Question → who to ask → one value per answer → pattern.
Variability in the data is the finding, not an error.
A collectible question names a concrete measurement; values come only from answers received.

lessons.title: Dot Plots
takeaways: A dot plot puts one dot per data value above a number line, stacking repeats.
Total dots = data-set size; stack height = that value's count; gaps = zero counts.
The plot loses nothing — the whole data set reads back from the dots.

lessons.title: Histograms
takeaways: A histogram groups data into equal-width bins; bar height = count in that bin.
Bar heights sum to the data size, but exact values are lost to the grouping.
Few distinct values → dot plot; many spread-out values → histogram.

lessons.title: The Shape of Data
takeaways: Describe plots with four words: peak (tallest), cluster (bunching), gap (empty), outlier (isolated).
Symmetric data mirrors around its peak; skewed data trails off to one side.
Outliers are real data — name them, don't erase them.

lessons.title: The Mean as Fair Share
takeaways: Mean = sum ÷ count — pool everything, share it out equally.
The mean can be a value nobody actually had; it's the balance point, not a member.
Backwards works too: mean × count = total, which uncovers missing values.

lessons.title: The Median as Middle
takeaways: Sort first, always — the median is the middle of the ORDERED list.
Odd count: the single central value. Even count: the mean of the middle pair.
The median only cares about position, not size — a fact that becomes its superpower next.

lessons.title: Choosing Mean vs Median
takeaways: The mean feels every value's size; one outlier can drag it far from the pack.
The median only counts positions, so it resists outliers — 6 → 6.5 while the mean leapt 6 → 10.
Outliers or skew → report the median; balanced data → the mean serves well.

lessons.title: Range: How Far Data Stretches
takeaways: Range = max − min: the fastest measure of spread.
It ignores every interior value — different data sets can share a range.
It has zero outlier resistance: one extreme day rewrites it.

lessons.title: Quartiles & the IQR
takeaways: Split sorted data at the median (set the median itself aside when the count is odd).
Q1 and Q3 are the halves' medians; IQR = Q3 − Q1.
Outliers own the endpoints but can't reach the fences — the IQR resists them, like the median does.

lessons.title: Same Center, Different Spread
takeaways: Data sets can share every center yet differ wildly: A and B both had mean AND median 7.
Spread broke the tie — IQR 4 vs 10, range 6 vs 12.
A full two-number description pairs one center with one spread.

lessons.title: Building a Box Plot
takeaways: A box plot draws the five-number summary: min, Q1, median, Q3, max.
The box spans Q1 to Q3 — the middle half — and its width is the IQR.
All four sections hold a quarter of the data, so width shows spread, never how many.

lessons.title: Comparing with Box Plots
takeaways: On a shared scale, median lines compare centres and box widths compare spread.
Equal medians with unequal boxes means the same typical value with different consistency.
Box plots hide individual values — use a dot plot when gaps or clusters matter.

lessons.title: Typical Distance: the MAD
takeaways: MAD = average of every value's distance from the mean; distances are always positive.
A small MAD means tightly clustered data; a large MAD means scattered data.
Pair mean with MAD and median with IQR — an extreme value moves the first pair, not the second.

lessons.title: Reading the Whole Picture
takeaways: Describe a distribution with shape + center + spread, in context and with units.
Symmetric data: mean ≈ median (here both 15), and either center serves.
A single number — however correct — is not a description.

lessons.title: Which Numbers Tell It Best
takeaways: Outliers or skew → the resistant pair: median + IQR.
Symmetric, clean data → mean + range serve honestly (and mean ≈ median anyway).
A mean far from the median is itself evidence: something is dragging it.

lessons.title: The Data Detective
takeaways: Question → data → picture → summary: the complete statistical workflow.
Shape chooses the summaries — outliers call for the median-IQR pair.
Report outliers as real data, in context units, never erased.

lessons.title: Exponent Notation
takeaways: An exponent counts how many copies of the base to multiply: 2^3 = 2 × 2 × 2 = 8.
The exponent does NOT multiply the base — 3^2 is 9, not 6.
Squaring uses exponent 2; cubing uses exponent 3.

lessons.title: Evaluating Powers
takeaways: Evaluate a power by multiplying the base by itself, one factor at a time.
Powers of 10 are 1 followed by that many zeros.
1 to any power is 1; any base to the power 1 is itself.

lessons.title: Order of Operations with Exponents
takeaways: Order: Parentheses, Exponents, Multiply/Divide, Add/Subtract.
2 + 3^2 = 11, but (2 + 3)^2 = 25 — grouping changes the result.
An exponent applies only to what's directly beneath it.

lessons.title: Variables Stand for Numbers
takeaways: A variable stands for an unknown or changing number; an expression is a rule built around it.
A number written against a variable multiplies it: 2n = 2 × n.
The same expression gives different outputs for different inputs.

lessons.title: Evaluating Expressions
takeaways: Evaluating = replacing each variable with its value, then computing in order.
Multiplication in 2n + 1 resolves before the addition; exponents on variables resolve first of all.
Substitute completely before computing anything.

lessons.title: Writing Expressions from Words
takeaways: Sum/more/increased → add; less/fewer/difference → subtract; twice/triple/of → multiply; per/half → divide.
"Less than" and "subtracted from" REVERSE the order: 3 less than x is x − 3.
When unsure, test the phrase with a real number.

lessons.title: Naming the Parts
takeaways: Terms are separated by + and −; factors are multiplied inside a term.
A coefficient is the number multiplying a variable; a constant has no variable at all.
Naming the parts is what lets you say precisely which piece you mean.

lessons.title: The Coefficients You Cannot See
takeaways: A bare variable has coefficient 1; a subtracted one has coefficient −1.
The sign in front of a term belongs to its coefficient.
Making the invisible 1 visible is what makes combining like terms reliable.

lessons.title: Reading an Expression Aloud
takeaways: 'The sum of' groups what follows — that is where brackets come from.
3(n + 2) and 3n + 2 are different expressions, and the words tell them apart.
A bracket can be viewed as one object, which makes counting copies easier than expanding.

lessons.title: The Distributive Property with Variables
takeaways: a(x + b) = ax + ab — distribute onto BOTH terms.
Factoring runs the identity backwards: pull the GCF out front.
Verify any expansion or factoring with a number substitution.

lessons.title: Combining Like Terms
takeaways: Like terms share the same variable part; combine by adding coefficients (3x + 2x = 5x).
Unlike terms never merge: 3x + 2 stays 3x + 2.
One matching value doesn't prove equivalence — test a second number.

lessons.title: Testing for Equivalence
takeaways: Equivalent expressions agree at EVERY input; one mismatch disproves the claim.
One lucky match (x + x = x² at 2) proves nothing — test twice, and try 0.
Distribution and like-terms are the identities that GUARANTEE equivalence.

lessons.title: What an Equation Says
takeaways: An equation claims two expressions are equal; a solution is the value making that claim true.
Test a candidate by substituting it in and checking both sides match.
Always verify a solution by substituting it back — solving and checking are two separate steps.

lessons.title: Solving with Addition & Subtraction
takeaways: To solve x + a = b, subtract a from both sides.
To solve x − a = b, add a to both sides.
Always check by substituting the solution back into the ORIGINAL equation.

lessons.title: Solving with Multiplication & Division
takeaways: To solve ax = b, divide both sides by a.
To solve x ÷ a = b, multiply both sides by a.
Every one-step equation follows the same principle: apply the OPPOSITE operation to both sides.

lessons.title: What an Inequality Says
takeaways: An inequality has infinitely many solutions — a range, not a single value.
Strict symbols (>, <) exclude the boundary; ≥ and ≤ include it.
"At least" and "at most" are inclusive language, matching ≥ and ≤.

lessons.title: Graphing Inequalities
takeaways: Open circle = strict (excludes boundary); closed circle = inclusive (includes it).
Arrow points right for bigger numbers (>, ≥), left for smaller (<, ≤).
A graph and its inequality carry the exact same information, two different ways.

lessons.title: Dependent and Independent Variables
takeaways: The independent variable is chosen freely; the dependent variable is computed from it.
Tables read independent-then-dependent; graphs plot independent on x, dependent on y.
Every rule like y = 3x or pay = 8h describes exactly this relationship.

lessons.title: How Many Fit?
takeaways: a ÷ (unit fraction) asks how many of that piece-size fit inside a.
Dividing by a fraction under 1 makes the answer BIGGER than the start.
Cut into the right-sized pieces first, then count.

lessons.title: Flip and Multiply
takeaways: Reciprocal swaps a fraction's top and bottom.
Keep the first fraction, flip the SECOND (the divisor), then multiply straight across.
Simplify the result to lowest terms.

lessons.title: Dividing Fractions in Context
takeaways: Convert every mixed number to an improper fraction FIRST.
Word problems are total ÷ piece size — find those two quantities.
Flip-and-multiply works exactly the same once fractions are improper.

lessons.title: Multi-Digit Division
takeaways: Multi-digit division uses the same steps as single-digit — just bigger estimates.
A remainder must always be smaller than the divisor.
