Check any division by multiplying the quotient by the divisor (plus the remainder).

lessons.title: Adding and Subtracting Decimals
takeaways: Pad decimals with trailing zeros so every number has the same number of places.
Add or subtract column by column, exactly like whole numbers.
The decimal point never moves — only the digits around it change.

lessons.title: Multiplying and Dividing Decimals
takeaways: Multiplying: count TOTAL decimal places across both factors, then place the point.
Dividing: shift both decimal points the same amount until the divisor is a whole number.
Shifting both points equally never changes the division's answer.

lessons.title: Greatest Common Factor
takeaways: A factor divides a number evenly; common factors divide both numbers.
The GCF is the LARGEST common factor — not just any shared one.
GCF = 1 means relatively prime; if one list sits inside the other, the GCF is the smaller number.

lessons.title: Least Common Multiple
takeaways: A multiple counts UP in steps; the LCM is the first multiple two numbers share.
Relatively prime → LCM is the product; one divides the other → LCM is the bigger number.
GCF (biggest shared divisor) and LCM (smallest shared multiple) point in opposite directions.

lessons.title: Factoring with the Distributive Property
takeaways: Pull the GCF out of a sum: a + b = GCF × (a÷GCF + b÷GCF).
The numbers inside are each original divided by the GCF.
Always verify by expanding back to the original sum.

lessons.title: The Number Line Goes Left
takeaways: The number line extends left of zero into the negatives.
Every number has an opposite — its mirror across zero, same distance away.
Taking the opposite twice returns the original number.

lessons.title: Comparing Negatives
takeaways: The number farther right on the line is always greater — even among negatives.
A bigger digit on a negative number means a SMALLER value (-8 < -3).
Every negative is less than zero and less than every positive.

lessons.title: The Four Quadrants
takeaways: Four quadrants, numbered counterclockwise from top-right: I(+,+), II(-,+), III(-,-), IV(+,-).
Plot x first, then y; the pair is always (x, y).
Points with a zero coordinate sit on an axis, in no quadrant.

lessons.title: Signs, and What a Flip Does to Them
takeaways: The pair of signs names the quadrant: (+,+) I, (−,+) II, (−,−) III, (+,−) IV.
Flipping the sign of x reflects across the y-axis; flipping y reflects across the x-axis.
A reflection never changes a point's distance from either axis — only which side it is on.

lessons.title: Absolute Value
takeaways: Absolute value is a number's distance from zero: |-3| = 3, |3| = 3.
It's always zero or positive — never negative.
Opposites share one absolute value; only zero has absolute value 0.

lessons.title: Comparing with Absolute Value
takeaways: "Greater" is about position: -2 > -8. "Farther from zero" is about absolute value: |-8| > |-2|.
For negatives, the bigger magnitude belongs to the SMALLER value.
Debt, depth, and temperature all need you to know which question you're answering.

lessons.title: Ordering Rational Numbers
takeaways: Integers, fractions, decimals, and negatives all share one number line.
Convert to a common form (usually decimals), then order left to right.
Among negatives, the bigger-looking number is the smaller value.

lessons.title: Two Quantities, One Relationship
takeaways: A ratio compares two quantities with "for every" — order matters.
The relationship holds as the group repeats: 3 : 2 stays true at 9 and 6.
Differences and lone counts aren't ratios; "for every" is the fingerprint.

lessons.title: Part, Part, Whole
takeaways: Add the parts to get the whole: 3 : 2 means groups of 5.
Part-to-whole puts the group total second: apples 3 : 5, oranges 2 : 5.
A ratio fixes shares, never exact counts.

lessons.title: Equivalent Ratios
takeaways: Multiply or divide BOTH parts by the same number — the relationship survives.
Adding the same number to both parts breaks a ratio (3 : 2 ≠ 5 : 4).
Test equivalence by shrinking both ratios to simplest form and comparing.

lessons.title: Ratio Tables
takeaways: Every table row = the base ratio × one number, applied to BOTH columns.
Adding the same amount to both columns breaks the table.
Any route through true rows works — take the easy arithmetic.

lessons.title: Double Number Lines
takeaways: Both lines share 0 — no head starts.
Stacked marks share one multiplier, up or down the line.
The line reads both ways: laps from minutes, minutes from laps.

lessons.title: Choose Your Tool
takeaways: Table for many rows; line for in-betweens; multiplier for one-shots.
Every tool multiplies both quantities — none of them add.
The shrink test verifies any answer: simplest form must match the original.

lessons.title: Ratio Pairs on the Plane
takeaways: Each row of a ratio table plots as a point: first column across, second column up.
Equivalent ratios land in a straight line through the origin.
The height of that line at x = 1 is the unit rate.

lessons.title: The Per-One Row
takeaways: A unit rate is the per-one row: divide both quantities by the count you want ONE of.
Every ratio hides two unit rates — the question picks the direction.
Per-one is the bridge: shrink to 1, then multiply out to any amount.

lessons.title: The Better Buy
takeaways: Convert every deal to the same per-one units, then compare.
Sticker price and package size both mislead; unit price doesn't.
Bigger isn't automatically cheaper per unit — divide every time.

lessons.title: Rates That Predict
takeaways: Rate × amount predicts totals; total ÷ rate recovers the amount.
Multi-step problems bridge through the per-one row: shrink first, then stretch.
Every prediction rides on "at this rate" — check that the pace actually holds.

lessons.title: Percent Means Per Hundred
takeaways: Percent means per 100: 25% = 25/100 = 1/4.
Convert a fraction by scaling to 100ths: 3/4 = 75/100 = 75%.
The friendly family (1/2, 1/4, 3/4, 1/10) makes most percents instant.

lessons.title: A Percent of a Number
takeaways: A percent of a number = the per-100 rate × the number: 30% of 40 = 12.
The 10% anchor speeds it up: find 10%, then scale.
A percent needs its whole — 30% of 40 ≠ 30% of 90.

lessons.title: Percents Over and Under
takeaways: 100% is the whole; under is a part, over exceeds it (150% of 20 = 30).
Work backwards from a part: 20% is 8 means the whole is 40.
Benchmarks (10%, 5%, 1%) make estimates quick.

lessons.title: Conversion Is a Ratio
takeaways: A conversion factor (12 in : 1 ft) is a ratio — scale it like any other.
Toward a smaller unit: multiply. Toward a bigger unit: divide.
Let the UNIT size, not the number size, choose the operation.

lessons.title: Chaining Conversions
takeaways: No direct rate? Chain two: hours → minutes → seconds.
Multiply toward smaller units at each link; divide toward bigger.
Compare quantities by converting both to the SAME unit first.

lessons.title: Ratios Capstone
takeaways: Ratios, equivalent ratios, unit rates, percents, and conversions are one idea in many outfits.
The wording points to the tool: "of" (percent), "per/each" (rate), "which deal" (unit price).
Multi-step problems chain the tools — solve one stage, carry it into the next.

lessons.title: Reading a Scale
takeaways: A scale like 1 cm = 4 m converts drawing lengths to real lengths.
Real length = drawing length × scale amount.
The scale is a unit rate: meters per centimeter.

lessons.title: From Real to Drawing
takeaways: Drawing → real: multiply by the scale amount.
Real → drawing: divide by the scale amount.
Decide the direction before computing.

lessons.title: How Area Scales
takeaways: Area picks up the scale factor twice: k becomes k².
Safest route: convert each side to real units, then multiply.
At 1 cm = 4 m, each cm² stands for 16 m².

lessons.title: Radius, Diameter, and π
takeaways: d = 2r and r = d ÷ 2.
π ≈ 3.14 is the same ratio for every circle.
Radius: center to edge. Diameter: across. Circumference: around.

lessons.title: Circumference
takeaways: C = 2πr from a radius; C = πd from a diameter.
The two formulas agree because d = 2r.
Round by multiplying the coefficient by 3.14.

lessons.title: Area of a Circle
takeaways: Area: A = πr² (square the radius).
From a diameter, halve to the radius first.
Around = circumference (2πr); inside = area (πr²).

lessons.title: Complementary and Supplementary
takeaways: Complementary: adds to 90°. Supplementary: adds to 180°.
Find a missing partner by subtracting from the pair's total.
C makes a Corner; S makes a Straight line.

lessons.title: Vertical and Adjacent Angles
takeaways: Vertical angles (across the crossing) are equal.
Adjacent angles at a crossing add to 180°.
One known angle unlocks all four (they total 360°).

lessons.title: Solving for Unknown Angles
takeaways: Corners give sum = 90; straight lines give sum = 180; verticals give equality.
Combine like terms before dividing.
Check by adding the solved angles back to the total.

lessons.title: Three Sides, One Triangle
takeaways: Three fixed sides (SSS) determine exactly one triangle, up to flips and turns.
Two sides with the angle BETWEEN them (SAS) also determine exactly one.
The two shorter sides must together exceed the longest, or no triangle exists at all.

lessons.title: When the Conditions Leave a Choice
takeaways: Two sides with a NON-included angle (SSA) can give two different triangles.
Three angles alone give infinitely many — shape without size.
Angles that do not sum to 180°, or sides that cannot reach, give none.

lessons.title: Constructing with Compass and Straightedge
takeaways: Equal compass radii force equal distances — that is why constructions prove rather than measure.
Arcs from both ends of a segment cross on its perpendicular bisector.
An SSS triangle is built by swinging one arc of each remaining length from each end of the base.

lessons.title: Unfolding a Prism
takeaways: A net is the solid's surface laid flat; adding its areas gives surface area.
A box's six faces come in three matching pairs, hence 2(lw + lh + wh).
Surface area is measured in square units; volume is not the same question.

lessons.title: Surface Area of Rectangular Prisms
takeaways: Surface area of a box is 2(lw + lh + wh), in square units.
Volume is lwh, in cubic units — the same three numbers answering a different question.
Doubling every dimension multiplies surface area by 4 and volume by 8.

lessons.title: Surface Area of Triangular Prisms & Pyramids
takeaways: A triangular prism has two matching triangular ends and three rectangular sides.
Lateral surface area of any prism is the end's perimeter times the prism's length.
A pyramid has one base and triangular faces meeting at an apex.

lessons.title: Volume of Right Prisms
takeaways: Volume of any right prism is base area × height, in cubic units.
The base's shape changes what you compute first, not the stacking rule.
Dividing volume by base area recovers the height.

lessons.title: Composite Areas
takeaways: Break a composite figure into shapes whose areas you already know.
Pieces present are added; pieces removed are subtracted.
Different valid cuts give the same total, which makes a second method a free check.

lessons.title: Area, Surface Area & Volume in Context
takeaways: Footprint area, surface area and volume answer different questions about the same solid.
Units identify the right measure: linear, square, or cubic.
Real problems usually name the measure indirectly — covering, filling, or bordering.

lessons.title: When Sides Make a Triangle
takeaways: Shorter pair > longest side — strictly greater.
Equal sums collapse flat (1, 2, 3 fails).
The third side lives strictly between the difference and the sum.

lessons.title: Slicing Solids
takeaways: Base-parallel cuts copy the base (cylinder → circle, pyramid → smaller square).
Vertical cuts through a tip make triangles; through a cylinder, rectangles.
One solid gives many sections — direction decides.

lessons.title: Geometry Roundup
takeaways: Convert with the scale first, then apply circle formulas.
Angle facts become equations; side sums decide triangles.
You now hold every 7.G tool — and the πr² behind Grade 8's volumes.

lessons.title: Dividing by a Fraction
takeaways: Unit rate = quantity ÷ time (or any two related amounts).
Dividing by a fraction: flip the second fraction, then multiply.
The unit rate isn't always a whole number.

lessons.title: Pace, Recipes, and Laps
takeaways: The flip-and-multiply rule applies to any two compared quantities.
The unit rate's name tells you which quantity is "per" the other.
Recipes, laps, and rates all use the same fraction-division method.

lessons.title: Finding Any Unit Rate
takeaways: Unit rate = first quantity ÷ second quantity.
Flip the second fraction, then multiply.
The result can be a whole number or a fraction — both are valid unit rates.

lessons.title: Testing a Table
takeaways: Compute y/x for every pair in the table.
All ratios equal means proportional; even one different ratio means not.
The constant ratio doesn't have to be a whole number.

lessons.title: Finding the Constant of Proportionality
takeaways: k is the shared ratio y/x across every pair in a proportional table.
k can be a whole number or a fraction.
Once you know k, y = k × x finds any missing value.

lessons.title: Tables in Real Situations
takeaways: Test every ratio before deciding if a table is proportional.
Not every real-world table is proportional — a flat fee breaks the pattern.
Once you know k, y = k × x predicts any new value.

lessons.title: Plotting a Proportional Relationship
takeaways: Every point on the line fits y = kx.
The line always passes through the origin (0, 0).
A bigger k makes a steeper line.

lessons.title: The Point That Shows the Unit Rate
takeaways: At x=1, the y-value IS the unit rate.
For any point, unit rate = y ÷ x.
This works whether you're plotting or reading a graph.

lessons.title: Reading a Story from a Graph
takeaways: Any point (x, y) on a proportional line gives rate = y ÷ x.
Know which axis is which before dividing.
Once you know the rate, you can predict any point on the line.

lessons.title: Writing the Equation y = kx
takeaways: Every proportional relationship is y = kx, with k the constant of proportionality.
k is y ÷ x from any row, the height at x = 1 on the graph, and the number in front of x.
With k known, the equation predicts any value without extending the table.

lessons.title: Tax and Tip
takeaways: Percent of a price = (percent/100) × price.
Total = original price + the percent amount.
The shortcut: multiply by (1 + percent/100) in one step.

lessons.title: Markup and Markdown
takeaways: Markup: new price = original + percent amount.
Markdown: sale price = original − percent amount.
Find the percent amount first, then add or subtract.

lessons.title: Percent Increase and Decrease
takeaways: Percent change = (new − old) ÷ old × 100.
A rise gives a positive percent; a fall gives a negative percent.
Always use the ORIGINAL value as the base.

lessons.title: Simple Interest
takeaways: I = P · r · t — principal times rate times time, with the rate as a decimal.
Interest and total owed are different questions: the total adds the principal back.
Simple interest grows in equal steps because the rate never touches the accumulated interest.

lessons.title: Commission and Fees
takeaways: Commission is a percent of the SALE, not of pay or of what remains.
Base pay plus commission means the percent applies only to the sales part.
A flat fee is not proportional — it does not double when the amount does.

lessons.title: Percent Error
takeaways: Percent error = size of the gap ÷ ACTUAL value, written as a percent.
It is never negative — over and under by the same amount give the same error.
It is what makes estimates of different sizes comparable at all.

lessons.title: Adding Same-Sign Integers
takeaways: Both positive: add normally.
Both negative: add the magnitudes, keep negative.
Same-sign jumps on a number line always go the same direction.

lessons.title: Adding Different-Sign Integers
takeaways: Subtract the smaller magnitude from the larger.
Keep the sign of whichever number has the bigger magnitude.
Opposites (same magnitude, different sign) always sum to 0.

lessons.title: Adding Any Two Integers
takeaways: Same sign: add magnitudes, keep the sign.
Different signs: subtract magnitudes, keep the bigger one's sign.
Opposites always sum to 0.

lessons.title: Subtracting Means Adding the Opposite
takeaways: a − b = a + (−b), always.
Subtracting a negative becomes adding a positive.
Once rewritten as addition, use the same-sign/different-sign rules.

lessons.title: Distance and Change on the Number Line
takeaways: Change = new value − old value.
A positive change means a rise; a negative change means a fall.
Rewriting as adding the opposite makes any change computable.

lessons.title: Adding and Subtracting Together
takeaways: Any subtraction can be rewritten as adding the opposite.
After rewriting, the addition rules from Chapter 1 handle everything.
Practice makes the rewrite automatic.

lessons.title: Multiplying Integers
takeaways: Same signs (both + or both −): product is positive.
Different signs: product is negative.
For 3+ factors, count the negatives — an odd count means negative.

lessons.title: Dividing Integers
takeaways: Same signs (both + or both −): quotient is positive.
Different signs: quotient is negative.
Division and multiplication use the identical sign rule.

lessons.title: Multiplying and Dividing Together
takeaways: Same signs: result is positive. Different signs: result is negative.
This rule works identically for multiplying and dividing.
For 3+ factors, count the negatives — odd is negative, even is positive.

lessons.title: Multiplying and Dividing Signed Fractions
takeaways: Same signs: positive result. Different signs: negative result.
Multiply fractions directly; divide by flipping and multiplying.
Always simplify the final fraction.

lessons.title: Adding and Subtracting Signed Decimals
takeaways: Same sign: add magnitudes, keep the sign.
Different signs: subtract magnitudes, keep the bigger one's sign.
Subtracting still means adding the opposite.

lessons.title: All Four Operations with Rational Numbers
takeaways: Integers, fractions, and decimals all use the identical sign rules.
Addition/subtraction: same-sign add-and-keep, different-sign subtract-and-keep-bigger.
Multiplication/division: same-sign positive, different-sign negative.

lessons.title: Estimating from a Sample
takeaways: Estimate = (trait count in sample ÷ sample size) × population size.
A random sample gives every member an equal chance of being chosen.
A biased sample (friends, convenience, self-selected) skews the estimate.

lessons.title: How Sample Size Affects Confidence
takeaways: Different random samples naturally give slightly different estimates.
Bigger samples tend to vary less and give more reliable estimates.
Tightly clustered estimates from several samples suggest a reliable true value.

lessons.title: Sampling in Real Situations
takeaways: Scaling a sample's ratio works the same in any real-world context.
Always check whether a sample was truly random or secretly biased.
Bigger random samples give more confidence in the estimate.

lessons.title: Are Two Groups Really Different?
takeaways: Gap in units = (difference in means) ÷ (variability measure).
A gap near 0 means the groups aren't meaningfully different.
A gap of several units suggests the groups barely overlap.

lessons.title: Visual Overlap and What It Means
takeaways: Heavy overlap matches a small gap-in-units (near 0).
Minimal overlap matches a large gap-in-units (several units).
The picture and the number should always tell a consistent story.

lessons.title: Comparing Two Populations in Real Situations
takeaways: The gap-in-units process works the same in any real-world comparison.
A small gap-in-units is itself a valid, useful conclusion.
A large gap-in-units points to a real, noticeable difference.

lessons.title: MAD as a Ruler
takeaways: The MAD is each group's typical wobble — use it as a ruler for the gap between centres.
Difference in MADs = (difference of means) ÷ MAD.
The same raw gap means more when the groups wobble less.

lessons.title: How Many MADs Apart?
takeaways: Means, then MADs, then gap ÷ MAD — the result is a plain number with no units.
Roughly: under 1 MAD is not convincing, about 2 MADs or more is a real gap.
Failing to show a difference is not the same as showing there is none.

lessons.title: Is the Gap Big Enough?
takeaways: When two groups' MADs differ a little, average them into one ruler.
Report the multiple, then say what it means in the situation — and never claim a cause from a comparison.
A real difference can still be too small to matter; the multiple and the raw size answer different questions.

lessons.title: How Likely Is It?
takeaways: Probability = favorable outcomes ÷ total outcomes.
0 is impossible, 1 is certain, 1/2 is an even chance.
Words like "likely" and "unlikely" describe the number, not replace it.

lessons.title: Estimating Probability from Trials
takeaways: Relative frequency = occurrences ÷ total trials.
Experimental probability can differ from theoretical probability.
More trials generally give a more reliable estimate.

lessons.title: Probability in Real Situations
takeaways: Theoretical probability: favorable outcomes ÷ total possible outcomes.
Experimental probability: occurrences ÷ total trials.
Watch the question's wording to know which one is being asked for.

lessons.title: Counting All the Outcomes
takeaways: Multiply the choices at each stage: 2 outcomes × 6 outcomes = 12.
This works for any number of stages, not just two.
You can double-check a small case by listing every outcome.

lessons.title: Compound Events
takeaways: Compound event probability = product of the individual probabilities, for independent events.
This matches counting matches out of the total sample space.
Independent means one event's outcome doesn't affect the other's.

lessons.title: Probability Models in Real Situations
takeaways: Counting principle: multiply the choices at each stage for the total outcomes.
Compound events: multiply the individual probabilities, for independent events.
Both tools apply to any real situation, whatever the context.

lessons.title: Distributing with Negative Coefficients
takeaways: The multiplier reaches every term inside the parentheses.
Use the sign rule: same signs positive, different signs negative.
Check by evaluating both forms at the same x-value.

lessons.title: Combining Like Terms with Negative Coefficients
takeaways: Add coefficients of matching terms using the same-sign/different-sign rule.
Constants and x-terms never combine with each other.
Distribute first if parentheses are present, then combine.

lessons.title: Simplifying Any Linear Expression
takeaways: Distribute before combining, always.
Use the sign rule (same=positive, different=negative) at every step.
Practice spotting which pattern you're facing before computing.

lessons.title: Factoring: Distribution Run Backwards
takeaways: Factoring asks one question: what do all the terms share?
Only the GREATEST common factor leaves a bracket with nothing left to pull out.
Check any factoring by distributing back — it must return the original.

lessons.title: The Multiplier Inside a Percent Increase
takeaways: a + 0.05a and 1.05a are the same value — a is 1a, so the coefficients simply add.
A multiplier above 1 is an increase; below 1, a decrease. 0.80 means 20% off.
Repeated changes multiply their multipliers, which is why 10% twice is 21%, not 20%.

lessons.title: Choosing the Form That Answers the Question
takeaways: Equivalent forms agree for every value; distributing or factoring is what proves it.
The factored form shows the number of groups; the expanded form shows the separate pieces.
Reading structure first often replaces a hard calculation with an easy one.

lessons.title: Undoing Addition, Then Multiplication
takeaways: Two-step equations need two undo-moves, in order.
Undo +/- first, then undo ×/÷.
Check by substituting the solution back into the original equation.

lessons.title: Equations with Negative Coefficients
takeaways: Undo addition/subtraction first, then divide by the coefficient.
Same signs when dividing give a positive solution.
Different signs when dividing give a negative solution.

lessons.title: Two-Step Equations in Real Situations
takeaways: Translate the story into an equation first.
Undo addition/subtraction, then undo multiplication.
The sign rules apply the same way regardless of the story.

lessons.title: Solving on the Balance
takeaways: An equation is a level beam: any move that touches only one side breaks the equality — and the beam shows it instantly.
The balance forces the solving order: clear loose units from both sides FIRST, split into equal groups LAST — which is why on paper you subtract before you divide.

lessons.title: Undo in the Right Order
takeaways: Undo the LAST step first — reverse the whole order, then flip every operation.
Dividing before subtracting splits the added number too: (51 − 9) ÷ 7, never 51 ÷ 7 − 9.

lessons.title: Distribute First, Then Solve
takeaways: Distribute before doing anything else.
After distributing, use the same two-step method as before.
Watch the signs carefully when distributing a subtraction.

lessons.title: Parentheses with Negative Multipliers
takeaways: A negative multiplier still distributes to every term.
Same signs give a positive term; different signs give a negative term.
After distributing, the two-step solving method is unchanged.

lessons.title: Mixed Parenthesized Equations
takeaways: Distribute first, regardless of the multiplier's sign.
The resulting equation solves exactly like the last chapter's two-step equations.
Verify by substituting the solution into the ORIGINAL, un-distributed equation.

lessons.title: Solving Two-Step Inequalities
takeaways: Undo addition/subtraction first, then divide.
Dividing by a POSITIVE number never flips the direction.
Check by testing a number from the solution set.

lessons.title: The Sign-Flip Rule
takeaways: The flip happens ONLY when multiplying or dividing by a negative.
Adding or subtracting never flips anything.
Test a number from your solution set in the original inequality to check.

lessons.title: Two-Step Inequalities in Real Situations
takeaways: Translate the story into an inequality first.
Undo addition/subtraction, then divide.
Flip the direction only when dividing by a negative.

lessons.title: Plotting Paired Data
takeaways: Each dot pairs two measurements: first across (x), then up (y).
One dot per item — keep the two numbers in order.
Scatter plots reveal relationships between two quantities.

lessons.title: Reading Association
takeaways: Positive: dots rise to the right (x up, y up).
Negative: dots fall to the right (x up, y down).
No association: no clear upward or downward direction.

lessons.title: Clusters, Outliers, and Form
takeaways: Clusters are groups of similar values; outliers are lone far-off dots.
Form is linear (straight) or nonlinear (curved).
Outliers can pull a summary line off the main pattern.

lessons.title: The Line of Best Fit
takeaways: It runs through the middle of the cloud, close to all dots.
It need not touch any dot — balance matters, not contact.
Its direction matches the association (rising or falling).

lessons.title: Judging a Good Fit
takeaways: Smaller total distance from dots to line means a better fit.
A good line is also balanced — dots split above and below.
Tight clouds allow closer fits than spread-out clouds.

lessons.title: Reading a Line's Equation
takeaways: The coefficient of x is the slope (steepness and direction).
The constant term is the y-intercept (value when x = 0).
A negative slope matches a negative association.

lessons.title: Making Predictions
takeaways: To predict, substitute the new x into y = mx + b.
Multiply the slope by x first, then add the intercept.
The line gives a likely y even for an x you never measured.

lessons.title: What Slope and Intercept Mean
takeaways: Slope = how much y changes for each extra unit of x (a rate).
Intercept = the value of y when x = 0 (a starting amount).
Reading both tells the data's real-world story.

lessons.title: How Far to Trust a Prediction
takeaways: Predictions inside the measured range are the most reliable.
Extrapolation — reaching far beyond the data — can mislead.
Real relationships may curve or level off outside the data.

lessons.title: Reading Two-Way Tables
takeaways: Each cell counts people in two categories at once (e.g. adult AND cat).
Row and column margins hold the totals; the corner is the grand total.
Add across a row or down a column to get its total.

lessons.title: Relative Frequency
takeaways: Relative frequency = cell ÷ total, as a fraction or percent.
Of the whole survey → divide by the grand total.
Of one row or column → divide by that row or column total.

lessons.title: Association in Categories
takeaways: Compare rates (relative frequencies), not raw counts, across groups.
Sharply different rates signal association between the categories.
Nearly equal rates mean little or no association.

lessons.title: The Leftover: Observed − Predicted
takeaways: Residual = observed − predicted: positive above the line, negative below, zero on it.
The sign says which way the line erred; the size says how badly.
The largest |residual| flags the point the model explains worst.

lessons.title: Reading the Leftovers
takeaways: A well-fit line leaves patternless residuals — boring leftovers are good news.
U-shape ⇒ curvature; one-sided ⇒ misplaced line; growing spread ⇒ trust varies with x.
The residual plot magnifies structure the raw scatter hides.

lessons.title: Better Line, Smaller Leftovers
takeaways: The best line makes residuals small AND balanced — near-zero sum, no pattern, no favored side.
Every adjustment trades misses; optimality is when no trade helps.
Least squares formalizes exactly this: minimize the summed squared leftovers.

lessons.title: What Powers of Ten Mean
takeaways: 10ⁿ (n positive) = 1 followed by n zeros.
10⁰ = 1, always.
10⁻ⁿ = 1/10ⁿ, a decimal with n zeros before the 1.

lessons.title: Multiplying and Dividing Powers of Ten
takeaways: Subtracting a negative exponent is the same as adding.

lessons.title: Powers of Ten and Place Value
takeaways: Thousands=10³, ones=10⁰, tenths=10⁻¹, hundredths=10⁻².
Any number can be written as a digit times a power of ten.
This 'digit × power of ten' form is exactly what scientific notation uses.

lessons.title: Same Base, Add the Exponents
takeaways: Multiplying powers of the same base adds exponents; dividing subtracts them.
The rules only apply when the base matches — 2⁴ · 3² cannot be combined.
A base with no written exponent has exponent 1.

lessons.title: A Power of a Power
takeaways: (a^m)^n = a^(m·n) — the outer exponent counts copies of the block.
(ab)^n = a^n b^n — the exponent reaches every factor inside the bracket.
(3x)² = 9x², not 3x²: the coefficient is inside, so it is squared too.

lessons.title: Zero and Negative Exponents
takeaways: a⁰ = 1 for any non-zero a — the descending pattern and the quotient rule both force it.
A negative exponent means a reciprocal: a⁻ⁿ = 1/aⁿ, never a negative value.
Adding exponents works straight through zero and into the negatives.

lessons.title: Evaluating Roots & Solving x² = p
takeaways: Squaring erases sign, so both +√p and −√p solve x² = p.
√p alone gives just the positive root; solving x²=p wants both signs.
This only works when p is a perfect square here — otherwise the roots are irrational (recall Chapter 2 of the last course!).

lessons.title: Cube Roots & Solving x³ = p
takeaways: ∛p asks: what number cubed gives p?
A negative number cubed stays negative, so cube roots of negatives are real, unlike square roots of negatives.
x³ = p always has exactly one real solution, unlike x² = p's two.

lessons.title: Roots in Context
takeaways: A physical length is always positive, so real-world square-root problems use only the positive solution.
Area (2D) problems set up side² = p; volume (3D) problems set up edge³ = p.
Cube-root context problems never have a sign ambiguity to resolve, since x³=p has just one real solution.

lessons.title: Writing Large Numbers in Scientific Notation
takeaways: Move the decimal left until one nonzero digit remains before it.
The exponent counts how many places the decimal moved.
The coefficient must satisfy 1 ≤ a < 10 — never 10 or more, never less than 1.

lessons.title: Writing Small Numbers in Scientific Notation
takeaways: Move the decimal right until one nonzero digit remains before it.
Count the places moved — that count becomes a negative exponent.
Numbers smaller than 1 always get a negative exponent in scientific notation.

lessons.title: Comparing Magnitudes
takeaways: A bigger exponent always means a bigger number, regardless of the coefficient.
Only compare coefficients when the exponents are equal.
Dividing two scientific-notation numbers answers 'how many times as much.'

lessons.title: Multiplying and Dividing in Scientific Notation
takeaways: Multiplying: multiply coefficients, add exponents.
Dividing: divide coefficients, subtract exponents.
If the coefficient lands outside [1, 10), shift a factor of 10 into the exponent.

lessons.title: Adding and Subtracting in Scientific Notation
takeaways: Unlike multiply/divide, exponents don't combine when adding or subtracting.
Convert to a shared exponent (usually the larger one) before combining coefficients.
Once exponents match, just add or subtract the coefficients.

lessons.title: Real-World Applications & Precision
takeaways: Total-from-rate problems multiply; combining differently-scaled quantities adds or subtracts.
Match exponents before adding/subtracting; add/subtract exponents when multiplying/dividing.
Don't report more precision than the original data supports.

lessons.title: What Is a Function
takeaways: One input → exactly one output means it's a function.
One input → several outputs means it's NOT a function.
Different inputs sharing an output is perfectly fine.

lessons.title: Functions from Tables and Pairs
takeaways: Scan the INPUT column for repeats.
A repeated input with different outputs means it's NOT a function.
Repeated outputs across different inputs are always fine.

lessons.title: The Vertical Line Test
takeaways: Cross more than once → two outputs for one input → NOT a function.
Cross at most once everywhere → IS a function.
Vertical lines and sideways U's fail; slanted lines and upright U's pass.

lessons.title: Rate of Change
takeaways: Rate of change = (output change) ÷ (input change).
Always reduce to the change for a single input step.
A decreasing output gives a negative rate of change.

lessons.title: Why a Line's Slope Is Constant
takeaways: Any two points on a line give the same slope.
Similar triangles on the line share the same rise/run ratio.
That shared ratio IS the line's slope.

lessons.title: Initial Value and y = mx + b
takeaways: m is the slope (rate of change); b is the initial value (output at x=0).
Read b straight from a table's x=0 row, or work backward using the slope.
Slope and initial value together determine the whole line.

lessons.title: One Function, Many Forms
takeaways: Equations, tables, graphs, and words can all show the same function.
Compare rate of change and initial value to tell if forms match.
Different presentation doesn't mean a different function.

lessons.title: Comparing Rates of Change
takeaways: Read the rate from an equation (coefficient of x) or a table (output change ÷ input change).
The bigger rate grows faster, regardless of form or initial value.
A big initial value does not mean a big rate of change.

lessons.title: Comparing Rate and Initial Value
takeaways: Rate and initial value are independent features to compare.
A function can start lower yet grow faster, overtaking later.
Setting two linear functions equal finds where they meet.

lessons.title: Linear vs. Nonlinear
takeaways: Linear functions graph as straight lines; nonlinear ones curve.
Check a table: equal differences → linear, changing differences → nonlinear.
A squared or higher power of the input makes a function nonlinear.

lessons.title: Reading Graph Shapes
takeaways: Up = increasing, down = decreasing, flat = unchanging.
Steeper = changing faster; gentler = changing slower.
A rising graph that flattens is still increasing, just more slowly.

lessons.title: Sketching Graphs from Stories
takeaways: Steady change → straight line; holding steady → flat; speeding up → steepening curve.
Read the story left to right and lay shapes in the same order.
Direction and order of stages both matter to the final sketch.

lessons.title: Keeping the Balance
takeaways: An equation is a balance — do the same to both sides.
Undo in reverse: subtract constants first, then divide by the coefficient.
Watch signs when dividing by a negative coefficient.

lessons.title: Variables on Both Sides
takeaways: Subtract the smaller x-term from both sides to collect x.
Then solve the leftover two-step equation as usual.
Every move happens on both sides to keep the balance.

lessons.title: Distribute, Then Solve
takeaways: Distribute the outside factor to EVERY term inside the parentheses.
The common slip is missing the second term — 3(x+4) = 3x+12, not 3x+4.
After distributing, combine like terms and solve as usual.

lessons.title: When There Is No Solution
takeaways: If x vanishes and you get a false statement (like 3 = 5), there's no solution.
This happens with equal x-coefficients but different constants.
Geometrically, it's two parallel lines that never meet.

lessons.title: When There Are Infinitely Many
takeaways: If x vanishes and you get a true statement (like 3 = 3), every x is a solution.
This happens when both sides simplify to the same expression.
Geometrically, it's one line drawn on top of itself.

lessons.title: Classifying Any Equation
takeaways: Different x-coefficients → one solution.
Same coefficients, same constants → infinitely many.
Same coefficients, different constants → none.

lessons.title: What Is a System?
takeaways: A system is two equations solved together.
The solution must make BOTH equations true, not just one.
Graphically, it's the intersection point of the two lines.

lessons.title: Solving by Graphing
takeaways: The crossing point of the two lines is the solution.
Set the expressions equal to find x, then plug in for y.
Always check the point in BOTH equations.

lessons.title: One, None, or Infinitely Many (Systems)
takeaways: Different slopes → one solution (lines cross).
Same slope, different intercepts → no solution (parallel).
Same slope AND intercept → infinitely many (same line).

lessons.title: The Substitution Method
takeaways: When one equation gives y = (expression), plug it into the other.
That leaves one variable — solve it exactly, no graph needed.
Substitution is precise where graphing only estimates.

lessons.title: Back-Substituting for y
takeaways: Solving gives x; back-substitute to find y.
Use the isolated (y = …) equation — it's the easy one.
Confirm the final point in BOTH equations.

lessons.title: Systems in the Real World
takeaways: Two relationships between two unknowns become two equations.
Substitute, solve for one unknown, back-substitute for the other.
Check both facts and answer the actual question asked.

lessons.title: What Makes a Number Rational
takeaways: Every rational number's decimal either stops or repeats a block forever.
A repeating remainder in long division is what forces the repeating digits.
0.333…, 0.4545…, and 0.875 are all rational — two repeat, one terminates.

lessons.title: Predicting Terminating vs. Repeating Decimals
takeaways: Only 2s and 5s in the simplified denominator means the decimal terminates.
Any other prime factor (3, 7, 11, …) forces a repeating decimal.
Always simplify the fraction BEFORE checking its denominator.

lessons.title: Converting a Repeating Decimal to a Fraction
takeaways: The power of 10 matches the repeating block's length (1 digit → ×10, 2 digits → ×100, …).
Subtracting the original x cancels the infinite repeating part.
Always simplify the resulting fraction by the greatest common factor.

lessons.title: A Number With No Exact Fraction
takeaways: √2 is the diagonal of a unit square, and no fraction squares to exactly 2.
Perfect-square roots (√4, √9, √16, …) are the rational exception.
A root is irrational exactly when its radicand isn't a perfect square.

lessons.title: Classifying Rational & Irrational
takeaways: Perfect-square roots and genuinely repeating decimals are rational, even when they look messy.
A decimal whose pattern keeps changing (never locking into one fixed block) is irrational.
π and non-perfect-square roots are the everyday examples of irrational numbers.

lessons.title: The Real Number Line Has No Gaps
takeaways: Between any two numbers, another number always fits.
Squaring two nearby decimals can trap an irrational number between them.
This narrowing technique works for any irrational, to any level of precision.

lessons.title: Estimating Square Roots Between Integers
takeaways: Find the perfect squares just below and just above n.
Compare distances to decide which whole number √n is closer to.
This bracketing technique works for any non-perfect-square n.

lessons.title: Locating Irrationals on the Number Line
takeaways: Test tenths (7.0², 7.1², 7.2², …) to narrow a bracket to one decimal place.
Every irrational number can be approximated to any precision this way.
The approximation never becomes exact — the true value never terminates or repeats.

lessons.title: Comparing & Estimating with Irrationals
takeaways: Convert radicals and fractions to decimals before comparing them.
Rational approximations (like 3.14 or 22/7) estimate irrational expressions.
Squaring a square root returns the original number exactly.

lessons.title: Sliding with Translations
takeaways: Right/up add to a coordinate; left/down subtract.
Apply the same shift to every point of the shape.
Size, shape, and orientation all stay the same — only position changes.

lessons.title: Flipping with Reflections
takeaways: Across the x-axis: (x, y) → (x, −y).
Across the y-axis: (x, y) → (−x, y).
The mirror image is congruent — same size and shape, flipped orientation.

lessons.title: Turning with Rotations
takeaways: 180° around the origin: (x, y) → (−x, −y).
90° counterclockwise: (x, y) → (−y, x).
Translations, reflections, and rotations all preserve size and shape.

lessons.title: Translations as Coordinate Rules
takeaways: A translation is (x, y) → (x + a, y + b), applied to every point alike.
Read the rule off a movement by subtracting the start from the end.
Translations compose by adding their vectors, and never change lengths or angles.

lessons.title: Reflections as Coordinate Rules
takeaways: Across the y-axis: (x, y) → (−x, y). Across the x-axis: (x, y) → (x, −y).
The coordinate that changes is the one measured perpendicular to the mirror.
Reflections keep every length and angle but reverse orientation.

lessons.title: Dilations as Coordinate Rules
takeaways: A dilation from the origin is (x, y) → (kx, ky) — every distance from the centre times k.
k > 1 enlarges, 0 < k < 1 shrinks, and the angles never change either way.
Rigid motions give congruent images; dilations give similar ones.

lessons.title: Congruent Shapes
takeaways: Congruent = mappable by translations, reflections, rotations.
Congruent shapes have equal corresponding sides and angles.
Resizing breaks congruence; rigid motions preserve it.

lessons.title: Dilations
takeaways: From the origin: multiply each coordinate by the scale factor.
Factor > 1 enlarges; factor between 0 and 1 shrinks.
A dilation changes size, so the image is similar, not congruent.

lessons.title: Similar Shapes
takeaways: Similar = mappable by a dilation (plus rigid motions).
Corresponding angles are equal; corresponding sides are proportional.
The common ratio of matching sides is the scale factor.

lessons.title: Angles and a Transversal
takeaways: Corresponding and alternate interior angles are equal.
Angles on a straight line (and co-interior angles) add to 180°.
Chaining these rules finds any of the eight angles.

lessons.title: Angles in a Triangle
takeaways: The three interior angles of any triangle sum to 180°.
Find a missing angle by subtracting the known ones from 180.
An exterior angle equals the sum of the two remote interior angles.

lessons.title: Angle-Angle Similarity
takeaways: Two pairs of equal angles guarantee similar triangles (AA).
The third angle matches automatically because all three sum to 180°.
Similar triangles have proportional sides — use the scale factor to find lengths.

lessons.title: Why the Theorem Works
takeaways: The hypotenuse is opposite the right angle — the longest side.
The squares on the two legs add up to the square on the hypotenuse.
That area relationship IS a² + b² = c².

lessons.title: Finding Missing Lengths
takeaways: Hypotenuse: add the leg-squares, then take the square root.
Missing leg: subtract the known leg-square from c², then take the root.
In these problems every answer is a whole number.

lessons.title: The Converse and Distance
takeaways: Converse: if a² + b² = c² (c longest), the triangle is right.
If the two smaller squares don't add to the biggest, it's not right.
Grid distance is the hypotenuse: d = √((Δx)² + (Δy)²).

lessons.title: Volume of a Cylinder
takeaways: V = πr²h — square the radius, then multiply by the height.
πr² is the base circle's area; h stacks it into a column.
Leave answers as a number times π, or round using π ≈ 3.14.

lessons.title: Volume of a Cone
takeaways: V = ⅓πr²h — find πr²h, then divide by 3.
Three cones exactly fill a cylinder with the same base and height.
The cone is always smaller — divide, don't multiply.

lessons.title: Volume of a Sphere
takeaways: V = 4⁄3 πr³ — cube the radius, times 4, divided by 3.
Spheres cube the radius; cylinders and cones square it.
Leave answers as a number times π, or round with π ≈ 3.14.

lessons.title: Absolute Value Is a Distance
takeaways: |x| is the distance from x to 0, which is why it is never negative.
Absolute value discards the side and keeps the size: |−6| = |6| = 6, but −6 ≠ 6.
Equal distances usually come in pairs — one on each side of zero.

lessons.title: The V-Shaped Graph
takeaways: y = |x| is a V: slope −1 into the vertex, slope +1 out of it.
The vertex (0, 0) is the graph's floor — distance cannot go below zero.
Mirror-image inputs have equal heights, so heights above the vertex are hit twice.

lessons.title: Shifting and Flipping the V
takeaways: The vertex sits where the expression inside the bars equals zero.
Inside the bars shifts horizontally and opposite to its sign; outside shifts vertically as written.
A minus in front flips the V into a peak.

lessons.title: Two Numbers Share a Distance
takeaways: |expression| = k splits into expression = k and expression = −k.
Treat everything inside the bars as a single quantity before splitting.
The two solutions sit symmetrically about the value that makes the inside zero.

lessons.title: No Solution, One, or Two
takeaways: |expression| = k has two solutions for k > 0, one for k = 0, and none for k < 0.
The count can be settled before any case-splitting.
Graphically the count is how many times a horizontal line meets the V.

lessons.title: Absolute Value Inequalities
takeaways: |x| < k is one band: −k < x < k.
|x| > k is two rays: x < −k or x > k — never a single chain.
Shifted versions center the band or the rays on whatever makes the inside zero.

lessons.title: A Function Defined in Pieces
takeaways: A piecewise function pairs each formula with the inputs it governs.
Evaluate by checking the condition first, then applying that branch.
Conditions must not overlap, or one input would get two outputs.

lessons.title: Graphing Piecewise Functions
takeaways: Draw each branch only over the inputs its condition names.
The boundary point belongs to the branch whose condition includes it: filled dot there, open circle on the other.
Branches that meet at different heights make the graph jump.

lessons.title: Steps, Brackets & Real Rules
takeaways: Step functions are piecewise rules whose branches are all flat.
Each branch rounds in the direction its rule states — started ounces round up.
Within a step the output carries no information about the exact input, only its range.

lessons.title: One Dataset's Shape, Two Datasets Compared
takeaways: A dot plot shows shape directly: peaks, symmetry, and how far an outlier's tail stretches.
Comparing groups needs both centre (median) and spread (IQR) — a higher average alone doesn't mean more consistent.
A narrow box is a tight cluster; a wide box is real variation, whatever the median says.

lessons.title: Fitting a Line, and Reading What It Says
takeaways: A fitted line minimizes the total size of the leftover gaps — it doesn't have to pass through every point.
Technology finds the identical line a careful hand-fit approximates, by testing every tilt for the smallest squared gaps.
Slope is always the rate of change; the intercept is always the value when the input is zero.

lessons.title: How Good Is the Fit? Residuals and Correlation
takeaways: A residual is actual minus predicted for ONE point — positive above the line, negative below.
The correlation coefficient r, from −1 to 1, summarizes every residual's pattern into a single strength score.
Strength is |r|, the distance from 0 — sign only tells you the direction of the trend.

lessons.title: Precise Enough — But Not More
takeaways: Combining measurements — adding, subtracting, computing a rate — never manufactures precision beyond the coarsest input.
A calculator's extra displayed digits are not automatically meaningful; they can be pure noise past what the data supports.
Match a reported result's precision to the LEAST precise measurement that built it, not the most precise.

lessons.title: Evaluating Exponential Functions
takeaways: f(x) = a · bˣ: a is the start, b is the per-step multiplier.
Raise b to the power x first, then multiply by a.
The initial value is f(0) = a, since b⁰ = 1.

lessons.title: Growth vs Decay
takeaways: b > 1 → growth (rising); 0 < b < 1 → decay (falling).
Decay shrinks by a constant factor but stays positive.
The base is the growth or decay factor.

lessons.title: The Constant Ratio
takeaways: Divide consecutive terms to find the base b.
Extend by multiplying by b — never add.
Constant difference = linear; constant ratio = exponential.

lessons.title: Growth Models
takeaways: P(x) = a · bˣ with b > 1 projects growth forward.
The starting amount is P(0) = a.
Apply the base once per period — multiply, don't add.

lessons.title: Decay Models
takeaways: V(x) = a · bˣ with 0 < b < 1 shrinks toward zero.
The starting amount is V(0) = a.
Apply the decay factor once per period.

lessons.title: Percent Growth & Decay
takeaways: Growth factor = 1 + rate; decay factor = 1 − rate.
Once you have the base, evaluate a · bˣ as usual.

lessons.title: Solving by Matching Bases
takeaways: bˣ = k: write k as a power of b, then x is that exponent.
Ask how many times b multiplies to reach k.
If bases match, the exponents must be equal.

lessons.title: Equations with a Coefficient
takeaways: Divide out the coefficient before matching bases.
The coefficient scales the output, not the exponent.
Then bˣ = k solves by rewriting k as a power of b.

lessons.title: Decay & Negative Exponents
takeaways: A fraction target (below 1) with base > 1 means a negative exponent.
1/bⁿ = b⁻ⁿ — negative exponents are repeated division.
With a decay base, targets above 1 flip the sign negative.

lessons.title: Reading Exponential Graphs
takeaways: The y-intercept is the initial value a (at x = 0).
b > 1 rises (growth); 0 < b < 1 falls (decay).
The curve approaches the asymptote y = 0 but never reaches it.

lessons.title: Comparing Growth
takeaways: Compare two models by evaluating both at the same x.
“Grows faster” = larger base, not larger start.
A larger base always overtakes eventually.

lessons.title: Exponential vs Linear
takeaways: Linear adds a fixed amount; exponential multiplies by a fixed factor.
Test a table: equal differences = linear, equal ratios = exponential.
Any exponential with b > 1 eventually overtakes any line.

lessons.title: Product & Quotient Rules
takeaways: Product rule: a^m · a^n = a^(m+n).
Quotient rule: a^m / a^n = a^(m−n).
The base never changes — only the exponent does.

lessons.title: Power of a Power & Products
takeaways: (a^m)^n = a^(mn) — multiply the exponents.
(ab)^n = a^n · b^n — the coefficient gets the power too.
Raise every factor inside, including hidden exponents of 1.

lessons.title: Zero & Negative Exponents
takeaways: a^0 = 1 for any nonzero base.
a^(−n) = 1/a^n — a reciprocal, never a negative value.
Keep exponent signs when adding or subtracting.

lessons.title: Degree & Like Terms
takeaways: Degree = highest exponent; leading coefficient sits on that term.
The constant term is the one with no variable (x^0).
Like terms share variable and exponent; only they combine.

lessons.title: Adding Polynomials
takeaways: Combine like terms: add coefficients of matching terms.
A missing term contributes a coefficient of 0.
Carry every sign through each column.

lessons.title: Subtracting Polynomials
takeaways: Distribute the minus across every term, then combine like terms.
Subtracting a negative adds: −(−5) = +5.
Flip all signs, not just the first, before combining.

lessons.title: Multiplying by a Monomial
takeaways: a·(b + c) = a·b + a·c across every term.
Coefficients multiply; exponents add.
Carry every sign as you distribute.

lessons.title: Multiplying Binomials (FOIL)
takeaways: Multiply every term of one binomial by every term of the other.
The middle term is Outer + Inner, with signs.
Watch signs on the Last product.

lessons.title: Special Products
takeaways: (a + b)² = a² + 2ab + b² — never forget the 2ab.
(a + b)(a − b) = a² − b² — the middle cancels.
Square coefficients too: (2x)² = 4x².

lessons.title: Factoring with the GCF
takeaways: Pull out the largest monomial dividing every term.
Include the variable at its lowest power.
Distribute back to check, keeping every sign.

lessons.title: Factoring Trinomials
takeaways: The two numbers become the constants in (x + p)(x + q).
A negative constant means opposite signs.
Always check by FOIL-ing back.

lessons.title: Difference of Squares
takeaways: a² − b² = (a + b)(a − b) — no middle term.
Coefficients can be squares too: 4x² = (2x)².
A sum of squares (a² + b²) does not factor this way.

lessons.title: Function Notation
takeaways: f(4) means substitute 4 for x in the rule.
Follow order of operations — powers and × before + and −.
The letter (f, g, h) is just a name.

lessons.title: Domain, Range & the Function Test
takeaways: Domain = set of inputs; range = set of outputs.
A function gives each input exactly one output.
Repeated outputs are fine; repeated inputs (with different outputs) are not.

lessons.title: Functions from a Table
takeaways: Find the rule by comparing inputs to outputs.
The rule works for inputs the table never listed.
Follow order of operations for multi-step rules.

lessons.title: Common Difference
takeaways: Find d by subtracting consecutive terms.
Extend by adding d to the last term.
d can be negative (decreasing) or zero.

lessons.title: The nth Term Formula
takeaways: Use (n − 1) steps — the first term is step zero.
The formula reaches any position directly.

lessons.title: Finding Terms & Positions
takeaways: Find a_1 and d, then use a_n = a_1 + (n − 1)d.
For a position, solve value = a_1 + (n − 1)d for n.
One rule replaces listing every term.

lessons.title: Common Ratio
takeaways: Find r by dividing consecutive terms.
Extend by multiplying the last term by r.
Geometric sequences grow faster than arithmetic ones.

lessons.title: The nth Term of a Geometric Sequence
takeaways: Use exponent (n − 1) — the first term has zero factors of r.
The formula reaches any position directly.

lessons.title: Reading a Geometric Rule
takeaways: Find a_1 and r, then use a_n = a_1 · r^(n − 1).
The exponent is (n − 1), counting from the first term.
One rule replaces multiplying step by step.

lessons.title: Arithmetic or Geometric?
takeaways: Arithmetic adds a constant (constant difference).
Geometric multiplies by a constant (constant ratio).
If neither is constant, it's neither type.

lessons.title: Choosing the Right Formula
takeaways: Arithmetic: a_n = a_1 + (n − 1)d.
Geometric: a_n = a_1 · r^(n − 1).
The wrong rule gives a badly wrong answer — classify first.

lessons.title: Growth in the Real World
takeaways: Constant addition → arithmetic; repeated multiplication → geometric.
Watch the words: "add/each" vs "double/triple/times."
Geometric growth overtakes arithmetic over time.

lessons.title: A Line Splits the Plane
takeaways: Every line splits the plane into two half-planes.
Side test: compare the point's y with the line's y at that x.
Bigger = above, smaller = below, equal = on.

lessons.title: Testing a Point
takeaways: An inequality's solutions fill a half-plane.
Test one off-boundary point: true → shade its side; false → shade the other.
(0, 0) is the witness of choice — unless it's on the line.

lessons.title: Solid or Dashed
takeaways: > and < : dashed boundary, excluded.
≥ and ≤ : solid boundary, included.
Line style and shaded side are separate decisions.

lessons.title: Two Fences
takeaways: A system's region = the intersection of its half-planes.
One failed test disqualifies a point completely.
Overlaps can be strips, wedges — or empty.

lessons.title: Corners of a Region
takeaways: A vertex is the simultaneous solution of two boundary equations.
Substitution and elimination find every corner exactly.
n boundaries pair up into at most n·(n−1)/2 crossings.

lessons.title: Is the Point In?
takeaways: Test every inequality; one failure evicts.
Non-strict fences admit their boundaries — corners included.
Naming the broken fence tells you how to repair a plan.

lessons.title: Feasible First
takeaways: Constraints are inequalities wearing work clothes.
The feasible region is every plan that passes all of them.
New constraints only shrink the region — and re-carve its corners.

lessons.title: The Corner Principle
takeaways: Linear objectives peak (and bottom out) at vertices.
Algorithm: find corners → score → keep the best.
Ties spread along an edge, but a corner always shares the crown.

lessons.title: A Real Plan
takeaways: Story → constraints → feasible region → corners → scores → best plan.
The winner used both resources fully — mixed plans often beat all-in ones.
Relaxing a binding constraint moves the corner and buys extra profit.

lessons.title: Slope as Steepness
takeaways: Slope = rise ÷ run — divide, never multiply or subtract.
Slope is a rate: how much y changes per 1 step in x.
A bigger slope means a steeper line.

lessons.title: Slope from Two Points
takeaways: Slope = (y₂ − y₁) ÷ (x₂ − x₁).
Subtract y's and x's in the SAME order or the sign flips.
Slopes may be fractions — reduce, don't round.

lessons.title: Positive, Negative, Zero & Undefined
takeaways: Uphill → positive; downhill → negative.
Horizontal → 0; vertical → undefined (never mix these up).
Undefined means the run is 0, so you can't divide.

lessons.title: Meet y = mx + b
takeaways: m is the slope (coefficient of x); b is the y-intercept (the constant).
b is the y-value when x = 0 — where the line meets the y-axis.
To evaluate, multiply m·x first, then add b.

lessons.title: Graphing from Slope-Intercept
takeaways: Start at (0, b), the y-intercept, on the y-axis.
Step by the slope: rise over run (down for a negative slope).
The x-intercept is different: it's where y = 0, found by solving.

lessons.title: x-intercept vs y-intercept
takeaways: y-intercept: x = 0, so it's b — read it straight off y = mx + b.
x-intercept: y = 0, so solve mx + b = 0 for x.
To build a line: slope in front of x, y-intercept at the end.

lessons.title: Point-Slope Form
takeaways: Point-slope form: y − y₁ = m(x − x₁).
Read it back by subtracting: y − 4 & x − 1 → point (1, 4).
A plus inside hides a negative coordinate: y + 2 means y₁ = −2.

lessons.title: Point-Slope to Slope-Intercept
takeaways: Convert point-slope → y = mx + b: distribute m, add y₁.
Shortcut: b = y₁ − m·x₁ (the slope never changes).
Backward: any point on y = mx + b gives a point-slope equation.

lessons.title: Standard Form Ax + By = C
takeaways: Standard form: Ax + By = C, integers, A ≥ 0.
Intercepts fast: x-int = C/A (set y = 0), y-int = C/B (set x = 0).
Slope from standard = −A/B; convert from y = mx + b by moving the x-term left.

lessons.title: Line from a Point and a Slope
takeaways: Find b with b = y₁ − m·x₁, then write y = mx + b.
The given point always lands back on the finished line.
Slope 0 makes a horizontal line, y = y₁.

lessons.title: Line Through Two Points
takeaways: Slope first: m = (y₂ − y₁)/(x₂ − x₁).
Then b = y₁ − m·x₁ with either point; write y = mx + b.
Same x on both points → vertical line x = that value (slope undefined).

lessons.title: Parallel & Perpendicular Lines
takeaways: Parallel lines share the same slope.
Perpendicular slopes are negative reciprocals: flip and negate, so m₁·m₂ = −1.
To write either line, take the right slope and find b = y₁ − m·x₁.

lessons.title: Where Line Meets Parabola
takeaways: An intersection satisfies both equations at once.
Set the expressions for y equal — the system becomes one quadratic.
A line meets a parabola 0, 1, or 2 times.

lessons.title: Substitution Does It
takeaways: Substitute the line into the curve.
Solve the quadratic that results.
Back-substitute for y — and audit in both equations.

lessons.title: Zero, One, or Two
takeaways: A line meets a parabola 0, 1, or 2 times.
Substitute, rearrange, read b² − 4ac: −, 0, + in that order.
Discriminant zero is tangency — merged crossings.

lessons.title: The Circle as an Equation
takeaways: x² + y² = r² collects the points at distance r from the origin.
Under, equal, over 25 sorts inside, on, outside.
Signs die under squaring — the rim is symmetric four ways.

lessons.title: A Line Through the Circle
takeaways: Substitute the line, square the binomial WITH its middle term.
Tidy, factor, back-substitute — then audit in the circle.
y² = k hands back ±√k: two roots unless k = 0.

lessons.title: Miss, Touch, Cross
takeaways: |height| vs radius: under cuts, equal grazes, over misses.
Tangency is the doubled root again — x² = 0 or discriminant 0.
Tilted lines answer to the same discriminant as parabolas did.

lessons.title: The Parent Parabola & Vertex Form
takeaways: y = a(x − h)² + k has vertex (h, k) and axis x = h.
(x − h) shifts right by h — mind the sign flip.
A negative a opens the parabola downward.

lessons.title: Graphing from Standard Form
takeaways: Axis of symmetry: x = −b/(2a).
Vertex y: substitute that x back into the equation.
a > 0 opens up (minimum); a < 0 opens down (maximum).

lessons.title: Stretch, Flip, and Shift
takeaways: a sets width and direction; |a| > 1 narrower, a < 0 opens down.
+ k shifts vertically; (x − h) shifts horizontally (right by h).
y = a(x − h)² + k has vertex (h, k).

lessons.title: The Zero-Product Property
takeaways: Zero-product property: set each factor to 0.
A factor (x − r) gives root r; (x + r) gives root −r.
The roots are where the parabola crosses the x-axis.

lessons.title: Factoring to Solve
takeaways: Find two numbers with product c and sum b.
Positive c, negative b → both negative; negative c → mixed signs.
Set each factor to zero to get the roots.

lessons.title: Special Products, Roots & the Graph
takeaways: x² − a² = (x − a)(x + a), with roots ±a.
Sum of roots = −b; product of roots = c.
Roots are the parabola's x-axis crossings, symmetric about the axis.

lessons.title: Solving by Square Roots
takeaways: x² = k gives x = ±√k — two solutions.
Never forget the negative root.
For (x − h)² = k, take the root then undo the shift.

lessons.title: The Quadratic Formula
takeaways: Compute b² − 4ac first, then apply ±.
Divide the whole numerator by 2a; fractional roots are fine.

lessons.title: The Discriminant
takeaways: D = b² − 4ac; watch the signs.
D > 0 two roots, D = 0 one, D < 0 none.
D = 0 means the parabola touches the x-axis at its vertex.

lessons.title: Projectile Motion
takeaways: Set h = 0 and solve for the launch and landing times.
The axis x = −b/(2a) is the time of maximum height.
Substitute that time back in for the maximum height.

lessons.title: Area Problems
takeaways: Dimensions × dimensions = area gives a quadratic.
Discard the negative root — a length must be positive.
Multiply back to check your dimensions.

lessons.title: Putting It Together
takeaways: Set = 0 and solve for times or dimensions; keep the valid root.
Use the vertex for a maximum or minimum value.
Use the discriminant when you only need the count.

lessons.title: Perfect Squares & Square Roots
takeaways: √ of a perfect square is a whole number (√81 = 9).
Memorize the perfect squares up to 144.
The largest perfect-square factor is the key to simplifying.

lessons.title: Simplifying with Factors
takeaways: Pull out the root of the largest perfect-square factor.
The leftover radicand should have no square factors.

lessons.title: Fully Simplified Form
takeaways: Keep pulling out squares until the radicand is square-free.
An outside coefficient multiplies the root you pull out.
Check every answer for a leftover perfect square.

lessons.title: Adding & Subtracting Like Radicals
takeaways: Like radicals: add or subtract the coefficients, keep the radical.
Unlike radicals can't be combined.
Simplify each radical first to reveal like terms.

lessons.title: Multiplying Radicals
takeaways: Coefficients multiply separately from radicands.
Simplify the product for any perfect square.

lessons.title: Distributing Radicals
takeaways: Each product may become a whole number.
Combine like radicals after simplifying.

lessons.title: Roots as Exponents
takeaways: a^(1/n) = the n-th root of a.
Ask: what number to the n-th power gives a?

lessons.title: The Power/Root Combo
takeaways: Root first keeps the numbers small.
Denominator = root, numerator = power.

lessons.title: Negative Rational Exponents
takeaways: a^(−m/n) = 1/a^(m/n) — take the reciprocal.
Do the root and power first, then flip.
A negative rational exponent gives a fraction below 1.

lessons.title: The Pythagorean Theorem
takeaways: c = √(a² + b²) for a right triangle.
Missing leg: a = √(c² − b²).
Add (or subtract) the squares, then take the root.

lessons.title: When the Answer is a Radical
takeaways: c² = a² + b²; take the root, then simplify.
A square-free radicand like √5 is already the final answer.

lessons.title: Distance Between Points
takeaways: d = √((Δx)² + (Δy)²).
Subtract coordinates to get the legs.
Simplify the radical if the distance isn't whole.

lessons.title: Two-Step Equations
takeaways: Undo operations in reverse order: last on, first off.
Undoing +5 means −5; undoing −5 means +5.
Every move happens to both sides.

lessons.title: Variables on Both Sides
takeaways: Collect x-terms first — subtract the smaller one.
Then it's the two-step routine you know.
Every move hits both sides.

lessons.title: Distribute, Then Solve
takeaways: Distribute to EVERY term, signs included.
Then combine like terms and run the two-step.
Dividing first is a legal shortcut when it's clean.

lessons.title: Equations with One Fraction
takeaways: A fraction is a division — undo it by multiplying.
Isolate the fraction, then clear it.
If you clear first, the multiplier hits EVERY term.

lessons.title: Clear with the LCD
takeaways: The LCD is the smallest number all denominators divide.
The LCD multiplies EVERY term, both sides.
After clearing, it's a whole-number solve.

lessons.title: Decimal Equations
takeaways: ×10 (or 100) shifts every decimal to whole.
Whole numbers shift too — zeros for everyone.
After the shift, it's the two-step you know.

lessons.title: Solving for a Variable
takeaways: Literal equations use the same moves as numeric ones.
Isolate your chosen letter; undo the rest in reverse.
Multiplied factor? Divide it away.

lessons.title: Rearranging with Fractions
takeaways: Clear a fraction first, then isolate your letter.
Subtract added terms before dividing.
Keep the whole numerator together over the divisor.

lessons.title: Multi-Step Literal Equations
takeaways: Undo layers in reverse, clearing fractions early.
Keep numerators together with parentheses.
A rearranged formula evaluates like any other.

lessons.title: Solving Inequalities
takeaways: Use the same moves; the < or > carries along.
The answer is a range, drawn as a ray.
Open circle for < >, filled for ≤ ≥.

lessons.title: The Flip Rule
takeaways: ×/÷ by a negative flips the inequality.
Adding or subtracting never flips.
Spot a negative coefficient before you divide.

lessons.title: Inequalities on Both Sides
takeaways: Collect, isolate, divide — the equation routine.
Flip only when dividing/multiplying by a negative.
Choose the side that keeps x positive to skip the flip.

lessons.title: Systems and Their Solutions
takeaways: A system is two equations solved together; the solution is where the lines cross.
The solution must satisfy every equation — check by substituting into both.
Sitting on just one line is not enough.

lessons.title: Solving by Graphing
takeaways: Draw each line from its y-intercept, stepping by its slope.
The crossing point is the solution — read its x and y.
Confirm the crossing by substituting into both equations.

lessons.title: One, None, or Infinitely Many
takeaways: Different slopes → exactly one solution.
Same slope, different intercept → no solution (parallel).
Same slope and intercept → infinitely many (same line).

lessons.title: Substitution When y Is Alone
takeaways: Replace y in the other equation with the isolated expression.
Solve the one-variable equation, then back-substitute for y.
Check the point in both equations.

lessons.title: Isolate First, Then Substitute
takeaways: Solve one equation for a variable — prefer coefficient 1.
Substitute the whole expression, in parentheses, into the other equation.
Distribute the minus sign carefully into a −y term.

lessons.title: Substitution in Action
takeaways: Isolate a variable, substitute, solve, back-substitute.
Distribute minus signs into substituted expressions.
Always confirm the solution in both equations.

lessons.title: Add or Subtract to Eliminate
takeaways: Opposite coefficients → add; matching coefficients → subtract.
When subtracting, distribute the minus to every term.
Solve the remaining variable, then back-substitute.

lessons.title: Scale One Equation First
takeaways: Multiply a whole equation to match a coefficient — it stays the same line.
Match a coefficient-1 variable by multiplying by the other's coefficient.
Then add (opposite) or subtract (matching) as before.

lessons.title: Scale Both, and Special Cases
takeaways: Multiply each equation to match a coefficient (aim for the LCM).
Both variables cancel to a false statement → no solution; to a true one → infinitely many.
Otherwise solve the remaining variable and back-substitute.

lessons.title: Totals and Differences
takeaways: A total gives x + y = sum; "x is k more than y" gives x − y = k.
A "times as much" fact gives x = (multiple)·y.
Assign x to the larger quantity to keep differences positive.

lessons.title: Counts and Values
takeaways: Count equation: x + y = total items (coefficients 1).
Value equation: price·x + price·y = total worth.
Substitute the count into the value equation and solve.

lessons.title: Choose a Method, Then Interpret
takeaways: Substitution when a variable is isolated; elimination when coefficients match or scale.
The solution is a pair — report the quantity the question wants.
Systems turn two-unknown stories into exact answers.

lessons.title: Central Angles & Arcs
takeaways: Central angle = arc measure, by definition; the full circle is 360°.
Minor (<180°, two letters), major (>180°, three letters), semicircle (exactly 180°).
Adjacent arcs add; ratios split 360° into equal parts.

lessons.title: Inscribed Angles
takeaways: Inscribed angle = half its arc = half the central angle on that arc.
Proof engine: radii make isosceles triangles; the exterior angle doubles at the center.
All inscribed angles on the same arc are congruent — the vertex may roam.

lessons.title: Thales' Theorem
takeaways: Thales: any inscribed angle on a diameter is 90° (half the 180° semicircle).
Converse: a 90° inscribed angle forces its chord to BE a diameter — hypotenuse through the center.
The acute pair are complements, and Pythagoras prices the diameter from the legs.

lessons.title: Chords & Their Arcs
takeaways: Congruent chords ↔ congruent central angles ↔ congruent arcs (SSS/SAS on the radii).
The 60° chord equals the radius — equilateral triangle, hexagon shortcut.
The diameter is the longest chord, cutting the 180° semicircle.

lessons.title: The Perpendicular from the Center
takeaways: The center's perpendicular bisects the chord AND its arc (HL + CPCTC).
Right-triangle engine: (half-chord)² + d² = r² — solve for any missing piece.
Converse: chord perpendicular bisectors pass through the center — two of them FIND it.

lessons.title: Chords & Distance
takeaways: Congruent chords ⇔ equidistant from the center — the engine (chord/2)² + d² = r² is one-to-one.
Closer ⇒ longer, from the diameter (d = 0) down to a point (d = r).
Real circles — tunnels, pipes — are chord problems wearing overalls.

lessons.title: Tangent Meets Radius
takeaways: Tangent line: exactly one shared point; perpendicular to the radius there (and conversely).
Tangent-length engine: PT = √(OP² − r²), right angle always at T.
Horizon sights and wheel contacts are tangent problems in costume.

lessons.title: The Two-Tangent Theorem
takeaways: PT₁ = PT₂ — HL on the radius triangles, CPCTC on the tangents.
OT₁PT₂ is a KITE: right angles at the touch points, so angle P + central = 180°, and OP bisects both.
Tangent segments chain: equal pairs at every external point.

lessons.title: Circumscribed Figures
takeaways: Circumscribed polygon: every side = sum of two adjacent tangent lengths; perimeter = 2(x + y + z).
Reverse: one tangent length + the sides unlocks all the rest.
Incircle center = angle bisectors' meeting (constructions course); right-triangle r = (a + b − c)/2.

lessons.title: Angles Inside & Outside
takeaways: Inside crossing: angle = half the SUM of the facing arcs (the average).
Outside vertex (secants/tangents): angle = half the DIFFERENCE, far minus near.
One story: center = full arc, rim = half, inside = half-sum, outside = half-difference.

lessons.title: The Tangent-Chord Angle
takeaways: Tangent-chord angle = half its intercepted arc — inscribed pricing at the boundary.
The two angles at the tangency point are supplements (arcs sum to 360°).
Diameter chord ⇒ 90°, recovering tangent ⊥ radius; far-side inscribed angles match the tangent-chord angle.

lessons.title: Power of a Point
takeaways: Inside: crossing chords, PA·PB = PC·PD — AA similarity via same-arc inscribed angles.
Outside: secants pair external × WHOLE; the tangent limit gives PT² = external × whole.
The matched product is the POWER of the point — one number for every line through P.

lessons.title: Arc Length
takeaways: Arc length = (θ/360) · 2πr — the degree share of the circumference.
It agrees exactly with trig's s = rθ (radians build the fraction into the unit).
Linear in BOTH θ and r; runs backward to find any missing piece.

lessons.title: Sector Area
takeaways: Sector area = (θ/360) · πr² — the degree share of the whole pie.
Radian form ½r²θ agrees, and reads as ½ · radius · arc.
Linear in θ but QUADRATIC in r — radius doublings quadruple slices.

lessons.title: Cyclic Quadrilaterals
takeaways: Cyclic quadrilateral: opposite angles supplementary — they halve complementary arcs of the full 360°.
The converse holds: supplementary opposite pairs guarantee a circumscribing circle.
Always cyclic from the quadrilateral cast: rectangles, squares, isosceles trapezoids; parallelograms only when they're rectangles.

lessons.title: Why All Circles Are Similar
takeaways: Circumference's '2r' piece is a straight multiple of r — it scales by exactly the same factor as the radius.
Area's 'r²' piece is built from r squared — it scales by the SQUARE of whatever factor the radius scales by.

Because π is the same universal constant for every circle, any two circles' measurements are connected by a single scale factor — which is exactly what makes every pair of circles similar, no conditions to check.

courses.title: Conditional Probability & the Rules of Chance

lessons.title: Events as Sets of Outcomes
takeaways: An event is a subset of the sample space; with equally likely outcomes, P(event) = count ÷ total.
A ∩ B = both at once; A ∪ B = at least one.
|A ∪ B| = |A| + |B| − |A ∩ B| — the overlap is counted twice unless you remove it.

lessons.title: Complements and "At Least One"
takeaways: P(not A) = 1 − P(A) — the complement rule.
The complement of "at least one" is "none", which is a single clean multiplication.
"At least one tail" is **not** the opposite of "at least one head" — complements can never overlap.

lessons.title: Mutually Exclusive vs Overlapping
takeaways: Mutually exclusive = zero shared outcomes = the events cannot co-occur.
For exclusive events, |A ∪ B| = |A| + |B|; otherwise you must subtract the overlap once.
Given a total and a "neither" count, you can solve backwards for the overlap.

lessons.title: The Addition Rule
takeaways: P(A ∪ B) = P(A) + P(B) − P(A ∩ B) — add, then take the overlap back once.
Mutually exclusive events are the special case where the overlap is 0 and plain addition is safe.
Before adding any two probabilities, ask: can both happen at the same time?

lessons.title: Two-Way Tables: Joint and Marginal
takeaways: Joint = one inner cell ÷ grand total. It answers both questions at once.
Marginal = one edge total ÷ grand total. It ignores the other question.
Every cell and every edge shares the same denominator, so the four inner cells sum to 1.

lessons.title: Or, And, Neither — on a Table
takeaways: "Or" on a table = a row plus a column, minus the cell where they cross.
"Neither" is the complement of "or": P(neither) = 1 − P(A ∪ B) — the cell you never shaded.
The rule and the raw cell counts must agree; disagreement means the overlap was mishandled.

lessons.title: Restricting the Sample Space
takeaways: Being told B happened deletes every outcome outside B. What survives is your new world.
P(A | B) = P(A ∩ B)/P(B) — the part of A inside B, over all of B.
The numerator can only shrink or stay the same, but the denominator shrinks too, so a conditional probability can go up or down.

lessons.title: Which Way Round? P(A|B) vs P(B|A)
takeaways: P(A | B) and P(B | A) share a numerator but divide by different groups — they are almost never equal.
The condition is the denominator. Find it before you compute anything.
"Of the X, some fraction are Y" means P(Y | X). Reversing it reverses the meaning.

lessons.title: The Multiplication Rule
takeaways: P(A ∩ B) = P(B) × P(A | B) = P(A) × P(B | A). Pick the conditional you know.
The second factor lives in the world where the first event already happened — that is why deck sizes shrink.
P(A) × P(B) is a special case that needs justifying, not a default.

lessons.title: Trees and Drawing Without Replacement
