takeaways: Multiply along a path (each branch is conditional on the ones before it); add across paths.
Without replacement, the second-stage denominators shrink — that shrinkage *is* the conditioning.
The leaves are mutually exclusive and always sum to 1, which gives you a free check and a complement shortcut.

lessons.title: What Independence Means
takeaways: A and B are independent when P(A | B) = P(A) — learning B moves nothing.
The relation is symmetric: test whichever direction has the easier numbers.
Independence must be checked against the numbers; "they seem unrelated" is not evidence.

lessons.title: The Product Test
takeaways: Independence ⟺ P(A ∩ B) = P(A) × P(B). It is a test, not an assumption.
Any gap between the predicted and the actual cell — surplus or shortfall — means dependence.
Assume independence only when you have a reason; otherwise the product silently invents a number.

lessons.title: Independent vs Mutually Exclusive
takeaways: Mutually exclusive: P(A ∩ B) = 0 and P(A | B) = 0 — maximal dependence, not independence.
Independent: P(A ∩ B) = P(A) × P(B) — the events must overlap, at exactly the product rate.
Exclusive gives an OR shortcut; independent gives an AND shortcut. Two words, two different rules.

lessons.title: Permutations: When Order Matters
takeaways: Fill slots one at a time and multiply the number of choices at each step.
If items cannot repeat, the pool shrinks by one each time — that is nPk, and n! when every item is placed.
Handle any restricted slot first; the free slots then take whatever is left.

lessons.title: Combinations: When Order Doesn't Matter
takeaways: C(n,k) = nPk / k! — count the ordered picks, then divide out the orderings you do not want.
Swap two chosen items: if nothing changes, it is a combination.
Choices made in separate groups multiply: choose the girls, choose the boys, multiply.

lessons.title: Probability by Counting
takeaways: P = favourable count / total count — and both counts must be done in the same style, ordered or unordered.
Split a favourable count into independent choices and multiply them.
For "at least one", count the single failing case and subtract from 1.

lessons.title: The Compass & Straightedge
takeaways: Straightedge draws lines (no marks); compass draws arcs and HOLDS a radius.
Copying a segment works because the compass keeps one unchanged length.
Constructions are recipes whose results are provably exact, not merely measured.

lessons.title: Constructing a Perpendicular Bisector
takeaways: Equal arcs from both endpoints cross at two points; their line is the perpendicular bisector.
Open wider than half so the arcs can meet.
It works because those crossing points are equidistant from A and B — and it gives midpoint AND right angle.

lessons.title: Constructing an Angle Bisector
takeaways: Arc across both sides, then equal arcs from those crossings, then draw the ray.
It works by SSS congruence of the two little triangles.
Bisector points are equidistant from the two SIDES — the angle cousin of the perpendicular bisector.

lessons.title: A Perpendicular at a Point
takeaways: Perpendicular at P: mark equal PA = PB, then arc equal radii from A and B to get Q.
It works because P and Q are both equidistant from A and B — the perpendicular-bisector logic.
It's really bisecting the 180° straight angle: two 90° halves.

lessons.title: A Perpendicular from a Point
takeaways: Perpendicular from P: arc to cut the line at C, D; equal arcs from C, D meet at E; draw PE.
PE is the perpendicular bisector of CD — P and E both equidistant from C and D.
That perpendicular is the shortest path from P, and E is P reflected over the line.

lessons.title: A Parallel through a Point
takeaways: Parallel through P: draw a transversal, then copy its angle to P in the corresponding spot.
Equal corresponding angles ⇒ parallel; alternate interior equal; co-interior sum to 180°.
Through a point off a line, exactly one parallel exists — existence by construction, uniqueness by angles.

lessons.title: Inscribing a Hexagon
takeaways: The circle's radius steps around it exactly six times — the hexagon needs no measuring.
It works because each center triangle (two radii + 60°) is equilateral, so the chord equals r.
Central angle 60°, interior angle 120°; joining alternate vertices gives the inscribed equilateral triangle.

lessons.title: The Square & the Triangle
takeaways: Square: perpendicular diameters → 4 vertices at 90°.
Equilateral triangle: every other hexagon mark → 3 vertices at 120°.
Equal central angles force equal chords — that's what makes each polygon regular.

lessons.title: Why Constructions Work
takeaways: Every arc guarantees equal radii — the seed fact of construction proofs.
Equal radii → congruent triangles (usually SSS) → the equal angles/sides you wanted.
A drawing shows; a proof guarantees — true regardless of drawing error.

lessons.title: Conjecture vs Proof
takeaways: Conjecture = a pattern you suspect; proof = reasoning that makes it certain.
One counterexample disproves a universal; no finite pile of examples proves one.
A proof reasons about all cases at once — which is why constructions need them.

lessons.title: The Two-Column Proof
takeaways: Two columns: every Statement sits beside the Reason that licenses it.
Reasons are givens, definitions, postulates, or already-proven lines — never guesses.
Order backward-only: no line may lean on a fact not yet established.

lessons.title: Proving Vertical Angles Equal
takeaways: Linear pair: two angles on a straight line sum to 180°.
Two linear pairs share an angle; cancelling it proves the vertical angles equal.
Now you can USE ∠1 = ∠3 with confidence — and with algebra.

lessons.title: The Transversal Angle Family
takeaways: A transversal on parallels makes just two angle sizes: a and 180 − a.
Corresponding and alternate pairs are EQUAL; same-side (co-interior) pairs are SUPPLEMENTARY.
Corresponding-angles is the anchor; the rest follow via vertical angles and linear pairs.

lessons.title: Proving the Transversal Theorems
takeaways: Alternate interior proof: corresponding angles + one vertical-angle step + transitivity.
Co-interior proof: alternate interior + one linear-pair step + substitution.
Equal conclusions use vertical angles; supplementary conclusions use linear pairs.

lessons.title: The Converses
takeaways: A converse swaps hypothesis and conclusion — and needs its own proof.
A true statement can have a false converse; the transversal converses happen to be true.
Forward theorems compute angles from parallels; converses prove parallels from angles.

lessons.title: The Distance Formula
takeaways: d = √((Δx)² + (Δy)²) — Pythagoras on the run-rise triangle.
Squares erase signs: distance is symmetric and unsigned.
Shared axis ⇒ just the coordinate gap; unknowns ⇒ square both sides and mind the ±.

lessons.title: The Midpoint Formula
takeaways: M = ((x₁ + x₂)/2, (y₁ + y₂)/2) — each coordinate splits its own gap.
Invert for endpoints: B = 2M − A.
The similar-triangle ratio 1/2 is why the halves synchronize — and diagonal-bisection puzzles already yield.

lessons.title: Distances at Work
takeaways: Classify triangles by MEASURING sides (isosceles: two distances match).
The Pythagorean converse on squared sides detects right angles without a protractor.
Axis-aligned sides cost one subtraction — which is why proofs place figures on the axes.

lessons.title: Partitioning a Segment
takeaways: P = A + k(B − A) with k = m/(m + n) — the m : n point measured FROM A.
Similar triangles guarantee the coordinate walk matches the segment ratio.
Direction is part of the ratio; midpoints are the k = 1/2 special case.

lessons.title: Parallel, Proved
takeaways: Translation carries a slope triangle intact between parallel lines: parallel ⇒ equal slopes.
Uniqueness (one point, one slope, one line) proves the converse — and upgrades shared-point equal slopes to collinearity.
Parallelogram completion: copy the displacement, and both slope pairs follow.

lessons.title: Perpendicular, Proved
takeaways: Rotating (a, b) to (−b, a) proves perpendicular slopes multiply to −1.
Complete test: product −1, OR vertical-meets-horizontal (the undefined exception).
Right angles, altitudes, and axis intercepts all fall to slope arithmetic — no protractor.

lessons.title: Classifying Triangles
takeaways: Side audit (squared distances): scalene / isosceles / equilateral — no roots needed.
Angle audit: slope product −1 OR Pythagorean converse — two independent right-angle certificates.
A coordinate proof = the numbers plus the definition they satisfy.

lessons.title: Classifying Quadrilaterals
takeaways: Base layer: parallelogram by slope pairs OR coinciding diagonal midpoints (usually fastest).
Upgrades: equal sides ⇒ rhombus; equal diagonals or a −1 slope product ⇒ rectangle; both ⇒ square.
Always the most specific name — with the computations as receipts.

lessons.title: Proofs for Every Figure
takeaways: General placement (origin + axes + symmetry) turns one computation into a theorem for every figure.
Varignon: side midpoints of ANY quadrilateral form a parallelogram — midsegments copy the diagonals at half length.
Special parents pass traits down: congruent diagonals (rectangle) ⇒ midpoint rhombus.

lessons.title: Perimeter on the Plane
takeaways: Perimeter = ordered sum of side distances — n vertices, n sides, home again.
Keep radicals exact (√20 = 2√5); decimalize once, at the end.
Axis-aligned sides are free reads; diagonals go through the distance formula.

lessons.title: Area by the Box Method
takeaways: Bounding box minus right-triangle corners — every cut has axis-aligned legs.
Cross-check areas by a second route (legs, g7 formulas): agreement is the proof of work.
The 44-area quadrilateral awaits a one-line method…

lessons.title: The Shoelace Formula
takeaways: Shoelace: ½|Σ(xᵢyᵢ₊₁ − xᵢ₊₁yᵢ)|, vertices in boundary order, wrap at the end.
Signed origin-triangles explain it; reversal flips sign (harmless), scrambling crosses the path (fatal).
Varignon bonus: the midpoint parallelogram holds exactly HALF its parent's area.

lessons.title: The Circle's Equation
takeaways: (x − h)² + (y − k)² = r² — chapter 1's distance formula wearing an equals sign.
Read carefully: the equation SUBTRACTS the center (signs flip out) and stores r SQUARED.
Build from center + point (r² by distance) or a diameter (center by midpoint, r by half).

lessons.title: On, Inside, Outside
takeaways: Substitute, then compare to r²: equal = on, less = inside, greater = outside.
No roots — squared distances rank exactly like distances (chapter 3's discipline).
Design radii by pinning a boundary point: r² = that point's evaluation.

lessons.title: Circles in Disguise
takeaways: Complete the square (from Algebra) to convert x² + y² + Dx + Ey + F = 0 into center-radius form.
The unmasked form feeds every earlier tool: position judging, distance, midpoint, tangency.
Line-meets-circle = substitute and solve; the root count IS the secant/tangent/miss trichotomy.

lessons.title: The Words We Don't Define
takeaways: Point, line, plane are described, never defined — they're the agreed starting stock.
Lines are named by any two points, in either order; collinear = on one line.
Exactly one line through two points = it exists AND no second one does.

lessons.title: Building Definitions
takeaways: Segment = two endpoints; ray = one endpoint, one direction (endpoint written FIRST).
A circle is a distance test: all points at exactly r from the center.
Angle names put the vertex in the middle; outer letters come one from each ray.

lessons.title: Symbols That Say Different Things
takeaways: Hats pick the object: line, ray, or segment; no hat = the length, a number.
Numbers take =; figures take ≅ — and m∠A is the number, ∠A the figure.
Intersections drop a rung: planes share a line, lines share at most a point.

lessons.title: Segment Addition & Midpoints
takeaways: Coordinates turn distance into arithmetic: PQ = positive difference.
B between A and C ⇒ AB + BC = AC — pieces tile the whole.
Midpoint = average of endpoint coordinates; half ↔ whole by doubling.

lessons.title: Angle Addition & Bisectors
takeaways: Interior ray ⇒ m∠PQR + m∠RQS = m∠PQS — piece + piece = whole.
A bisector's pieces are CONGRUENT: halve the whole, double a half.
For a missing piece, first name the whole — right angle 90°, straight angle 180°.

lessons.title: Algebra Meets Geometry
takeaways: "Between/interior" ⇒ pieces ADD to the whole; "bisects/midpoint" ⇒ pieces are EQUAL.
Solving for x is halfway — substitute back for the length or measure asked.
Sanity check every answer: the pieces must really rebuild the whole.

lessons.title: Translations as Functions
takeaways: A transformation is a function: preimage in, image (with a prime) out.
Translation rule slots act on their own letters: (x + a, y + b).
Find a rule by image − preimage; chain rules by ADDING shifts.

lessons.title: Reflections as Functions
takeaways: x-axis: (x, −y); y-axis: (−x, y) — flip the coordinate that measures distance to the axis.
y = x: swap the coordinates, no sign changes.
The mirror line is the perpendicular bisector of every PP′ — and its own points are fixed.

lessons.title: Rotations as Functions
takeaways: CCW rules: 90° (−y, x) · 180° (−x, −y) · 270° (y, −x) — positive means counterclockwise.
270° CCW and 90° CW are the same turn in different words.
Rotations compose by ADDING angles: 90 then 90 is 180.

lessons.title: Composing Rigid Motions
takeaways: A composition feeds one motion's output into the next — and rigid chains stay rigid.
Order can matter: test a point through both orders before assuming it doesn't.
Glide reflection = slide + mirror over a line parallel to the slide — the last rigid motion in the cast.

lessons.title: Line Symmetry
takeaways: Line symmetry = a reflection mapping the shape onto ITSELF; test by folding.
Regular n-gon: exactly n lines; circle: infinitely many; scalene: none.
Diagonals mirror the SQUARE but not the rectangle — the classic miscount.

lessons.title: Rotational Symmetry
takeaways: Rotational symmetry: some turn under 360° maps the shape onto itself.
order × smallest angle = 360° — each dial reads from the other.
Mirrors and turns are independent: the parallelogram turns but never folds.

lessons.title: Congruence, Defined
takeaways: Congruent = some rigid motion maps one figure exactly onto the other.
Rigid motions preserve distance AND angle — so all parts match for free.
Dilations change distances: same shape, different size — similarity, not congruence.

lessons.title: Find the Motion
takeaways: Read the pattern: constant shifts = translation; sign flips/swaps = mirrors and turns.
Confirm the candidate on EVERY point — one point can lie.
Unequal distances end the case: no rigid motion, no congruence.

lessons.title: Corresponding Parts
takeaways: Letter order encodes the pairing: 1st↔1st, 2nd↔2nd, 3rd↔3rd — trust it over any picture.
Measurements teleport only between POSITIONAL partners.
Rewrites must drag partners to matching slots: ΔCAB ≅ ΔFDE.

lessons.title: The Interior Angle Sum
takeaways: Fanning from one vertex splits an n-gon into n − 2 triangles.
Interior angle sum = (n − 2) × 180°; reverse it with n = sum/180 + 2.
A missing angle is the total sum minus the angles in hand.

lessons.title: Exterior Angles: One Full Lap
takeaways: Exterior angles of any polygon sum to 360° — walking the boundary is one full turn.
At each vertex, interior + exterior = 180° (straight line).
Regular polygon: n × (each exterior) = 360, so n = 360 ÷ exterior.

lessons.title: Regular Polygons
takeaways: Regular n-gon: each interior = (n − 2) × 180/n; each exterior = 360/n.
Reversing from an interior angle: supplement first, then n = 360/exterior.
Tilings work when corner angles divide 360° — triangles, squares, hexagons.

lessons.title: Opposite Sides
takeaways: Definition: both pairs of opposite sides parallel — everything else is proved.
One diagonal + alternate interior angles + ASA ⇒ two congruent triangles ⇒ opposite sides congruent (CPCTC).
Equal opposite sides turn side-expressions into solvable equations.

lessons.title: Opposite & Consecutive Angles
takeaways: Opposite angles of a parallelogram are congruent (CPCTC again).
Consecutive angles are supplementary — co-interior between the parallel rails.
Given one angle: opposite copies it, both neighbors supplement it, and all four total 360°.

lessons.title: The Diagonals Bisect Each Other
takeaways: Parallelogram diagonals bisect each other: AO = OC and BO = OD.
They need NOT be equal, perpendicular, or angle-bisecting — those are rectangle/rhombus upgrades.
Midpoint equalities turn diagonal expressions into equations; remember to answer for the length asked.

lessons.title: Rectangles
takeaways: Rectangle = parallelogram + one right angle; supplements spread it to all four.
New property: congruent diagonals (bisection is inherited) — all four half-diagonals equal.
The diagonal is a hypotenuse: √(w² + ℓ²), Pythagoras style.

lessons.title: Rhombi
takeaways: Rhombus = parallelogram + all sides congruent; perimeter = 4 × side.
Diagonals: perpendicular AND vertex-angle-bisecting (bisection of each other is inherited).
Half-diagonals + side form right triangles — Pythagoras converts between them.

lessons.title: Squares
takeaways: Square = rectangle ∩ rhombus: all right angles AND all congruent sides.
Diagonals inherit everything: congruent, perpendicular, mutually bisecting, corner-splitting into 45°s.
s√2 converts side to diagonal; divide by √2 to go back.

lessons.title: Trapezoids
takeaways: Trapezoid (our convention): EXACTLY one parallel pair; bases parallel, legs not.
Along each leg, base angles are supplementary — the surviving transversal fact.
Isosceles trapezoids add congruent base-angle pairs and congruent diagonals.

lessons.title: The Trapezoid Midsegment
takeaways: Midsegment: joins the legs' midpoints; parallel to both bases; m = (b₁ + b₂)/2.
Backward form: missing base = 2m − known base.
Shrink one base to 0 and the triangle midsegment theorem falls out — same idea, matured.

lessons.title: Kites
takeaways: Kite: two pairs of congruent CONSECUTIVE sides; symmetry along one diagonal.
Diagonals perpendicular; the axis bisects the cross diagonal (one-way); non-vertex angles congruent.
Area = ½·d₁·d₂ — half the diagonal bounding box (rhombi included).

lessons.title: Proving a Parallelogram
takeaways: Tests: both side pairs ≅, both angle pairs ≅, diagonals mutually bisect, or ONE pair both ≅ and ∥.
The mixed-pairs shortcut fails — the isosceles trapezoid is the standing counterexample.
Equal rods crossing at midpoints = rectangle: tests stack with ch3 upgrades.

lessons.title: Always, Sometimes, Never
takeaways: Up the tree: always. Down the tree: sometimes. Across disjoint branches: never (exclusive convention).
The square holds dual citizenship: always a rectangle AND always a rhombus.
Regular quadrilateral = square: ch1's angle formula meets the hierarchy.

lessons.title: The Quadrilateral Capstone
takeaways: Marks first: what's the MOST SPECIFIC name the evidence forces?
Opposite pairs → parallelogram family; consecutive pairs → kite; one parallel pair + congruent legs → isosceles trapezoid.
The certified name unlocks exactly its theorems — never compute past the evidence.

lessons.title: The Pythagorean Theorem
takeaways: a² + b² = c² — and c is always the hypotenuse, the longest side.
Missing hypotenuse: add the leg-squares. Missing leg: subtract from the hypotenuse-square.
Rectangles' diagonals, ladders, and straight-line distances all hide right triangles.

lessons.title: The Converse & Classifying Triangles
takeaways: Converse: a² + b² = c² certifies a right angle from side lengths alone.
c² < a² + b² → acute; c² > a² + b² → obtuse; equality → right.
Triples (3-4-5, 5-12-13, 8-15-17…) and their multiples are instant right triangles.

lessons.title: 45-45-90 Triangles
takeaways: 45-45-90 sides always sit in the ratio 1 : 1 : √2.
Leg → hypotenuse: multiply by √2. Hypotenuse → leg: divide by √2.
A square's diagonal = side × √2 — the classic appearance.

lessons.title: 30-60-90 Triangles
takeaways: 30-60-90 sides sit in the ratio 1 : √3 : 2 (short : long : hypotenuse).
Route conversions through the short leg: hyp ÷ 2, short × √3, long ÷ √3.
An equilateral triangle's altitude = (side/2)·√3.

lessons.title: Sine, Cosine & Tangent
takeaways: Similar right triangles (AA) make each side ratio depend on the ANGLE alone.
SOH-CAH-TOA: sin = opp/hyp, cos = adj/hyp, tan = opp/adj — all measured from θ.
Swap acute angles and opposite/adjacent swap: sin of one = cos of the other.

lessons.title: Finding a Side
takeaways: Pick the ratio containing exactly your known side and your unknown side.
Unknown on top → multiply; unknown on the bottom (hypotenuse) → divide.
Sanity check: the hypotenuse is always the longest side.

lessons.title: Finding an Angle
takeaways: sin⁻¹, cos⁻¹, tan⁻¹ each undo their ratio: feed the ratio, receive the angle.
Match the inverse to the side pair you actually have — legs only means tan⁻¹.
Acute angles sum to 90°: one inverse computation unlocks both.

lessons.title: Solving Right Triangles Completely
takeaways: Angle + side: trig ratios give the missing sides; 90°-complement gives the angle.
Two sides: Pythagoras → third side; inverse trig → an angle; complement → the last.
Always audit with a² + b² = c² and the longest-side rule.

lessons.title: Angles of Elevation & Depression
takeaways: Elevation looks up, depression looks down — both from the HORIZONTAL, never the vertical.
Depression from A to B = elevation from B to A (alternate interior angles).
Height + horizontal distance are legs, so tangent usually runs the show.

lessons.title: Height Problems
takeaways: Sketch, mark the horizontal, label sides FROM the angle — then it's ordinary solving.
Instruments read from eye level: add eye height for total height.
Strings, ladders, and sight lines are hypotenuses (sine/cosine); ground-and-height pairs are legs (tangent).

lessons.title: Shadows, Wires & Surveys
takeaways: Shadows: tan(sun angle) = height/shadow — solve for either piece.
Wires and cables are hypotenuses: divide by sine (or cosine) to size them.
Two readings from different spots pin an unreachable height: equate the two h-expressions.

lessons.title: How the Ratios Relate
takeaways: Quotient: tan θ = sin θ / cos θ — the hypotenuses cancel.
Pythagorean: sin²θ + cos²θ = 1 — one ratio determines the other.
Cofunction: sin θ = cos(90° − θ) — complements trade sine for cosine.

lessons.title: The Law of Sines
takeaways: a/sin A = b/sin B = c/sin C in EVERY triangle — sides scale with opposite sines.
One matched side-angle pair anchors the ratio; the 180° sum supplies missing angles.
Audit: biggest side faces biggest angle.

lessons.title: The Law of Cosines
takeaways: SAS: c² = a² + b² − 2ab·cos C, with C the INCLUDED angle.
SSS: cos C = (a² + b² − c²)/(2ab); a negative cosine flags an obtuse angle.
At C = 90° the correction dies and Pythagoras returns.

lessons.title: Choosing the Tool & Trig Area
takeaways: Right angle → SOH-CAH-TOA / Pythagoras. Matched side-angle pair → Law of Sines. SAS or SSS → Law of Cosines.
Area = ½·a·b·sin C — the included sine builds the height for free.
Every tool here is similarity's child: the angle fixes the ratio, and the ratio measures the world.

lessons.title: Dilations & Scale Factor
takeaways: A dilation scales distances from a center: OP′ = k·OP.
It preserves angles and shape; lengths scale by k, so the image is similar.
k > 1 enlarges, 0 < k < 1 reduces; from the origin, multiply both coordinates by k.

lessons.title: What Similarity Means
takeaways: Similar (~): corresponding angles equal, corresponding sides proportional.
Congruence is similarity with scale factor 1; the ratio links every side pair.
Perimeter scales by k, area by k² — the squared growth is easy to forget.

lessons.title: The AA Criterion
takeaways: AA: two pairs of equal angles ⇒ similar triangles (the third angle follows).
Similarity needs no side; it gives same shape, not necessarily same size.
AA powers indirect measurement — shadows and reflections share angles.

lessons.title: The SAS Similarity Criterion
takeaways: SAS~: two proportional sides + the included angle equal ⇒ similar.
It follows from dilation: scale the small triangle and it matches by SAS congruence.
Ideal for nested/overlapping triangles that share the included angle.

lessons.title: The SSS Similarity Criterion
takeaways: SSS~: all three side pairs in the SAME ratio ⇒ similar (no angle needed).
Pair smallest-to-smallest, largest-to-largest before dividing.
Congruent SSS is the special case with ratio 1.

lessons.title: Choosing a Criterion
takeaways: AA for angles, SAS~ for two sides + included angle, SSS~ for three sides.
Free parts: shared angles (reflexive), parallel-line angles.
Prove similar, then write and solve a proportion for the unknown.

lessons.title: The Side-Splitter Theorem
takeaways: Side-Splitter: a line ∥ one side cuts the others in equal ratios (AD/DB = AE/EC).
It works because the parallel creates a similar triangle (AA).
Match ratio styles; the midsegment is the 1 : 1 special case.

lessons.title: The Converse & Parallel Lines
takeaways: Converse: a proportional split ⇒ the line is parallel to the third side.
Three parallel lines cut transversals in equal ratios.
Angle Bisector Theorem: BD/DC = AB/AC — the same proportional idea.

lessons.title: Proportions in Figures
takeaways: Read the marks: parallel ⇒ side-splitter, bisector ⇒ adjacent-side ratio, angles ⇒ similarity.
Anchor correspondence on equal angles before writing ratios.
Identify config → name theorem → one proportion → solve.

lessons.title: Three Similar Triangles
takeaways: The altitude to the hypotenuse makes two small triangles, each similar to the whole (AA).
All three share angles, so they're similar — same shape, different sizes.
This configuration even proves the Pythagorean theorem.

lessons.title: The Geometric Mean
takeaways: Geometric mean of a, b is √(ab) — where a/x = x/b.
Altitude = geometric mean of the two hypotenuse segments: h = √(p·q).
Leg = geometric mean of the whole hypotenuse and its adjacent segment: √(hyp × adj).

lessons.title: Solving Right Triangles
takeaways: Altitude from the two segments; each leg from the hypotenuse and its adjacent segment.
Sketch and label p, q, and the hypotenuse before choosing a relationship.
Cross-check the result with the Pythagorean theorem.

lessons.title: Indirect Measurement
takeaways: Shadows: person and object make similar triangles by AA (right angle + sun-ray angle).
Mirrors: equal reflection angles make similar triangles even in shade.
Match height↔height and shadow↔shadow, write one proportion, solve.

lessons.title: Scale Drawings & Models
takeaways: Scale drawings are similar copies; multiply drawing × scale for reality, divide to reverse.
Maps, blueprints, and models all use a stated length ratio.
Length scales by the ratio, AREA by its square, volume by its cube.

lessons.title: Area & Perimeter Ratios
takeaways: Perimeter (and any length) scales by k; area scales by k².
To get the side ratio from an area ratio, take the square root.
This is why a 16-inch pizza is four times an 8-inch one, not twice.

lessons.title: Dilations and Parallel Lines
takeaways: A segment not passing through the centre of dilation comes out parallel to its original direction.
Dilation changes every length by the scale factor k, but preserves every angle exactly.
The parallel property holds for any scale factor and any centre — the only requirement is that the segment misses the centre.

lessons.title: Cross-Sections, Formalized
takeaways: Cylinder: circle (parallel to base), rectangle (parallel to axis), ellipse (slant).
Cone: shrinking circles, apex-cut triangle, slant ellipses. Sphere: circles ALWAYS, greatest through the center.
Off-center sphere slices obey r²ₛₗᵢᶜₑ = R² − d² — Pythagoras inside the solid.

lessons.title: Solids of Revolution
takeaways: Rectangle (side on axis) → cylinder; right triangle (leg on axis) → cone; semicircle (diameter on axis) → sphere.
The AXIS is part of the problem: swapping legs swaps 100π for 240π.
Offset regions sweep holes — rings and tubes, priced later by subtraction.

lessons.title: Reasoning from Sections
takeaways: Patterns identify: constant circles ⇒ cylinder, shrinking ⇒ cone (similarity runs the rate), all-circles ⇒ sphere.
A great circle exposes the true radius; off-center slices pay π(R² − d²).
Constant slice RATIOS (circle-in-square = π/4) will become volume ratios next.

lessons.title: Cavalieri's Principle
takeaways: Cavalieri: same height + equal cross-sections at EVERY level ⇒ equal volumes.
Oblique prisms and cylinders cost the same as their upright twins — V = Bh with VERTICAL height.
Slant edges are decoys: extract h by Pythagoras before any volume recall.

lessons.title: Cavalieri at Work
takeaways: Constant section ratio k at every level ⇒ volume ratio k (the π/4 cylinder-in-prism).
Oblique cones inherit the ⅓ for free; curvy solids with known sections price like their straight twins.
The method: align heights, relate sections at every level, conclude.

lessons.title: What Cavalieri Doesn't Say
takeaways: Cavalieri certifies volume ONLY — shearing preserves volume but grows lateral surface (12 → 13 per side).
The converse fails: equal volumes never promise matching slices (post vs block).
'Every level' is strict — barrels beat end-matched cylinders in the unchecked middle.

lessons.title: Prism to Cylinder
takeaways: Cylinder volume = Bh, justified: constant sections + Cavalieri against any equal-base prism.
The argument covers oblique cylinders and ANY constant-section solid (tunnels, troughs).
Half or partial sections scale the price by their ratio.

lessons.title: The One-Third Story
takeaways: Seed: a cube tiles into THREE congruent pyramids — ⅓Bh is a tiling fact.
Spread: similarity shrinks all pyramid/cone sections by (z/h)² — Cavalieri transfers the ⅓ everywhere, oblique included.
Leftover: cylinder minus cone = ⅔ — remember its ring sections.

lessons.title: The Sphere Surrenders
takeaways: Slice identity: hemisphere disk π(r² − h²) = drilled-cylinder ring πr² − πh² at every height.
Cavalieri: hemisphere = cylinder − cone = ⅔πr³; doubling gives V = (4/3)πr³.
Every recall from Grade 8 is now a theorem — slice law + Cavalieri + the ⅓.

lessons.title: Adding Solids
takeaways: Composite volume = sum of the pieces across clean (matched-radius) seams.
Standard compounds: silo (cylinder + hemisphere), capsule (cylinder + sphere-in-two-halves), ice-cream (cone + hemisphere).
Reverse problems: subtract known pieces to expose the unknown dimension.

lessons.title: Subtracting Solids
takeaways: Hollow volume = outer minus removed: tubes π(R² − r²)h, bores, carved cavities.
R² − r², never (R − r)² — areas subtract, radii don't.
Bends are free (Cavalieri); mixed exact-and-π answers are normal bookkeeping.

lessons.title: Surfaces of Composites
takeaways: New prices: sphere 4πr² (dome 2πr²), cylinder wall 2πrh (an unrolled rectangle).
Seam circles count ZERO times — interior faces never bill.
Hollows expose extra faces: tubes bill outer + inner walls + end rings.

lessons.title: k, k-Squared, k-Cubed
takeaways: Lengths ×k, areas/surfaces ×k², volumes/capacities/masses ×k³ — sort the quantity before scaling.
Formulas encode it: r³ in the sphere is the k³ law in algebra.
Run it backwards with roots: volume ratio 27 ⇒ length ratio ∛27 = 3.

lessons.title: Density & Design
takeaways: Density = mass ÷ volume: the material's identity card (steel 7.8, water 1, pine 0.6).
Mass = density × justified volume; float when average density < 1 (hollowing lowers it — ships).
Density is scale-invariant: k³ over k³.

lessons.title: Modeling with Solids
takeaways: Surface costs (paint, metal, heat): k². Volume costs (capacity, fill, weight): k³.
Surface-to-volume falls as 1/k — big tanks are cheap per liter, small animals eat constantly.
Design inverts the formulas: capacity ⇒ r by roots.

lessons.title: Shortcuts to Congruence
takeaways: A criterion guarantees a rigid motion exists without checking all 6 parts.
SSS (3 sides), SAS (2 sides + INCLUDED angle), ASA (2 angles + INCLUDED side).
AAS reduces to ASA because two angles determine the third.

lessons.title: The One That Fails
takeaways: SSA is ambiguous — a side can swing to two positions, giving two triangles.
AAA gives similar (same shape, any size), never guaranteed congruent.
Valid criteria: SSS, SAS, ASA, AAS — each has at least one side.

lessons.title: Criteria & CPCTC
takeaways: A congruence proof: first a criterion (SSS/SAS/ASA/AAS), then CPCTC for the parts.
CPCTC is valid only AFTER congruence is established.
Match corresponding parts by letter POSITION, not by the picture.

lessons.title: The Hypotenuse-Leg Criterion
takeaways: HL: a right angle, equal hypotenuse, and one equal leg ⇒ congruent.
It escapes SSA ambiguity because Pythagoras forces the second leg uniquely.
HL is SAS in disguise — two legs with the included right angle.

lessons.title: Proof Practice with CPCTC
takeaways: Embed target parts in two triangles, prove congruence, then release with CPCTC.
Free parts: shared sides (reflexive), vertical angles, right angles.
CPCTC unlocks only parts NOT already used in the congruence proof.

lessons.title: Overlapping Triangles
takeaways: Overlapping triangles: pull them apart; the shared side or angle is reflexively equal.
Two-step proofs relay a CPCTC part from the first congruence into the second.
Plan backward: find the triangles holding the target, then what proves them congruent.

lessons.title: The Isosceles Base Angles Theorem
takeaways: Base Angles Theorem: equal legs ⇒ equal base angles (opposite those legs).
Proof: bisect the apex angle → two SAS-congruent triangles → CPCTC.
The apex segment is bisector, median, altitude, and perpendicular bisector all at once.

lessons.title: The Converse & Equilateral Triangles
takeaways: Converse: equal base angles ⇒ equal legs (proves a triangle isosceles from angles).
Equilateral ⇔ equiangular for triangles; each angle is 60°.
The equilateral-equiangular equivalence is special to triangles.

lessons.title: The Midsegment Theorem
takeaways: A midsegment joins two side-midpoints; it's parallel to the third side and half its length.
The third side is double the midsegment; the midpoint triangle has half the perimeter.
Three midsegments split a triangle into four congruent half-scale triangles.

lessons.title: Circumcenter & Incenter
takeaways: Circumcenter: perpendicular bisectors meet; equidistant from vertices; center of circumscribed circle.
Incenter: angle bisectors meet; equidistant from sides; center of inscribed circle.
Incenter is always inside; circumcenter can fall outside an obtuse triangle.

lessons.title: Centroid & Orthocenter
takeaways: Centroid: medians meet; balance point; 2:1 split; coordinates = vertex average.
Orthocenter: altitudes meet; no equidistance property; can fall outside.
Circumcenter, centroid, orthocenter are collinear on the Euler line.

lessons.title: Choosing the Right Center
takeaways: Lines: perp bisectors→circumcenter, angle bisectors→incenter, medians→centroid, altitudes→orthocenter.
Properties: circum=equidistant from vertices, in=equidistant from sides, centroid=balance point.
Always inside: centroid and incenter; circumcenter and orthocenter can fall outside (obtuse).

lessons.title: The Triangle Inequality
takeaways: Triangle Inequality: any two sides must sum to more than the third.
Third side is bounded: |a − b| < third < a + b.
Largest angle sits opposite the largest side.

lessons.title: The Hinge Theorem
takeaways: Hinge Theorem: equal two sides, larger included angle ⇒ longer third side.
It's the SAS inequality — equal angle gives equal (SAS congruence), bigger angle gives bigger.
Converse: longer third side ⇒ larger included angle.

lessons.title: Inequalities in Proofs
takeaways: Within one triangle: bigger side ⇔ bigger opposite angle.
Exterior angle inequality: an exterior angle exceeds either remote interior (it equals their sum).
Across two triangles sharing two sides: the hinge theorem compares third sides.

lessons.title: Building a Perfect Square
takeaways: (x + p)² = x² + 2px + p², so the constant is (b/2)².
The sign of b vanishes when squared — the constant is always positive.
The number inside the folded square is b/2, sign intact.

lessons.title: Completing the Square to Solve
takeaways: The added constant goes to BOTH sides of the equation.
The left side folds to (x + b/2)²; square roots finish it.
x = −b/2 ± √k — two roots, symmetric around −b/2.

lessons.title: Vertex Form by Completing the Square
takeaways: On an expression (not an equation), compensate on the SAME side: +9 − 9.
Vertex form hands you the vertex and the max/min instantly.
The y-intercept (x = 0 value) is NOT the vertex height.

lessons.title: Meet i
takeaways: i² = −1 by definition.
√(−k) = i√k: pull the −1 out as i.
x² = −k has the two solutions ±i√k.

lessons.title: Powers of i
takeaways: i¹ = i, i² = −1, i³ = −i, i⁴ = 1, then repeat.
For iⁿ, only the remainder of n ÷ 4 matters.
Remainder 0 means a whole number of laps: the value is 1.

lessons.title: Complex Numbers & the Plane
takeaways: Real part a and imaginary part b are both plain real numbers.
Purely real numbers live on the horizontal axis; purely imaginary on the vertical.
The imaginary PART of a + bi is b, not bi.

lessons.title: Adding & Subtracting
takeaways: (a + bi) ± (c + di) = (a ± c) + (b ± d)i.
A minus sign distributes to BOTH parts of the second number.
a + bi is already simplified — the parts are unlike terms.

lessons.title: Multiplying Complex Numbers
takeaways: (a + bi)(c + di) = (ac − bd) + (ad + bc)i.
Pure imaginary × pure imaginary = real (sign flipped).
The i² term is the one everyone forgets — it changes the REAL part.

lessons.title: Conjugates & Division
takeaways: Conjugate of a + bi is a − bi — flip only the imaginary sign.
(a + bi)(a − bi) = a² + b², always real, never negative.
To divide: multiply top and bottom by the bottom's conjugate, then split the parts.

lessons.title: Square Roots of Negatives in Equations
takeaways: x² = −k gives x = ±i√k — two purely imaginary roots.
(x − h)² = −k gives x = h ± i√k — real center h, imaginary spread.
Complex roots verify by substitution, with i² = −1 doing the work.

lessons.title: The Formula Goes Complex
takeaways: D < 0 gives √D = i√|D| and a conjugate pair of roots.
The ÷2a divides BOTH the real and imaginary parts.
x = −b/(2a) ± (√|D|/(2a))i — center and spread.

lessons.title: The Full Discriminant Story
takeaways: D > 0: two distinct real roots; D = 0: one repeated; D < 0: a conjugate pair.
'No real solutions' really means 'both solutions went complex'.
D = 0 designs perfect squares: b² = 4ac.

lessons.title: Sum & Product with Complex Roots
takeaways: a ± bi sums to 2a and multiplies to a² + b².
Both results are real — that's why real-coefficient quadratics can host complex roots.
Sign trap: sum = MINUS b.

lessons.title: Building Quadratics from Roots
takeaways: Sum 2a → middle term −2a·x; product a² + b² → constant.
One complex root of a real quadratic reveals the other: its conjugate.
Verify builds by substitution — the cancellation is exact.

lessons.title: Choosing the Best Method
takeaways: Bare square → roots; friendly factors → factor; even b → complete; always → formula.
D < 0 predicts a conjugate pair before any solving starts.
Dividing by a first often simplifies everything.

lessons.title: A Number Attached to Chance
takeaways: A random variable assigns a number to each outcome of a chance experiment.
Its possible values are fixed by the experiment and should be listed first.
Several outcomes may share one value, so values are rarely equally likely.

lessons.title: The Probability Distribution
takeaways: A distribution pairs every possible value with its probability.
Probabilities are never negative and must total exactly 1.
Disjoint values add, so a missing entry is recoverable from the rest.

lessons.title: The Long-Run Average
takeaways: Expected value multiplies each value by its probability and adds: a weighted average.
It need not be a possible outcome — a fair die expects 3.5.
It always lies between the smallest and largest possible values.

lessons.title: Computing Payoffs
takeaways: The cost to play is a negative payoff and must be netted into every outcome.
Expected net multiplies each net payoff by its probability and adds.
The sign says who the game favours; the size says by how much per play.

lessons.title: Is the Game Fair?
takeaways: A fair game has expected net exactly 0.
Win frequency is irrelevant — a 1-in-10 game is fair if it pays 9 to 1.
Setting expectation to zero solves for the fair payout or price.

lessons.title: Deciding by Expectation
takeaways: Expectation compares repeated options; over many plays the higher expected value wins.
It scales with repetitions: n plays expect n times the per-play value.
It ignores risk of ruin and non-monetary value, which is why negative-expectation insurance is rational.

lessons.title: Meet the Parent Functions
takeaways: The parents: y = x, y = x², y = |x|, y = √x, y = x³.
|x| has a sharp corner; x² is the smooth look-alike; √x only takes x ≥ 0.
Every later function is a parent moved, flipped, or stretched.

lessons.title: Domain: the Allowed Inputs
takeaways: Polynomials accept every real number.
Square root: set the inside ≥ 0 and solve.
Fraction: exclude any x that zeroes the denominator.

lessons.title: Range: the Possible Outputs
takeaways: x², |x|, and √x all have range y ≥ 0; x and x³ hit every real y.
A vertical shift moves the range's floor by the same amount.
A flip (−x²) turns the floor into a ceiling.

lessons.title: Vertical Shifts
takeaways: f(x) + k slides the graph up k; f(x) − k slides it down k.
Every point moves equally — compute the parent, then shift.
The shape never changes; only the position does.

lessons.title: Horizontal Shifts
takeaways: f(x − h) slides right h; f(x + h) slides left h.
The key point lands where the inside equals 0.
Evaluate inside-out: shift the input, then apply the parent.

lessons.title: Combining Shifts
takeaways: y = (x − h)² + k has its vertex at (h, k).
The vertex height is the minimum for an upward-opening graph.
Vertical shifts never change the domain; the inside does.

lessons.title: Reflections
takeaways: y = −f(x): every (x, y) becomes (x, −y).
y = f(−x): every (x, y) becomes (−x, y).
Compute the parent first, then apply a front minus.

lessons.title: Stretches & Compressions
takeaways: y = a·f(x): apply the parent first, then multiply by a.
|a| > 1 stretches (steeper); 0 < |a| < 1 compresses (wider).
Negative a stretches AND flips in one move.

lessons.title: Reading the Full Rule
takeaways: y = a(x − h)² + k: three dials, one graph.
The vertex is (h, k); negative a makes it a maximum.
Evaluate inside-out: subtract h, square, multiply by a, add k.

lessons.title: Adding & Subtracting Functions
takeaways: (f + g)(x) = f(x) + g(x); same idea for −, ·.
Order matters in subtraction: (f − g) puts f's output first.
Both functions receive the same raw input x.

lessons.title: Composition: Feeding One into Another
takeaways: f(g(x)): g first, then f.
Swapping the order usually changes the answer.
Track the intermediate value — it's the inner output.

lessons.title: Composition Formulas
takeaways: f(g(x)): replace f's x with ALL of g's expression.
A single numeric plug-in exposes a wrong formula.
To solve f(g(x)) = c, undo the outer steps first.

lessons.title: Undoing a Function
takeaways: If f(a) = b, then f⁻¹(b) = a.
f⁻¹(x) is NOT 1/f(x) — ⁻¹ on a function name means undo.
Undo multi-step functions in reverse order.

lessons.title: Finding an Inverse Rule
takeaways: Undo operations in reverse order — last step of f is undone first.
Swap and solve: y = f(x) → x = f(y) → solve for y.
Always check: feeding f⁻¹'s answer back through f should return the original x.

lessons.title: Graphs & Verification
takeaways: (a, b) on f becomes (b, a) on f⁻¹ — reflection across y = x.
Verify inverses by composing: f(f⁻¹(x)) must simplify to plain x.
Horizontal line test: two hits at one height means no inverse function without restricting the domain.

lessons.title: Building the Undo Machine
takeaways: An inverse reverses the ORDER of the steps and flips each one — last on, first off, like shoes and socks.
The two classic mistakes are now visible moves: undoing in f's own order, and reversing without flipping. The sample value catches both — it only comes home when both are right.

lessons.title: The Exponent-Finder
takeaways: Read log_b x as 'b to what power gives x?'
Base stays the base in both forms; the log's value is the exponent.
Logs name exact solutions when no base-matching works.

lessons.title: Evaluating Logarithms
takeaways: log_b 1 = 0 and log_b b = 1, for every base.
Reciprocal inside ⟺ negated exponent.
Bare 'log' means base 10.

lessons.title: The Logarithmic Graph
takeaways: Domain x > 0 — zero and negatives have no log.
Every log graph passes (1, 0) and (b, 1).
Transformation grammar applies: the wall follows the inside's zero.

lessons.title: The Product Property
takeaways: log_b(MN) = log_b M + log_b N, straight from adding exponents.
No rule exists for log(M + N).
Condensing can turn messy pieces into a clean single log.

lessons.title: Quotient & Power Properties
takeaways: log_b(M/N) = log_b M − log_b N.
log_b(Mᵖ) = p log_b M — the equation-solving superpower.
Roots ride the same rule with fractional powers.

lessons.title: Expand & Condense Fluency
takeaways: When condensing, coefficients become exponents BEFORE any merge.
Quotients of logs and logs of sums have NO rules — witness values expose fakes.
Clean numeric answers often hide inside condensed products.

lessons.title: Change of Base
takeaways: The formula is the power property in disguise.
Estimate with bracketing powers before trusting a decimal.
A clever shared base can make the formula exact.

lessons.title: Solving Exponential Equations
takeaways: Taking logs of both sides is legal — equal numbers have equal logs.
The power property converts an exponent hunt into a division.
Bracket with integer powers to sanity-check every decimal.

lessons.title: Solving Log Equations
takeaways: log_b(inside) = k ⟺ inside = b^k.
Condensing widens the domain — the final check narrows it back.
Every inside must be POSITIVE at any accepted solution.

lessons.title: The Number e
takeaways: More frequent compounding climbs toward e, never past it.
eˣ is an ordinary exponential between 2ˣ and 3ˣ.
e⁻ˣ decays: the negative exponent flips the base below 1.

lessons.title: The Natural Log
takeaways: ln 1 = 0, ln e = 1, ln(eˣ) = x, e^(ln x) = x.
All three log properties carry over verbatim.
Rewrite inputs as powers to reuse given ln values.

lessons.title: Solving with e and ln
takeaways: eˣ = k solves as x = ln k; ln x = k solves as x = eᵏ.
Coefficients divide off before either inverse is applied.
Check log INPUTS for positivity — a negative x can still be valid.

lessons.title: Continuous Growth: A = Pe^(rt)
takeaways: Coefficient = start; exponent coefficient = continuous rate (sign = direction).
Doubling time (ln 2)/r ignores the principal entirely.
'How long?' and 'what rate?' are both one ln away.

lessons.title: Half-Life
takeaways: Whole half-lives: divide repeatedly; fractional ones: fractional exponents.
Half a half-life leaves ≈ 71%, not 75% — decay compounds.
Non-matching targets fall to ln, like every exponential equation.

lessons.title: Logarithmic Scales
takeaways: Each step of 1 is ×10 underneath — steps add, factors multiply.
Fractional gaps give in-between factors (1.5 steps ≈ 32×).
The log properties compute real measurements — this is the course, applied.

lessons.title: Polynomial Functions & Their Shape
takeaways: Evaluate by substituting: powers first, then coefficients, then signs.
At most n zeros for degree n.
At most n − 1 turning points.

lessons.title: End Behavior
takeaways: Even degree: ends match. Odd degree: ends oppose.
Positive lead: right end up. Negative lead: right end down.
Lower-degree terms never change the ends.

lessons.title: Leading-Term Domination
takeaways: Higher degree beats bigger coefficient in the long run.
Trailing terms become rounding error as |x| grows.
To read end behavior, cover everything after the leading term.

lessons.title: Zeros from Factored Form
takeaways: Zeros = solutions of f(x) = 0 = x-intercepts.
A factor (x − c) gives the zero c; (x + c) gives −c.
Constant multipliers stretch the graph but never add or move zeros.

lessons.title: Multiplicity: Bounce or Cross
takeaways: Multiplicity = the factor's exponent.
Even multiplicity: the graph touches and turns back; odd: it passes through.
Degree = sum of all multiplicities — every polynomial of degree n has n zeros counting repeats.

lessons.title: The Factor & Remainder Theorems
takeaways: Remainder of f ÷ (x − c) is f(c) — no division needed.
f(c) = 0 ⟺ (x − c) is a factor.
Watch the sign: a zero at −2 means the factor (x + 2).

lessons.title: Polynomial Long Division
takeaways: Each pass kills the current leading term.
The remainder's degree is below the divisor's.
Multiply-back and the Remainder Theorem are two independent checks.

lessons.title: Synthetic Division
takeaways: The box holds c from (x − c) — flip the sign you see in (x + c).
The bottom row IS the quotient, one degree down; its last entry is the remainder.
f(c) cross-checks the remainder every time.

lessons.title: Division Meets the Theorems
takeaways: Substitution finds the first factor (Factor Theorem).
Synthetic division drops the degree by one.
The leftover quadratic may factor, need the formula — or go complex (D < 0).

lessons.title: GCF & Quadratic Form
takeaways: 'Completely' means no factor left factorable.
Treat x² as the unknown to factor x⁴ + bx² + c.
A pulled-out x is a genuine factor — it contributes the zero 0.

lessons.title: Factoring by Grouping
takeaways: Grouping works exactly when both pairs expose the SAME binomial.
The leftover quadratic may factor further — or go complex (x² + k).
Expansion is the universal check.

lessons.title: Sum & Difference of Cubes
takeaways: a³ ± b³ = (a ± b)(a² ∓ ab + b²): Same, Opposite, Always Plus.
The trinomial partner always has D < 0 — one real zero per cube pattern.
Take cube ROOTS to find a and b; square and multiply for the partner.

lessons.title: Sketching from Factored Form
takeaways: Degree and lead come from multiplying the factors' leading terms.
Sign can only change at an odd-multiplicity zero.
One sample point pins the sign of a whole zero-free interval.

lessons.title: Turning Points & Degree
takeaways: Turning points ≤ degree − 1, always.
Matching ends: even degree, odd turn count. Opposing ends: odd degree, even turn count.
Coefficients change steepness, never the turn budget.

lessons.title: Building & Using Polynomial Models
takeaways: One factor per zero, sign flipped; square it for a bounce.
Degree = the sum of all multiplicities (FTA's guarantee).
Real models: each dimension of a problem becomes a factor.

lessons.title: Between Radicals & Exponents
takeaways: The root index becomes the exponent's denominator.
Unit fractions are bare roots: x^(1/n) = ⁿ√x.
Root first when evaluating — the numbers stay small.

lessons.title: Exponent Rules Go Rational
takeaways: Fraction arithmetic replaces integer arithmetic; the rules don't change.
Reciprocal exponents cancel to x¹ — the future equation-solving move.
Work inside parentheses first.

lessons.title: Simplifying Variable Radicals
takeaways: √(xⁿ) = x^(n/2); even powers exit whole.
Odd powers split: largest even part out, one factor stays.
Numbers and variables simplify independently, then recombine.

lessons.title: Rationalizing Denominators
takeaways: Rationalizing multiplies by a clever 1 — the value never changes.
Finish with ordinary fraction reduction.
Simplifying the radical before rationalizing keeps numbers small.

lessons.title: Binomial Radical Products
takeaways: √a · √a = a: watch products go rational.
Like radicals in the result combine by coefficient.
Squaring keeps its middle term: (a + b)² = a² + 2ab + b².

lessons.title: Conjugates & Binomial Denominators
takeaways: Flip only the radical's sign to form the conjugate.
Binomial denominators rationalize by conjugate; monomial ones by the bare root.
Watch for a negative denominator flipping signs at the end.

lessons.title: The Square-Root Function
takeaways: Domain x ≥ 0 (no negatives under the root), range y ≥ 0 (principal roots).
The function √ returns ONE value; the equation x² = k has two.
Going backward through √ means squaring.

lessons.title: Domains of Radical Functions
takeaways: Solve inside ≥ 0 as a one-step inequality for the domain.
The graph starts where the inside equals zero.
A negative x-coefficient points the domain leftward (x ≤ ...).

lessons.title: Transforming Radical Graphs
takeaways: The start point moves like a vertex: inside opposite, outside as written.
Outside shifts set the range's floor (or ceiling, after a flip).
A leading minus turns the start into a maximum.

lessons.title: Square Both Sides
takeaways: Squaring undoes an isolated root — never square a sum.
Coefficients divide off before the square.
A principal root can't equal a negative — spot the no-solution case early.

lessons.title: Extraneous Solutions
takeaways: Extraneous roots satisfy the SQUARED equation, not the original.
They're usually legal inputs with a sign mismatch, not domain errors.
Predict: the side equal to a √ must be ≥ 0.

lessons.title: Radical = Radical & Beyond
takeaways: Root = root: one squaring clears both.
Odd powers (cubing) preserve signs — no extraneous risk.
Even-power solves end with a mandatory check.

lessons.title: Solving with Reciprocal Powers
takeaways: x^(m/n) = k solves as x = k^(n/m).
Evaluate k^(n/m) root-first to keep numbers small.
Isolate the power, undo the exponent, then unwrap any inside shifts.

lessons.title: The Even-Numerator ±
takeaways: Even numerator: x = ±k^(n/m) — two real solutions (for k > 0).
Even-numerator powers can never equal a negative: no solution.
Odd numerator: exactly one real solution, sign preserved.

lessons.title: Radical Models
takeaways: Evaluate root-first; solve isolate-then-square.
√-growth dampens: ×4 inside is only ×2 outside.
Real quantities keep the check honest — negative candidates rarely make sense.

lessons.title: Rational Expressions & Excluded Values
takeaways: Excluded values come from the BOTTOM only; a zero top just outputs 0.
Factor the denominator to catch every exclusion.
Some denominators (like x² + 4) never vanish — nothing excluded.

lessons.title: Simplify by Factoring
takeaways: Only FACTORS cancel — terms glued by + or − never do.
A number test exposes any illegal cancellation instantly.
The simplified form inherits every original exclusion.

lessons.title: Opposite Factors: the −1 Trick
takeaways: b − a = −(a − b): rewrite, then cancel normally.
Addition reversals are identical — no sign cost.
One numeric test settles any sign doubt.

lessons.title: Multiplying Rational Expressions
takeaways: Diagonal cancels are legal — a product is one big fraction.
Cancel BEFORE multiplying to keep expressions small.
Every denominator that ever appeared contributes its exclusions.

lessons.title: Dividing Rational Expressions
takeaways: Only the divisor flips; the first fraction is kept.
A bare divisor flips to 1-over-it.
The divisor's numerator zeros become NEW exclusions.

lessons.title: Mixed Operations & Restriction Tracking
takeaways: Exclusions come from every original bottom AND every divisor's top.
Cancellation never un-bans an input.
When everything cancels, the answer is a constant — on the legal domain.

lessons.title: Like Denominators
takeaways: Never add a denominator to itself — it's a label.
−(a − b) = −a + b: the classic sign trap.
Factor the combined numerator — it often cancels the bottom.

lessons.title: Building the Polynomial LCD
takeaways: Blind multiplication overshoots whenever factors are shared.
Repeated factors take the HIGHEST power, never the sum.
Convert by multiplying with missing-factor-over-itself.

lessons.title: Adding & Subtracting, Unlike Denominators
takeaways: Each top gains exactly its missing factors.
A fraction already on the LCD converts by 1 — leave it alone.
Factor the combined numerator; cancellations hide there.

lessons.title: The Reciprocal Function
takeaways: Near the vertical asymptote outputs explode; far away they flatten.
Shifts move the asymptote pair exactly like a start point.
1/x's range misses exactly one value: 0.

lessons.title: Holes vs Vertical Asymptotes
takeaways: Cancelled factor → hole; surviving factor → vertical asymptote.
A hole's height comes from the SIMPLIFIED form at that x.
Squared factors can survive their own cancellation — still a wall.

lessons.title: Horizontal Asymptotes
takeaways: top < bottom: y = 0; equal: lead ratio; top > bottom: none.
Only leading terms matter far out — the rest fades.
Horizontal rails can be crossed mid-graph; vertical walls cannot.

lessons.title: Solving by Clearing the LCD
takeaways: LCD-clearing can mint phantoms at denominator zeros — always check.
Clearing may raise the degree: expect quadratics.
Identities solve to 'everything except the exclusions'; contradictions to nothing.

lessons.title: Proportions & Work Rates
takeaways: a/b = c/d ⟺ ad = bc — one move clears both bottoms.
A t-hour job means a 1/t-per-hour rate.
Joint time beats the fastest solo time — a built-in sanity check.

lessons.title: Inverse & Joint Variation
takeaways: Inverse: y = k/x, constant product xy = k.
Joint: z = kxy — proportional to the product.
Two-step ritual: solve for k, then substitute.

lessons.title: Two Ways to Give a Rule
takeaways: Recursive: a start plus a next-from-previous instruction.
Explicit: position n straight to the term, no chain.
Both describe the SAME sequence — they just answer different questions fast.

lessons.title: Working the Chain
takeaways: aₙ₋₁ always means the term right before the one you're building.
Recursion covers rules no single nth-term formula does — like “double, add one.”
Its cost: distant terms need the whole chain. The explicit form is the cure.

lessons.title: Converting Between Forms
takeaways: Arithmetic: start once + (n − 1) hops of d. Geometric: start once × rⁿ⁻¹.
Explicit → recursive just reads the start and the hop back out.
Test n = 1 and n = 2 — two cheap checks catch the (n − 1) slip.

lessons.title: Meet the Sigma
takeaways: Below the sigma: where the counter starts. Above: where it stops. Beside: the rule each k feeds.
Evaluate by unrolling — substitute, list, add.
The index letter is a dummy, and even a constant rule runs once per counter value.

lessons.title: Evaluating Sigma Sums
takeaways: Run the counter bottom-to-top; both ends are included.
Term count = upper − lower + 1 — the fencepost fact.
A constant factor slides out: Σ 4k = 4·Σ k.

lessons.title: Writing Sums in Sigma Form
takeaways: Find the rule: (step)·k + leftover, pinned by the first term.
Find the bounds: the counter values producing the first and last terms.
Index shifts give many correct forms — expanding a few terms verifies any of them.

lessons.title: Gauss's Shortcut
takeaways: Ends pair to the same value — (a₁ + aₙ) every time.
Sₙ = n(a₁ + aₙ)/2: n terms, half as many pairs.
The write-it-twice proof shows exactly where the ÷ 2 comes from.

lessons.title: The Two Sum Formulas
takeaways: Ends known → S = n(a₁ + aₙ)/2. Start-step-count known → S = n/2·(2a₁ + (n−1)d).
The second form is the first with aₙ rebuilt — they always agree.
Every problem starts by extracting a₁, d, n.

lessons.title: Arithmetic Series at Work
takeaways: Extract a₁, d, n from the story — they're always there.
Sigma sums with rules like 2k + 3 are arithmetic series: fold them.
Term vs total: “in row 8” is a₈; “in all” is S₈.

lessons.title: Why Adding Powers Needs a New Trick
takeaways: Gauss's fold dies on geometric sums — the pairs don't match.
Multiply by r and subtract: the whole middle cancels, only edges survive.
The subtraction leaves (r − 1)S — one division finishes.

lessons.title: The Geometric Sum Formula
takeaways: Sₙ = a₁(1 − rⁿ)/(1 − r), for r ≠ 1.
rⁿ uses the term COUNT; the last term uses rⁿ⁻¹ — keep them straight.
Growing or shrinking r — the formula handles both.

lessons.title: Geometric Series at Work
takeaways: Doubles/triples/× each round → geometric; extract a₁, r, n.
Sigma rules shaped a₁·rᵏ⁻¹ are geometric series in uniform.
Test the pattern first — equal gaps fold, equal ratios shift-and-subtract.

lessons.title: When Adding Forever Settles Down
takeaways: An infinite geometric series converges exactly when |r| < 1.
Partial sums climb toward a ceiling they never cross.
The sign of r sets alternation; the SIZE of r decides the fate.

lessons.title: The Infinite Sum Formula
takeaways: S = a₁/(1 − r) — the finite formula with its vanishing rⁿ erased.
Check |r| < 1 FIRST; on divergent series the formula outputs garbage.
Backwards: a₁ = S(1 − r).

lessons.title: Forever Sums in the Wild
takeaways: Repeating decimals are infinite geometric series: single repeats land over 9.
Motion totals (bounces, swings) are forever-sums — mind what's traveled once vs twice.
Pick the tool by pattern and stopping: fold, finite formula, or a₁/(1 − r).

lessons.title: How the Data Was Made
takeaways: Random sampling licenses generalising to a population; random assignment licenses claiming a cause.
Observational studies report association, however large they are.
Ask of any headline: what was randomised — nothing, the sample, or the treatment?

lessons.title: Bias, and Why a Bigger Sample Cannot Save You
takeaways: Variability is random scatter around the truth; bias is a systematic miss. Sample size only touches the first.
Undercoverage, nonresponse, voluntary response and loaded wording all change WHO is in the sample.
A tiny margin of error on a biased poll is a precise wrong answer — the most dangerous kind.

lessons.title: Designing an Experiment That Can Answer
takeaways: Control answers "compared with what?"; random assignment removes lurking variables; blinding removes expectation; replication removes fluke.
Random assignment buys cause. Random sampling buys reach. They are different coins.
A comparison group that was not built by coin is not a control group — it is a second observational study.

lessons.title: The Statistic Wobbles
takeaways: The parameter p is fixed and unseen; the statistic p̂ is computed and moves with every sample.
Honest random samples disagree with each other. That scatter is sampling variability, not error.
An unbiased method produces a pile centred on the truth — even though almost none of its individual polls hit it.

lessons.title: The Sampling Distribution
takeaways: The sampling distribution is the set of all answers your method could produce; one poll is a single dot from it.
An honest method centres the pile on the truth. Sample size controls only the width.
Width falls with √n: quadruple the sample to halve the wobble — which is why precision gets expensive fast.

lessons.title: Putting a Number on the Wobble
takeaways: SE = √(p(1−p)/n) is the typical distance from a poll to the truth; about 95% of polls land within 2 SE of it.
p(1−p) peaks at p = 0.5, so pollsters quote that worst case — which is where the familiar ±3 on a 1,000-person poll comes from.
The wobble depends on the sample size, never on the population size.

lessons.title: The Margin of Error
takeaways: Margin of error ≈ 2 × SE, and it turns a point estimate into a range of plausible values.
Only n (and, out of your control, p) move it — the population size does not.
The margin measures random wobble and nothing else. It is blind to bias by construction.

lessons.title: What "95% Confident" Actually Counts
takeaways: The parameter is fixed; the interval is random. So "95%" describes how often the METHOD captures the truth.
Any one interval either contains the truth or it does not — you are borrowing the method's track record.
Higher confidence means a wider interval. Only more data improves confidence and precision together.

lessons.title: Reading a Poll Without Being Fooled
takeaways: A lead smaller than the margin is a lead the poll cannot see — the bands overlap and a tie stays on the table.
The gap between two estimates is noisier than either estimate, so it needs a bigger margin, not the same one.
Ask how people were chosen BEFORE you ask how many — bias cannot be repaired downstream.

lessons.title: The Bell That Wobble Builds
takeaways: Stacked sample statistics form a symmetric mound — the normal distribution — with its peak on the truth.
Bigger samples narrow the bell; they never move its center or break its symmetry.
The bell belongs to accumulations (averages, totals) — single fair outcomes keep their own shapes.
68 – 95 – 99.7: the shares within one, two, three σ of the mean, for every normal curve.
Symmetry halves anything: one tail is half of what both tails hold.
Any band's share comes from subtracting memorized levels — no new facts needed.

lessons.title: z: Distance Measured in Wobbles
takeaways: z = (x − μ)/σ: distance in wobbles, sign for side — comparable across any two scales.
The empirical rule restates cleanly: 68% within |z| ≤ 1, 95% within |z| ≤ 2.
'How unusual is unusual' becomes a threshold check at |z| = 2.

lessons.title: What Chance Alone Produces
takeaways: Shuffle the labels while keeping the scores: that simulates a world where the treatment did nothing.
The pile of shuffled gaps centres on 0 and shows exactly what chance can manufacture.
If the real gap sits far out in that pile's tail, 'chance alone' becomes a poor explanation — which is not the same as proof.

lessons.title: How Unusual Is Unusual?
takeaways: p-value = the chance of data at least this extreme IF the no-effect story were true. It is not the chance that the story is true.
p < 0.05 is a convention, and it lets about 1 in 20 null results through by luck.
Many tests, one reported winner: that is how noise gets published. Count the tests, not just the finding.

lessons.title: What "Significant" Does Not Say
takeaways: Significance rules out chance. It says nothing about the SIZE of the effect — and a huge sample makes trivial effects significant.
It is not proof (about 1 in 20 clears the bar by luck) and it does not generalise beyond the population sampled.
It never buys causation. Only random assignment does that.

lessons.title: Reading a Study's Design
takeaways: What was randomised — nothing, the sample, or the treatment? That fixes the ceiling on every claim.
A claim can travel down the ladder of designs, never up.
Always ask who was in the study and what the comparison group was. A result with no comparison is not a result.

lessons.title: When the Number Is Right and the Claim Is Wrong
takeaways: A claim may not reach beyond the population that was actually sampled.
A model is evidence only inside the range of its data — extrapolation is assumption, not inference.
"95% accurate" is P(positive | disease). For a rare disease, P(disease | positive) can be tiny.

lessons.title: The Statistics Detective
takeaways: Design first (what was randomised?), then who was left out, then the wobble, then whether the effect clears it, then whether it matters.
Bias is invisible to the margin of error, and significance is invisible to the question of size.
The numbers tell you what is real and how big. Whether it is worth doing is a judgement — and it stays yours.

lessons.title: Three Ratios in a Right Triangle
takeaways: Opposite, adjacent, hypotenuse — all named relative to YOUR angle.
SOH-CAH-TOA: sin = opp/hyp, cos = adj/hyp, tan = opp/adj.
Similar triangles share ratios — sin, cos, tan depend only on the angle.

lessons.title: Solving for Sides
takeaways: Pick the ratio whose two sides are the known one and the wanted one.
Known hypotenuse ⇒ multiply; wanted hypotenuse ⇒ divide — and sanity-check its length.
No hypotenuse in the story ⇒ tangent.

lessons.title: Finding the Angle
takeaways: Inverse trig recovers the angle from a ratio — and sin⁻¹ is an inverse, not a reciprocal.
Match the two KNOWN sides to their ratio, then invert that one.
The two acute inverses must total 90° — a free error check.

lessons.title: The Radian
takeaways: One radian = the angle whose arc is one radius; 2π of them fill a turn.
Radians are a pure arc÷radius ratio — the unit circle formulas demand them.
Anchor 180° = π; the conversion factor points 180 at the unit you want.

lessons.title: Degrees ↔ Radians, Fluently
takeaways: 30-45-60-90 ↔ π/6, π/4, π/3, π/2 — denominators count copies in 180°.
Read nπ/d as n steps of size 180/d degrees.
Angles run negative (clockwise) and past 2π (extra laps).

lessons.title: Arc Length
takeaways: s = rθ — arc equals radius times angle, radians only.
Degrees in the problem? Convert BEFORE the formula, every time.
Rolling wheels obey the same law: distance = rθ.

lessons.title: Coordinates on the Unit Circle
takeaways: Unit circle: cos θ = x, sin θ = y — every angle now has values.
A-S-T-C gives each quadrant's positive function; coordinates explain why.
tan = y/x, the radius's slope — undefined where x = 0 (90°, 270°).

lessons.title: Reference Angles
takeaways: Reference angle: the acute gap to the X-axis — never the y-axis.
Q2: 180−θ · Q3: θ−180 · Q4: 360−θ (same shapes with π in radians).
Magnitude from the reference, sign from A-S-T-C.

lessons.title: Exact Values
takeaways: Sines climb √1/2, √2/2, √3/2 across 30-45-60; cosines run it backward.
Any angle: reference for magnitude, A-S-T-C for sign, table for the value.
π-fraction denominators name the family: 6 → 30s, 4 → 45s, 3 → 60s.

lessons.title: The Wave from the Circle
takeaways: sin x is the circle's height unrolled — periodic, period 2π, swinging ±1.
Cosine is the same wave entering at its peak; sine enters at the midline, rising.
Any wave: midline = (max+min)/2, amplitude = (max−min)/2.

lessons.title: Amplitude & Midline
takeaways: y = a sin x + d: amplitude |a| (vertical stretch), midline y = d (vertical shift).
Max = d + |a|, min = d − |a| — and the reads reverse to recover a and d.
Negative a reflects over the midline; amplitude stays positive.

lessons.title: Period & Writing Rules
takeaways: Period = 2π/b — bigger b, faster wave, shorter repeat.
Designing: b = 2π/period; check b × period = 2π.
y = a sin(bx) + d assembles amplitude, speed, and midline independently.

lessons.title: The Ferris Wheel
takeaways: h(t) = (axle) − (radius) cos t models a bottom-boarding wheel.
Midline = axle height, amplitude = radius — formula parts ARE wheel parts.
Any max/min data fits: average for the midline, half-span for the amplitude.

lessons.title: Fitting Waves to the World
takeaways: Data gives a and d: half-span and average of the extremes.
Real repeat time gives b = 2π/period — hours and seconds welcome.
The finished model predicts: evaluate the inside first, then swing and shift.

lessons.title: The Pythagorean Identity
takeaways: sin²θ + cos²θ = 1 — the unit circle's equation wearing trig names.
Recover the missing function in squares; let the quadrant pick the root's sign.
From triangle ratios to radians, the circle, the wave, and the world — one idea, unrolled.

lessons.title: Powers of a Sum
takeaways: (a + b)ⁿ is not aⁿ + bⁿ — cross terms appear and they are not optional.
(a + b)ⁿ expands into n + 1 terms, with a's power falling as b's rises.
For n = 2 the coefficients are 1, 2, 1; for n = 3 they are 1, 3, 3, 1.

lessons.title: Pascal's Triangle
takeaways: Rows are numbered from 0; row n gives the coefficients of (a + b)ⁿ.
Each interior entry is the sum of the two above it, and each row is symmetric.
Row n's entries sum to 2ⁿ, which checks a freshly built row.

lessons.title: Why Combinations Appear
takeaways: Every term of (a + b)ⁿ is one choice of a-or-b from each bracket.
The coefficient of aⁿ⁻ᵏbᵏ is C(n,k) — the number of such choices.
Pascal's row n, position k, IS C(n,k), and its symmetry is the complement rule.

lessons.title: The Binomial Theorem
takeaways: (a + b)ⁿ = Σ C(n,k)·aⁿ⁻ᵏ·bᵏ for k from 0 to n.
Every term's exponents total n — a one-second check on any written term.
For substituted binomials the powers act on the whole quantity, coefficients included.

lessons.title: Finding a Single Term
takeaways: The general term is C(n,k)·aⁿ⁻ᵏ·bᵏ, with k read off the power of b.
Row symmetry can hide a wrong k — anchor it to b every time.
The term with exponent k sits in position k + 1.

lessons.title: Binomials Meet Probability
takeaways: (p + q)ⁿ expands to the binomial distribution: term k is the chance of exactly k successes.
C(n,k) counts the paths; pᵏqⁿ⁻ᵏ weighs each one.
Because p + q = 1, the terms sum to 1 and account for every outcome.

lessons.title: The Parabola: Focus and Directrix
takeaways: A parabola = points equidistant from a focus and a directrix.
Vertex at origin: x² = 4py, focus (0, p), directrix y = −p.
p is the focal length; larger p widens the curve.

lessons.title: Shifted Parabolas & Orientation
takeaways: (x − h)² = 4p(y − k): vertex (h, k), focus (h, k + p), directrix y = k − p.
Squared y → opens sideways: (y − k)² = 4p(x − h).
The sign of p sets the opening direction.

lessons.title: The Reflective Property
takeaways: Parallel rays reflect to the focus; focus-sourced rays leave parallel.
Dishes, headlights, and solar cookers all exploit this.
Focal length p tunes the dish's depth and focus distance.

lessons.title: The Ellipse: Two Foci and a String
takeaways: Ellipse = points whose distances to two foci sum to 2a.
Standard form x²/a² + y²/b² = 1 with a > b.
The larger denominator marks the major (long) axis direction.

lessons.title: Foci, Axes & the a-b-c Relationship
takeaways: Ellipse: c² = a² − b², so foci are c from center, always inside.
Foci lie ON the major axis: (±c, 0) or (0, ±c).
Rearrange to find any of a, b, c from the other two.

lessons.title: Shifted Ellipses & How Round They Are
takeaways: Shift the center to (h, k): (x − h)²/a² + (y − k)²/b² = 1.
Foci move with the center: (h ± c, k) or (h, k ± c).
Eccentricity e = c/a in [0, 1): 0 ≈ circle, near 1 ≈ elongated.

lessons.title: The Hyperbola: A Difference of Distances
takeaways: Hyperbola: |r₁ − r₂| = 2a (constant difference of focal distances).
Standard form has a MINUS: x²/a² − y²/b² = 1 (or y² positive for vertical).
Vertices at (±a, 0) — the positive term's variable.

lessons.title: Asymptotes & the Guiding Box
takeaways: Asymptotes: y = ±(b/a)x — the diagonals of the a-by-b guiding box.
Hyperbola focus rule ADDS: c² = a² + b² (foci beyond the vertices).
The box (±a, ±b) frames the whole curve.

lessons.title: Foci, Orientation & Eccentricity
takeaways: Foci on the opening axis at distance c > a (beyond the vertices).
Orientation = the positive term's variable (x² horizontal, y² vertical).
Eccentricity e = c/a > 1 for every hyperbola.

lessons.title: Reading the Second-Degree Form
takeaways: General form: Ax² + Cy² + Dx + Ey + F = 0.
A = C → circle; same sign, A ≠ C → ellipse.
Opposite signs → hyperbola; one squared term missing → parabola.

lessons.title: Completing the Square to Standard Form
takeaways: Complete the square on x-terms and y-terms separately, balancing both sides.
Circle/parabola: read center directly; ellipse/hyperbola: divide to make RHS = 1.
The completed form exposes center, radius, or a and b.

lessons.title: Hyperbolas & Parabolas from General Form
takeaways: Hyperbola: move the constant, divide to RHS = 1, keep the minus.
Parabola: isolate the lone square (y² = 4px), no division.
Coefficient signs (Ch4 opener) predict the finish before you start.

lessons.title: Eccentricity Unifies the Conics
takeaways: Eccentricity e orders every conic on a single scale.
e = 0 circle, 0 < e < 1 ellipse, e = 1 parabola, e > 1 hyperbola.
Bigger e means a more open curve.

lessons.title: The Focus-Directrix View
takeaways: Every conic: (distance to focus)/(distance to directrix) = e.
Ratio < 1 ellipse, = 1 parabola, > 1 hyperbola.
Directrix at x = a/e; it vanishes to infinity as e → 0 (circle).

lessons.title: Conics in the Sky
takeaways: Kepler: planets ride ellipses with the Sun at one focus.
e < 1 orbits are bound and repeat; e ≥ 1 paths escape forever.
Parabolic reflectors focus parallel rays — conic geometry, applied.

lessons.title: Average Rate of Change
takeaways: Average rate of change = (f(b) − f(a))/(b − a).
Divide by the input CHANGE b − a, never by b.
A line's average rate of change is its slope on every interval.

lessons.title: Secant Lines: Seeing the Rate
takeaways: A secant's slope equals the average rate of change between its two points.
Falling endpoint heights mean a negative average rate.
A horizontal secant means zero average change — not a constant function.

lessons.title: Interpreting Rates: Units & Meaning
takeaways: Units of a rate: output units per input unit.
The sign is the direction: negative means the quantity is falling.
Always subtract later − earlier, top and bottom.

lessons.title: Where a Function Rises and Falls
takeaways: Increasing = graph climbs left-to-right; decreasing = it falls.
Report intervals with x-values, never heights.
Turning points are where the behavior switches.

lessons.title: Peaks & Valleys: Extrema
takeaways: Local extrema beat their neighbors; absolute extrema beat the whole graph.
Report both coordinates: where (x) and what value (y).
Unbounded growth means no absolute maximum exists.

lessons.title: Reading a Whole Graph
takeaways: Read behavior, extrema, domain/range, and story together.
Range comes from extrema PLUS end behavior — local bumps don't cap it.
With units, every point is a sentence: x is when/where, y is how much.

lessons.title: Even & Odd: The Symmetry Test
takeaways: Even: f(−x) = f(x), mirror in the y-axis.
Odd: f(−x) = −f(x), half-turn about the origin.
Test with the letter −x; a single point can only DISPROVE.

lessons.title: Piecewise Functions
takeaways: Find the branch whose condition your input satisfies, then use only that rule.
Boundary inputs follow the inequality symbols exactly.
Solving backwards: every candidate must satisfy its own branch's condition.

lessons.title: Absolute Value & Step Functions
takeaways: |x| = −x for x < 0, x for x ≥ 0 — the flip makes negatives positive.
Step functions are constant branches: flat shelves with jumps.
To split |inside|, break at inside = 0 and flip the negative side.

lessons.title: Composition: Order Matters
takeaways: f(g(x)): g runs first; its output feeds f.
f(g(x)) ≠ g(f(x)) in general — order changes the function.
To build the rule, substitute the whole inner formula.

lessons.title: The Domain of a Composition
takeaways: x must enter g, AND g(x) must enter f.
Solve inner-function restrictions first, then exclude x where g's output breaks f.
Never read the domain off a simplified formula.

lessons.title: Decomposing & Modeling with Composition
takeaways: Decompose by asking what happens to x first (inner) and last (outer).
Real models compose: each function's output is the next one's input.
Check any decomposition numerically at one value.

lessons.title: One-to-One & the Horizontal Line Test
takeaways: One-to-one: no two inputs share an output.
Horizontal line test: any double-crossing line kills the inverse.
Strictly increasing or decreasing functions always pass.

lessons.title: Restricting the Domain
takeaways: Restrict to a strictly rising or falling piece to gain an inverse.
Any interval straddling a turning point keeps collisions.
Inverses swap domain and range.
