lessons.title: Verifying Inverses: the Composition Identity
takeaways: f(g(x)) = x AND g(f(x)) = x — both, as algebra — proves inverses.
One numeric round trip is evidence, not proof; one failure is disproof.
Graphs of inverses mirror across y = x: (a, b) ↔ (b, a).

lessons.title: Comparing Functions Across Representations
takeaways: A function's properties — rate of change, intercepts, values — exist independent of whether it's shown as a graph, table, or equation.
Each representation has its own fastest way to extract a given property: subtraction in a table, substitution in an equation, tracing on a graph.
Comparing two functions means finding the SAME property in each one's own representation, then comparing the numbers directly.

courses.title: Precalculus: Limits & the Doorway to Calculus

lessons.title: The Idea of a Limit: Approaching a Value
takeaways: A limit is the value f(x) approaches as x nears a.
Limits can exist at holes, where f itself is undefined.
The value f(a) doesn't decide the limit — the approach does.

lessons.title: Reading Limits from Tables & Graphs
takeaways: Numerical tables: approach a from both sides; watch outputs settle.
Graphically: trace both branches to the shared y-height (ignore open circles).
No hole? Direct substitution gives the limit.

lessons.title: When a Limit Fails to Exist
takeaways: A limit exists only when left and right approaches AGREE.
Failures: a jump (sides disagree), unbounded blow-up, or endless oscillation.
Matching one-sided limits ⇒ the two-sided limit exists.

lessons.title: Direct Substitution & the Limit Laws
takeaways: Continuous at a ⇒ lim(x→a) f(x) = f(a): just substitute.
Limit laws split sums, products, and quotients across the limit.
The quotient law needs the denominator's limit ≠ 0.

lessons.title: The 0/0 Form: Factor and Cancel
takeaways: 0/0 is indeterminate — a signal to factor, not an answer.
Factor numerator and denominator, cancel the shared factor, then substitute.
Cancelling is valid because x nears a without equalling it.

lessons.title: Rationalizing to Resolve Limits
takeaways: A root in a 0/0 form: multiply by the conjugate.
(√A − B)(√A + B) = A − B² erases the root and cancels the trouble factor.
Match the tool to the obstacle: factor for polynomials, conjugate for roots.

lessons.title: One-Sided Limits
takeaways: lim(x→a⁻) approaches from the left; lim(x→a⁺) from the right.
The two-sided limit exists ⟺ the one-sided limits are equal.
Disagreeing sides ⇒ a jump, and the two-sided limit DNE.

lessons.title: Limits at Infinity & Horizontal Asymptotes
takeaways: Limit at infinity = where f heads as x grows; it's the horizontal asymptote.
Degrees: top < bottom → 0; equal → leading ratio; top > bottom → ±∞.
This turns pra's asymptote rules into limit statements.

lessons.title: End Behavior: The Full Picture
takeaways: Top degree > bottom → ±∞ (unbounded, no horizontal asymptote).
Top < bottom → 0; equal → leading-coefficient ratio.
The leading terms alone settle end behavior at ±∞.

lessons.title: Continuity at a Point
takeaways: Continuous at a: f(a) defined, limit exists, and limit = f(a).
For continuous functions, the limit is just f(a) (substitution).
Discontinuities are where one of the three conditions breaks.

lessons.title: Classifying Discontinuities
takeaways: Removable: a fillable hole — the limit exists but f(a) doesn't match.
Jump: one-sided limits disagree — no two-sided limit.
Infinite: the function blows up to ±∞ (vertical asymptote).

lessons.title: The Intermediate Value Theorem
takeaways: IVT: a continuous f on [a, b] hits every value between f(a) and f(b).
Sign change on [a, b] ⇒ a root in (a, b) — existence without solving.
Continuity is required; a jump can skip over values.

lessons.title: Average Rate of Change
takeaways: Average rate of change = secant slope (f(b) − f(a))/(b − a).
With b = a + h it's the difference quotient (f(a + h) − f(a))/h.
Shrinking h nudges the secant toward a single-point rate.

lessons.title: The Derivative as a Limit
takeaways: Derivative f′(a) = lim_{h→0} (f(a + h) − f(a))/h (the difference quotient's limit).
The secant pivots into the tangent as h → 0.
For f(x) = x², f′(a) = 2a — an instantaneous rate at every point.

lessons.title: Limits Everywhere: Series & the Road Ahead
takeaways: An infinite sum is the limit of its partial sums.
The geometric formula a/(1 − r) computes that limit (recall series).
The same limit machine powers derivatives, infinite sums, and — ahead in calculus — areas under curves; you've built the doorway.

lessons.title: A New Address System
takeaways: Polar (r, θ): distance r from the pole, angle θ from the polar axis.
Addresses aren't unique — add 2π, or negate r and shift θ by π.
Negative r points along the opposite ray.

lessons.title: Polar → Rectangular: Drop the Triangle
takeaways: x = r cos θ, y = r sin θ — the triangle's legs.
Signs of cos/sin place the quadrant automatically.
Negative r plugs straight in; no special rules.

lessons.title: Rectangular → Polar: Watch the Quadrant
takeaways: r = √(x² + y²); tan θ = y/x.
arctan lands in (−π/2, π/2) — add π whenever x < 0.
Sketch the quadrant to confirm the angle points the right way.

lessons.title: The Simplest Polar Graphs
takeaways: r = a: circle of radius a at the pole. θ = c: line through the pole.
r = 2a cos θ: circle center (a, 0); r = 2a sin θ: circle center (0, a).
Both shifted circles pass through the origin.

lessons.title: Rose Curves & the Petal Rule
takeaways: r = a cos(nθ) / a sin(nθ): rose with petal length |a|.
n odd → n petals; n even → 2n petals.
cos aligns a petal with the polar axis; sin rotates the bloom.

lessons.title: Limaçons & Cardioids
takeaways: Limaçon r = a ± b·trig θ; shape from a/b: <1 loop, =1 cardioid, 1–2 dimpled, ≥2 convex.
r = 0 gives the cusp (cardioid) or the inner loop's crossing.
Max r = a + b; min r = a − b.

lessons.title: Complex Numbers in Polar Form
takeaways: z = r(cos θ + i sin θ) with r = √(a² + b²), θ from b/a plus a quadrant check.
a = r cos θ, b = r sin θ — the Ch1 conversion formulas.
Polar form makes multiplication and powers easy — next.

lessons.title: Multiply by Rotating: De Moivre
takeaways: Multiply: multiply moduli, add arguments.
De Moivre: [r(cosθ + i sinθ)]ⁿ = rⁿ(cos nθ + i sin nθ).
Track where nθ lands on the circle to get the sign right.

lessons.title: nth Roots: Points on a Circle
takeaways: n nth-roots: modulus r^(1/n), arguments (θ + 2πk)/n, spaced 2π/n.
Roots of unity are n evenly spaced points on the unit circle, including 1.
Equal spacing means the roots are the vertices of a regular n-gon.

lessons.title: Parametric Equations: Curves Over Time
takeaways: Parametric form: x = x(t), y = y(t); the point traces a curve as t moves.
Direction and speed depend on the parametrization, not just the shape.
Parametric curves can violate the vertical line test — loops and doubling-back are fine.

lessons.title: Eliminating the Parameter
takeaways: t appears simply → solve for t and substitute.
t inside sin/cos → square and add via sin²t + cos²t = 1.
The rectangular equation shows the shape; the parametrization added the motion.

lessons.title: Writing Parametrizations & Orientation
takeaways: Any y = f(x): parametrize with x = t, y = f(t).
Circle radius R: x = R cos t, y = R sin t (counterclockwise).
Negate the sine to reverse orientation to clockwise.

lessons.title: Projectile Motion: Two Independent Clocks
takeaways: Horizontal: x = vₓ·t (constant velocity).
Vertical: y = v_y·t − ½g t² (a downward parabola in t).
The two motions are independent; vertical velocity is 0 at the peak.

lessons.title: Peak, Flight Time, and Range
takeaways: Time to peak = v_y/g; max height = v_y²/(2g).
Flight time = 2·t_peak (level ground); range = vₓ · flight time.
Symmetry makes the fall mirror the rise.

lessons.title: The Parabolic Path: Eliminating Time
takeaways: Eliminate t (t = x/vₓ) to get y as a downward parabola in x.
The path's roots give launch and landing; the vertex sits at their midpoint.
Parametric form separates WHEN (timing) from WHERE (shape) — the course's throughline.

lessons.title: The Rational Root Theorem: the Candidate List
takeaways: Candidates are ±p/q: p | constant, q | leading coefficient.
Reduce fractions and drop duplicates.
The list is complete for rational zeros — but nothing on it is guaranteed.

lessons.title: Putting Candidates on Trial
takeaways: Candidate c is a zero iff f(c) = 0 (Factor Theorem).
Synthetic division tests AND divides in one pass.
Each found root drops the degree by one.

lessons.title: The Full Pipeline: List, Test, Divide, Finish
takeaways: List → test → divide → finish the quadratic.
A zero p/q corresponds to the factor (qx − p).
Multiply back to verify — always.

lessons.title: The Fundamental Theorem: How Many Zeros Must Exist
takeaways: Degree n ⇒ exactly n complex zeros, counted with multiplicity.
Missing real zeros are hiding off the real line, never absent.
Distinct zeros ≤ degree; multiplicities fill the gap.

lessons.title: Mirror Pairs: the Conjugate Zero Theorem
takeaways: Real coefficients ⇒ non-real zeros come in conjugate pairs.
Odd degree ⇒ at least one real zero.
A conjugate pair multiplies to a real quadratic: (x − a − bi)(x − a + bi).

lessons.title: Building Polynomials from Mixed Zeros
takeaways: Pair non-real zeros; each pair becomes x² − (sum)x + product.
Real zeros each add one linear factor.
Minimal degree = real zeros + 2 × (number of pairs).

lessons.title: When the Asymptote Tilts
takeaways: Gap −1 or less: y = 0. Gap 0: y = leading ratio. Gap +1: slant.
Gap +2 or more: no line-shaped asymptote at all.
The slant line is the division's quotient.

lessons.title: Finding the Slant by Division
takeaways: Divide; the quotient (degree 1) is the slant asymptote.
The remainder term is the curve-to-line gap — and it dies far out.
Multiply back to verify every division.

lessons.title: The Full Asymptote Portrait
takeaways: Verticals/holes come from the bottom's zeros; the far-out line from the degree gap.
Only vertical asymptotes are uncrossable.
Crossings of the slant happen exactly where the remainder gap equals zero.

lessons.title: The Sign Chart
takeaways: Zeros cut the line; sign is constant on each piece.
One test point per interval decides its sign.
Strict excludes the zeros; inclusive keeps them.

lessons.title: The Multiplicity Shortcut
takeaways: Odd multiplicity flips the sign; even doesn't.
Anchor one interval (far right is easiest), then walk.
Even zeros can puncture a strict-inequality solution.

lessons.title: Polynomial Inequalities from Scratch
takeaways: Move everything to one side before charting — signs only compare to zero.
Never divide by a variable expression; factor it out instead.
Strict vs inclusive changes endpoints only, never intervals.

lessons.title: Rational Sign Charts: Two Kinds of Critical Points
takeaways: Cuts = top's zeros ∪ bottom's zeros.
The sign can flip at an excluded value via the asymptote jump.
Test one point per interval, exactly as with polynomials.

lessons.title: The Boundary Rule: Zeros Close, Excluded Values Never
takeaways: Numerator zeros may close under ≥/≤; denominator zeros never join.
Never multiply an inequality by a variable denominator.
A cancelled common factor still leaves the point excluded (hole).

lessons.title: Rearranging: One Fraction, Then Chart
takeaways: Zero on one side, then ONE fraction over a common denominator.
Cuts come from the combined top and bottom.
Boundary rule still reigns: zeros may close, excluded values never.

lessons.title: Phase Shift: Sliding the Wave
takeaways: sin(x − C): slide right C; plus inside slides left.
With a B, factor first — shift = constant ÷ B.
Verify any shift by tracking one landmark point.

lessons.title: The Full Sinusoid: Four Dials
takeaways: Max/min = D ± A; period = 2π/B; start the shape at x = C.
Reading a graph: D and A from extremes, B from the period, C from a rising crossing.
Peaks sit a quarter-period after each rising midline-crossing.

lessons.title: Graphing One Clean Period
takeaways: Quarter-period steps from x = C place all five key points.
Heights cycle midline, D+A, midline, D−A, midline.
Negative A runs the same dots with peak and trough swapped.

lessons.title: Cosine's Graph: Starting at the Top
takeaways: cos 0 = 1: cosine begins at its peak.
Five points: peak, midline, trough, midline, peak.
All four dials behave exactly as in sine.

lessons.title: One Wave, Two Names
takeaways: cos x = sin(x + π/2); sin x = cos(x − π/2).
Anchor cosine at a peak, sine at a rising midline-crossing.
Any sinusoid has both names; pick the cheaper one.

lessons.title: Reflections & Equivalent Rules
takeaways: π-slide = reflection: sin(x + π) = −sin x, cos(x ± π) = −cos x.
Full-period slides (±2π) change nothing.
Audit equivalences with the dials plus one test point.

lessons.title: Tangent: the Wave That Isn't
takeaways: tan = sin/cos: walls where cos = 0, zeros where sin = 0.
Period π — the double sign-flip cancels in the quotient.
Each branch climbs from −∞ through 0 to +∞.

lessons.title: Exact Values & Life Near a Wall
takeaways: tan(π/6), tan(π/4), tan(π/3) = 0.58, 1, 1.73 — from the sin/cos ratios.
Left of a wall: +∞; right of it: −∞.
Within a branch, tangent strictly increases.

lessons.title: Transforming Tangent
takeaways: Period of tan(Bx) is π/B; walls solve (inside) = π/2 + kπ.
A steepens branches — tangent has no amplitude.
Slides move zeros and walls together, unchanged in spacing.

lessons.title: Arcsine: a Rescued Inverse
takeaways: arcsin inverts sine's restricted climb on [−π/2, π/2].
Domain [−1, 1], range [−π/2, π/2]; negatives handled directly.
Candidate angles outside the branch are discarded by definition.

lessons.title: Arccosine: a Different Branch Entirely
takeaways: arcsin: range [−π/2, π/2]. arccos: range [0, π] — never negative. arctan: range (−π/2, π/2).
Branches are chosen to avoid each function's turning points or walls.
Tangent's walls become arctan's horizontal asymptotes y = ±π/2.

lessons.title: The Inverse Graphs & the y = x Mirror
takeaways: Inverse graphs are branch reflections: swap every (a, b) to (b, a).
arcsin & arctan climb through (0, 0); arccos descends through (0, π/2).
Walls mirror into fences: arctan lives strictly between y = ±π/2.

lessons.title: Round Trips & the arcsin(sin x) Trap
takeaways: sin(arcsin v) = v always (v in [−1, 1]).
arcsin(sin x) = x only for x in [−π/2, π/2]; otherwise it returns the branch angle with x's sine.
Quadrant II inputs map to π − x; negative sines map to negative branch angles.

lessons.title: Mixed Compositions & the Helper Triangle
takeaways: Set θ = the inner inverse; its definition labels two triangle sides.
Pythagoras supplies the third; read off the outer function.
Branch ranges fix the sign: cos(arcsin v) = +√(1 − v²) always.

lessons.title: Solving: One Answer from the Inverse, All Answers from the Circle
takeaways: Inverse functions return ONE branch solution; the circle supplies its twins.
Pairings: sine → π − x₁; cosine → 2π − x₁; tangent → x₁ + kπ.
Isolate the trig function before inverting — coats off first.

lessons.title: General Solutions: the +2πk Move
takeaways: General solution = each [0, 2π) twin + 2πk.
k ranges over ALL integers, negatives included.
Solutions per window = (families) × (turns in the window).

lessons.title: Tangent's Ladder & Merging Families
takeaways: Tangent: one family, step π.
Sine/cosine twins merge into a π-step family only when exactly π apart (e.g. cos x = 0, sin x = 0).
Test a rung before trusting any merge.

lessons.title: Ladders for Transformed Angles
takeaways: Write the ladder for the INSIDE, then solve linearly for x.
Divide or shift the k-term along with everything else.
B compresses both spacing and step: more solutions per window.

lessons.title: Six Functions from Two
takeaways: tan = sin/cos; sec = 1/cos, csc = 1/sin, cot = cos/sin.
The 'co' naming crosses: csc pairs with sin, sec with cos.
Simplify by rewriting everything in sine and cosine.

lessons.title: The Pythagorean Family
takeaways: Divide sin²+cos²=1 by cos²θ → tan²+1 = sec²; by sin²θ → 1+cot² = csc².
Rearranged: sec²−1 = tan², csc²−1 = cot², 1−sin² = cos².
Spotting a Pythagorean pair is the master simplification move.

lessons.title: Proving Identities: Working One Side
takeaways: Transform ONE side only — never operate across the equals sign.
Convert to sine/cosine, or spot a Pythagorean collapse first.
A numeric check catches proof slips instantly.

lessons.title: Sum & Difference: New Angles from Old
takeaways: sin(A ± B) = sinA cosB ± cosA sinB.
cos(A ± B) = cosA cosB ∓ sinA sinB — the sign FLIPS.
Split any special-combo angle (75°, 15°) into 45° ± 30°.

lessons.title: Tangent Sums & Cofunctions
takeaways: tan(A ± B) = (tanA ± tanB)/(1 ∓ tanA tanB) — denominator sign opposite.
Cofunction: sin(90° − θ) = cos θ, cos(90° − θ) = sin θ.
The sum formulas PROVE the cofunction identities.

lessons.title: Applying Sum & Difference: Simplify and Prove
takeaways: Recognize sinA cosB ± cosA sinB → sin(A ± B); the cosine patterns likewise.
Compressing avoids evaluating individual pieces.
Shift/reflection identities are sum formulas in disguise.

lessons.title: Double-Angle: One Angle, Twice
takeaways: sin 2θ = 2 sinθ cosθ; cos 2θ = cos²θ − sin²θ.
The quadrant of θ sets the signs of the doubled results.
Read backwards, 2 sinθ cosθ compresses to sin 2θ.

lessons.title: The Three Faces of cos 2θ
takeaways: cos 2θ = cos²θ − sin²θ = 1 − 2sin²θ = 2cos²θ − 1.
Pick the face matching your given info or your cancellation goal.
Backwards, they give power-reduction: sin²θ = (1 − cos2θ)/2, cos²θ = (1 + cos2θ)/2.

lessons.title: Double-Angle in Action
takeaways: Expand any 2θ so the whole expression shares one angle.
For equations: rearrange to a product = 0 and factor — never divide by a trig factor.
A quadratic in cos x or sin x is the usual payoff.

lessons.title: Quadratics in Disguise
takeaways: Substitute u = sin x (or cos x) and factor the quadratic.
Solve each branch with twin/ladder rules.
Discard any branch demanding |value| > 1.

lessons.title: Mixed Functions: Convert First
takeaways: Convert with a Pythagorean identity so only one trig function remains.
Aim the substitution at the squared term, keeping the linear term's function.
Expand double angles first, then factor to a product = 0.

lessons.title: Traps: Extraneous & Lost Roots
takeaways: Squaring can add extraneous roots — always check in the original.
Dividing by a trig factor loses roots — factor to a product = 0 instead.
Both traps stem from non-reversible operations.

lessons.title: Vectors: Size and Direction Together
takeaways: A vector ⟨a, b⟩ bundles magnitude and direction.
Magnitude = √(a² + b²), always ≥ 0 — the sign lives in the direction.
Vectors model directed quantities: velocity, force, displacement.

lessons.title: Direction Angles & Building Components
takeaways: Direction angle from components: tan θ = b/a with a quadrant check.
Components from size & angle: a = |v|cos θ, b = |v|sin θ.
The quadrant of ⟨a, b⟩ decides which angle the arctan really means.

lessons.title: Displacement: Vectors Between Points
takeaways: Displacement A→B = ⟨x_B − x_A, y_B − y_A⟩ (tip minus tail).
Equal vectors share components regardless of location.
The zero vector ⟨0, 0⟩ has length 0 and undefined direction.

lessons.title: Adding Vectors: Tip to Tail
takeaways: Add/subtract vectors componentwise: ⟨a±c, b±d⟩.
Tip-to-tail: the resultant runs start-to-end of the chain.
The magnitude of a sum is NOT the sum of magnitudes (unless aligned).

lessons.title: Scalar Multiplication: Stretch and Flip
takeaways: k⟨a, b⟩ = ⟨ka, kb⟩: length scales by |k|.
k < 0 reverses direction; k > 0 preserves it.
Unit vector û = v/|v| has length 1 and points along v.

lessons.title: Unit Vectors & Combining Motions
takeaways: Rebuild a vector at any length: (length)·û.
Combine independent motions by adding component vectors.
A balancing (equilibrium) force is the negative of the resultant.

lessons.title: The Dot Product: Vectors to a Number
takeaways: Dot product ⟨a, b⟩ · ⟨c, d⟩ = ac + bd, a scalar.
Positive → acute, zero → perpendicular, negative → obtuse.
Perpendicular to ⟨a, b⟩ is ⟨b, −a⟩ (dot product 0).

lessons.title: The Angle Between Two Vectors
takeaways: cos θ = (u · v)/(|u| |v|); then θ = arccos of that.
cos θ = 1 → parallel (0°); cos θ = −1 → antiparallel (180°); 0 → perpendicular.
Special cosines (√2/2, 1/2, √3/2) flag 45°, 60°, 30°.

lessons.title: Work: The Dot Product at Play
takeaways: Work W = F · d — only the force component along the motion counts.
Perpendicular force → zero work; aligned → maximal; opposing → negative.
The dot product u·v = |u||v|cos θ measures one vector's shadow on the other.

lessons.title: Matrices & the Matrix-Vector Product
takeaways: Add/scale matrices entry by entry.
Matrix-vector product: each output = a row dotted with the vector.
[[a,b],[c,d]]·⟨x,y⟩ = ⟨ax+by, cx+dy⟩.

lessons.title: Determinant & Inverse
takeaways: Determinant = ad − bc; it scales area and flags invertibility.
det = 0 → singular, no inverse (the plane collapses).
Inverse = (1/det)[[d, −b], [−c, a]].

lessons.title: Solving Systems with Matrices
takeaways: Write a system as M·⟨x, y⟩ = ⟨constants⟩; solve with M⁻¹ or Cramer's rule.
Cramer: replace a column with the constants, take determinants, divide by det M.
det = 0 → no unique solution (matches elimination stalling).

lessons.title: Matrices as Transformations
takeaways: A matrix maps (x, y) → (x′, y′) via the matrix-vector product.
Its columns are the images of ⟨1, 0⟩ and ⟨0, 1⟩.
Scalings and reflections are simple diagonal/swap matrices.

lessons.title: Rotation Matrices
takeaways: Rotation by θ: [[cos θ, −sin θ], [sin θ, cos θ]].
Rotation is rigid: it preserves every length and angle.

lessons.title: Composing Transformations
takeaways: Compose transformations by multiplying matrices: 'B then A' = A·B.
Each product entry is a row of A dotted with a column of B.
Order matters (not commutative); two reflections can equal a rotation.

lessons.title: Finding the Suspects
takeaways: A critical point is where f′ = 0 OR f′ does not exist. Both kinds can hide an extremum.
Finding them is algebra; classifying them is calculus, and they are separate steps.
x³ has a critical point that is neither a peak nor a valley. The suspect was innocent.

lessons.title: The First-Derivative Test
takeaways: + → − is a maximum. − → + is a minimum. No sign change is a saddle, not an extremum.
An EVEN root of f′ is a critical point with no sign change — the bounce rule, now saying something about peaks.
You built this machinery in precalculus. Calculus just pointed it at f′.

lessons.title: Endpoints and the Extreme Value Theorem
takeaways: On a closed, bounded interval a continuous function ALWAYS attains a maximum and a minimum.
They hide only at critical points or at endpoints — an endpoint maximum need not have a flat tangent.
The closed-interval method is a finite checklist: evaluate, compare, done.

lessons.title: Concavity and the Second Derivative
takeaways: f″ > 0 bends upward, f″ < 0 bends downward. Direction (f′) and bend (f″) are independent.
An inflection point needs f″ to CHANGE SIGN, not merely to equal zero — x⁴ is the counterexample.
Three functions, three sign charts: f says where, f′ says which way, f″ says how it bends.

lessons.title: The Second-Derivative Test
takeaways: f′(c) = 0 with f″(c) > 0 is a minimum; with f″(c) < 0, a maximum.
f″(c) = 0 is genuinely inconclusive — x⁴, −x⁴ and x³ all produce it and are all different.
The first-derivative test never fails, and it is the only one that can classify a corner.

lessons.title: Putting the Three Charts Together
takeaways: f says where the curve sits, f′ says which way it goes, f″ says how it bends. Three questions, three charts.
A single x can be a critical point AND an inflection — the labels are independent.
Sketching is deduction, not plotting: only one curve is consistent with all three charts.

lessons.title: Rolle's Theorem
takeaways: Rolle: continuous, differentiable, f(a) = f(b) ⇒ some c inside has f′(c) = 0.
Every hypothesis is load-bearing — |x| − 1 breaks the conclusion with a single corner.
Between consecutive roots of f there is always a root of f′, which lets the derivative COUNT the function's roots.

lessons.title: The Mean Value Theorem
takeaways: f′(c) = [f(b) − f(a)]/(b − a) for some c inside. Rolle is the special case where the secant is flat.
At some instant, your instantaneous rate equalled your average rate — which is why the speeding ticket sticks.
It is an EXISTENCE theorem: it says c is there, not where it is.

lessons.title: What the MVT Buys
takeaways: f′ > 0 ⇒ increasing, and f′ = 0 everywhere ⇒ constant. Both are PROVED by the MVT, not assumed.
That second fact is why + C describes the whole family of antiderivatives, with no exceptions.
A bound on f′ becomes a bound on f — you can constrain a function you have never seen.

lessons.title: End Behaviour and Asymptotes
takeaways: Rational functions: compare degrees for the horizontal asymptote; a vanishing denominator (with a surviving numerator) gives a vertical one.
A hole keeps its limit; an asymptote destroys it. Same widget, same verdict, as in limits.
Polynomials: the leading term decides both ends, and everything else is a rounding error at large |x|.

lessons.title: The Full Sketch
takeaways: Zeros, ends, sign of f′, sign of f″ — assemble them and only one curve fits.
The charts constrain each other, so a contradiction tells you exactly which one to recheck.
Critical points, inflections and turning points are three different counts, and they rarely agree.

lessons.title: Reading f From a Graph of f′
takeaways: A graph of f′ is not a graph of f. Every instinct will read it wrongly, and every instinct must be resisted.
Above the axis → f rises. Crossing the axis → f has an extremum. Rising → f is concave up.
A touch without a crossing is a saddle — the same distinction that has decided every chapter of this course.

lessons.title: Setting Up an Optimisation
takeaways: Write the quantity, use the constraint to reach ONE variable, state the physical domain, then differentiate.
The formula will happily return nonsense outside the domain — the domain is what stops you reporting it.
Once you are down to one variable on a closed interval, it is the closed-interval method from chapter 1.

lessons.title: The Open-Top Box
takeaways: V = x(12 − 2x)² on 0 < x < 6, and V′ = 12(x − 2)(x − 6) settles it: a maximum of 128 at x = 2.
The other critical point, x = 6, is an empty box — the algebra offers it and the domain rejects it.
Always compare with the endpoints. Here they are degenerate; in the next problem they may not be.

lessons.title: Applied Optimisation
takeaways: The constraint eliminates a variable; the domain rejects the impossible answers; the derivative finds the candidates.
ALWAYS compare with the endpoints — a curve that is still climbing when the range runs out has its maximum at the edge.
Equal shares turn up again and again (10 × 10, and half the fence each way). It is worth noticing when it happens.

lessons.title: From One Slope to Every Slope
takeaways: The derivative is a FUNCTION: one slope for every input, not one number for one point.
f′(x) = lim(h→0) [f(x+h) − f(x)]/h — and the cancellation must happen before h reaches 0.
f′ hands you the tangent line for free: the curve gives the point, the derivative gives the slope.

lessons.title: Reading f′ Off the Shape of f
takeaways: Sign of f′ = direction of f; size of f′ = steepness. Height never enters.
f′ = 0 marks a critical point — a suspect, not a conviction. x³ flattens at 0 and keeps climbing.
To convict a critical point you must look at f′ on BOTH sides of it.

lessons.title: Where the Derivative Fails
takeaways: Differentiable ⇒ continuous. The converse is false, and |x| at 0 is the counterexample.
Corners, cusps, vertical tangents and discontinuities all destroy f′.
Differentiable means locally straight: zoom in far enough and the curve becomes its tangent.

lessons.title: The Power Rule
takeaways: d/dx[xⁿ] = n·xⁿ⁻¹ — the exponent drops in front, the power falls by one.
It holds for negative and fractional exponents, so rewrite roots and reciprocals as powers first.
Simplify before you differentiate: many quotients are powers in disguise.

lessons.title: Constants, Sums and Multiples
takeaways: Constants differentiate to 0; constant multiples factor straight out.
Sums split term by term, which makes every polynomial routine.
There is NO product rule of the form f′g′, and no quotient rule of the form f′/g′. Both are false.

lessons.title: The Second Derivative
takeaways: f″ is the rate at which the slope changes: position → velocity → acceleration.
f′ > 0 with f″ < 0 is moving forward while slowing down. Direction and change-of-direction are different questions.
f″ > 0 means the curve bends upward, which is how a flat point is convicted as a minimum.

lessons.title: The Product Rule
takeaways: (uv)′ = u′v + uv′ — each factor takes a turn changing while the other holds still.
The tiny corner du·dv dies in the limit: it is a product of two small things.
f′g′ is not a rule. Test it on x²·x³ and watch it give 48 where the truth is 80.

lessons.title: The Quotient Rule
takeaways: (u/v)′ = (u′v − uv′)/v². The order of the subtraction decides the sign of the whole answer.
The minus and the square both fall out of differentiating v⁻¹ — nothing was invented.
Simplify first where you can: many quotients are powers in disguise.

lessons.title: Choosing and Combining the Rules
takeaways: Identify the outermost operation first: sum, product, or quotient.
Expand or cancel whenever it is cheap — the rules are always available but rarely the fastest road.
When rules nest, work outside in and never run two rules in one line.

lessons.title: The Chain Rule
takeaways: dy/dx = (dy/du)(du/dx) — each stage scales what the last one delivered, so the scalings multiply.
Differentiate the outside, leave the inside alone, then MULTIPLY BY THE DERIVATIVE OF THE INSIDE.
Evaluate the outer derivative where the inside LANDS: f′(g(a)), never f′(a).

lessons.title: Chains Within Chains
takeaways: Longer chains change nothing: one factor per layer, multiplied together, outside in.
When rules combine, the OUTERMOST operation decides which rule comes first.
Implicit differentiation is just the chain rule: every y you differentiate costs you a dy/dx.

lessons.title: Implicit Differentiation in Practice
takeaways: An implicit derivative in terms of BOTH x and y is the honest answer — it is what lets one formula serve a curve with two branches.
A product of x and y needs the product rule AND the chain rule together: d/dx[xy] = y + x·y′.
The recipe never changes: differentiate every term, collect the y′ terms, divide.

lessons.title: e^x and ln x
takeaways: (eˣ)′ = eˣ — the slope equals the height at every point. That property is what DEFINES e.
(ln x)′ = 1/x: still rising at every x, but ever more slowly.
With the chain rule: (e^u)′ = e^u·u′ and (ln u)′ = u′/u.

lessons.title: The Trig Derivatives
takeaways: (sin x)′ = cos x and (cos x)′ = −sin x. Four differentiations return you to the start.
The minus sign is forced: cosine starts at a peak and falls.
Radians are not a preference. In degrees, (sin x)′ picks up a factor of π/180 and every formula turns ugly.

lessons.title: Inverses and the Reciprocal Slope
takeaways: (f⁻¹)′(b) = 1/f′(a), where f(a) = b — reflecting across y = x swaps rise and run.
Find the matching point FIRST. Evaluating f′ at the wrong place is the error this rule invites.
The inverse trig derivatives are just this rule applied, and the trig vanishes when you do it.

lessons.title: Position, Velocity, Acceleration
takeaways: s says where, v = s′ says how fast and which way, a = s″ says whether that is changing.
v = 0 means momentarily at rest. Turning round is a stronger claim — it needs v to change SIGN.
a > 0 does NOT mean speeding up. That comparison is the next lesson.

lessons.title: Speeding Up or Slowing Down
takeaways: Speeding up ⟺ v and a have the SAME sign. Slowing down ⟺ opposite signs.
A reversing car with negative acceleration is speeding up — backward, and faster.
Speed is |v|, and 'deceleration' is a trap: it means a < 0, which is not the same as slowing down.

lessons.title: Distance Travelled vs Displacement
takeaways: Displacement is s(b) − s(a). Total distance adds the length of every leg as a positive number.
Split the journey wherever v changes sign — those are the turns, and only there.
In the next course: displacement is ∫v dt, and total distance is ∫|v| dt. The absolute value does this by hand-work automatically.

lessons.title: Related Rates: the Chain Rule With Time Hidden
takeaways: Differentiate the RELATION with respect to t; every variable picks up a d/dt, exactly as in implicit differentiation.
Geometry supplies the equation. Calculus only differentiates it.
Substitute the instant's numbers LAST. Doing it first freezes a variable and sends its rate to zero.

lessons.title: The Sliding Ladder
takeaways: The relation is geometry (Pythagoras). The calculus only differentiates it with respect to t.
dy/dt = −(x/y)(dx/dt), and the minus sign is the physics: the top slides DOWN.
As the ladder flattens, x/y grows — so the top falls faster and faster while the foot moves at a constant speed.

lessons.title: Choosing the Relation
takeaways: Ask what varies, and what ties them together. Geometry supplies the relation; calculus only differentiates it.
Reduce to one variable BEFORE differentiating, using the shape's fixed proportions.
Label the diagram with variables, never numbers. The numbers belong in the final line.

lessons.title: The Tangent as an Approximation
takeaways: L(x) = f(a) + f′(a)(x − a) — the tangent line, used as a stand-in for the curve near a.
It works because differentiable means locally straight. Zoom in and the curve BECOMES the line.
f″ tells you the direction of your error in advance: concave up undershoots, concave down overshoots.

lessons.title: Differentials and Error
takeaways: dy = f′(x)·dx — a small input change buys an output change of about f′(x) times as much.
For y = xⁿ, the RELATIVE error is multiplied by n. Cubing triples it; a square root halves it.
Run it backwards to set tolerances: decide the error you can accept in the output, and the rule tells you how precisely to measure the input.

lessons.title: When Linearisation Fails
takeaways: The error grows like (x − a)²: double the distance and you quadruple the error.
It is proportional to |f″| — the curvature is what pulls the curve away from its tangent.
No derivative, no tangent, no linearisation. A corner cannot be approximated by a line.

lessons.title: L'Hôpital: 0/0 Explained at Last
takeaways: If f/g → 0/0, then lim f/g = lim f′/g′. Zoom in and both curves become their tangents, so the ratio becomes the ratio of slopes.
CHECK THE FORM FIRST. Applied to a non-indeterminate limit, the rule gives a confident wrong answer — (x²+1)/(x+1) at 0 is 1, and the rule says 0.
It is not the quotient rule: differentiate top and bottom SEPARATELY. And re-check the form before each repeat application.

lessons.title: The Other Indeterminate Forms
takeaways: The rule speaks only 0/0 and ∞/∞. Every other indeterminate form must be REWRITTEN into one of them.
0·∞ becomes a quotient by pushing one factor downstairs; 1^∞ yields to logarithms.
ln x ≪ any power of x ≪ eˣ — and L'Hôpital is what proves the hierarchy.

lessons.title: Instructions a Curve Obeys
takeaways: dy/dx = f(x, y) is an INSTRUCTION at every point, and a solution is any curve that obeys it.
There are infinitely many solutions — one per starting point — and the initial condition picks one. That is the + C, drawn.
The field exists even when no formula does. Most differential equations cannot be solved with symbols; their curves exist anyway.

lessons.title: The Curve That Never Moves
takeaways: An equilibrium is where the right-hand side is ZERO: dy/dx = 0 for every x, so the solution never moves.
Stable equilibria attract nearby curves; unstable ones repel them — and the field shows which, with no algebra at all.
Solutions can never cross, because a point has only one instruction. That is why nothing gets past the ceiling.

lessons.title: Separating the Variables
takeaways: Separable means the right-hand side is (a function of x) × (a function of y). Get the y's left, the x's right, integrate both.
One + C, not two — and apply the initial condition as early as you can.
Dividing by y discards the equilibrium y = 0. The algebra loses it; the slope field never would.

lessons.title: Why Growth Is Exponential
takeaways: dy/dt = ky — the rate is proportional to the amount — FORCES y = y₀e^(kt). Exponential growth is not a species of curve; it is what that sentence implies.
Negative k gives decay, and the half-life T = ln2/k does not depend on how much you started with.
Algebra 1 handed you bˣ as a fact. This is where it comes from.

lessons.title: When the Rate Runs Out of Room
takeaways: dP/dt = kP(1 − P/K): nearly exponential when P is small, stopping dead at the ceiling K.
Equilibria at 0 (unstable) and K (stable). Every positive solution runs to K, from above or below.
The inflection sits at K/2 — the fastest growth is at HALF the carrying capacity, not at the top.

lessons.title: Euler's Method: Walking the Field
takeaways: yₙ₊₁ = yₙ + h·f(xₙ, yₙ): read the slope, take a step, re-read the slope. Repeat.
It is C2's tangent-line approximation, used once per step — so it undershoots a concave-up curve and overshoots a concave-down one.
Halving h roughly halves the error. Most differential equations in the world are solved this way, or by its smarter descendants.

lessons.title: Estimating with Rectangles
takeaways: Rectangles turn an impossible area into an easy sum — at the cost of an error you can predict.
On a rising curve the left rule always undershoots and the right rule always overshoots.
The trapezoid rule is exact on a straight line, because a slanted top is a straight line.

lessons.title: Trapping the Area
takeaways: left sum ≤ true area ≤ right sum, and the gap [f(b) − f(a)]·h shrinks like 1/n.
Only ONE number survives being squeezed from both sides forever — and the integral is DEFINED as that number.
∫ f(x) dx is a fossil of the construction: a stretched S for the sum, f(x) for the height, dx for the vanishing width.

lessons.title: The Definite Integral
takeaways: ∫ₐᵇ f dx is DEFINED as the limit of Riemann sums — not as a formula.
Adjacent intervals add; reversing the limits flips the sign (because dx is a signed width).
The integral is SIGNED: area below the axis counts as negative. For geometric area, integrate |f|.

lessons.title: The Accumulation Function
takeaways: A(x) = ∫ₐˣ f(t) dt is a FUNCTION — the area swept out so far.
The variable of integration is a dummy; only the endpoint survives.
A(b) − A(a) is the area between a and b. Remember that subtraction: it is about to do a great deal of work.

lessons.title: Reading A Off f
takeaways: f > 0 → A rises. f = 0 → A is flat. f < 0 → A falls.
Turning points of A sit exactly on the sign changes of f.
Accumulation is signed: A can go negative, and 'area' below the axis is subtracted.

lessons.title: The Integral of a Rate Is a Total
takeaways: ∫ (rate) dt = the total change. Multiply the units of the height by the units of dx and the meaning appears.
The plain integral gives NET change (displacement); ∫|f| gives the total amount that moved (distance).
Flow → volume, current → charge, marginal cost → total cost. It is always height × width, summed.

lessons.title: FTC Part 1: The Slope of the Area
takeaways: A′(x) = f(x): the slope of the accumulation IS the height of the function.
So d/dx[∫ₐˣ f(t) dt] = f(x) — the two operations annihilate, and you never compute the integral.
The lower limit only shifts A by a constant, and constants have no slope.

lessons.title: FTC Part 2: Evaluating With an Antiderivative
takeaways: ∫ₐᵇ f dx = F(b) − F(a), for ANY antiderivative F of f.
The +C cancels in the subtraction, so always take the simplest antiderivative.
This is why calculus is USEFUL: the rectangles define the integral, and the antiderivative computes it.

lessons.title: Why the Two Halves Are One Theorem
takeaways: Part 1 (A′ = f) and Part 2 (∫ₐᵇ f = F(b) − F(a)) are one fact: differentiation and integration are inverse.
Part 2 falls out of Part 1 in four lines — A is an antiderivative, constants cancel, A(a) = 0.
Every derivative rule is now an antiderivative rule, read backwards.

lessons.title: Reversing the Power Rule
takeaways: ∫ xⁿ dx = xⁿ⁺¹/(n + 1) + C, for n ≠ −1. Always check by differentiating back.
The + C is a whole family of parallel curves — the derivative destroyed that information and antidifferentiation cannot invent it.
In a definite integral C cancels, so ignore it. In an indefinite one it is part of the answer.

lessons.title: Pinning Down the Constant
takeaways: ∫ f dx is a FAMILY of curves; an initial condition picks one out of it.
The derivative destroys vertical position, so no amount of calculus can recover it — only a given point can.
Integrate twice and you meet two constants, which need two conditions to pin down.

lessons.title: The Antiderivative Library
takeaways: ∫eˣ = eˣ, ∫(1/x) = ln|x|, ∫cos = sin, ∫sin = −cos. The minus on the last is where the errors live.
n = −1 is not an arbitrary exception: the power rule literally divides by zero there, and ln|x| fills the hole.
Always differentiate your answer back. It is the cheapest check in mathematics.

lessons.title: Undoing the Chain Rule
takeaways: If the integrand contains an inside function AND (a constant times) its derivative, substitute u = the inside.
du = u′ dx. A missing CONSTANT can be fixed out front; a missing VARIABLE cannot.
Always check by differentiating your answer — the chain rule should hand back the integrand.

lessons.title: Changing the Limits
takeaways: Change variable, change limits: feed each x-limit through u.
Or substitute back to x and use the original limits — but NEVER mix a u-integral with x-limits.
A linear inside (kx + c) always costs a factor of 1/k, which is the inner derivative being paid back.

lessons.title: Choosing u
takeaways: What is inside something? Is its derivative present, up to a constant? If both, that is your u.
Constants may be moved across the integral sign. Variables may not — which is why a missing x is fatal.
Substitution is a tool, not an obligation: knowing when it fails (∫cos(x²) dx) is half of using it well.

lessons.title: Area Between Two Curves
takeaways: Area between curves = ∫(top − bottom) dx. Only the strip's HEIGHT has changed from C4.
The limits are where the curves meet — precisely where the height reaches zero.
A negative answer means you subtracted the wrong way. If the curves cross INSIDE the interval, split there.

lessons.title: Spinning a Strip Into a Disc
takeaways: Revolve a strip about the x-axis and it sweeps out a disc of radius f(x) and thickness dx.
V = π∫[f(x)]² dx — square the FUNCTION, slice by slice, then integrate. Never square the finished integral.
Slice, measure the slice, add them up. Only the measurement ever changes.

lessons.title: The Washer: a Disc With a Bite Out of It
takeaways: A washer's face is π(R² − r²) — subtract the AREAS, never the radii.
R is the far curve from the axis and r is the near one, so the hole is what the gap under the region sweeps out.
Area, disc, washer: same slicing, same summing, three measurements. Work out what ONE slice is worth and the integral writes itself.

lessons.title: Known Cross-Sections
takeaways: No revolution is needed. Stand ANY shape on the slices and the method is unchanged.
Write the area of ONE cross-section in terms of x, then integrate it. That is the whole method.
π appears only when the slice is round. Square slices have no π — which is a useful sanity check.

lessons.title: The Average Value of a Function
takeaways: f_avg = (1/(b − a))∫ₐᵇ f dx — add with an integral, then divide by the width.
It is the height of the rectangle with the SAME AREA as the region: level the curve without spilling anything.
The Mean Value Theorem for Integrals says the function actually ATTAINS its average — C3's theorem, one level up.

lessons.title: Motion Revisited: ∫v and ∫|v|
takeaways: Displacement = ∫v dt. Total distance = ∫|v| dt.
To compute ∫|v|, find where v changes sign, integrate on each piece, and add the MAGNITUDES.
It is not a new idea — it is the hand method from C2, written as a machine.

lessons.title: Differentiating a Parametric Curve
takeaways: dy/dx = (dy/dt)/(dx/dt) — the dt's cancel, and the curve may loop as much as it likes.
Horizontal tangent: dy/dt = 0. Vertical tangent: dx/dt = 0. (Both zero is a cusp, and undecided.)
The second derivative is NOT the ratio of second derivatives. It is d/dt[dy/dx] ÷ dx/dt — and getting that wrong is the classic error.

lessons.title: Arc Length: a Sum of Tiny Hypotenuses
takeaways: L = ∫√((dx/dt)² + (dy/dt)²) dt — every tiny piece of arc is a hypotenuse, and the integral adds them up.
The integrand is the SPEED, so arc length is ∫ speed dt: the total distance travelled.
It is C5's ∫|v| dt in two dimensions, where the magnitude is now Pythagorean.

lessons.title: Polar Area: the Slices Are Triangles
takeaways: A polar region is swept from the origin, so its natural slice is a thin WEDGE — a triangle, not a rectangle.
A = ∫½r²dθ, and the ½ is the triangle. Losing it is the classic error, and a circle will catch you every time.
Slice, measure one slice, add them up. The sentence never changed; only the measurement did.

lessons.title: Motion as a Vector
takeaways: r = ⟨x, y⟩; v = ⟨x′, y′⟩; a = ⟨x″, y″⟩. Differentiate component by component.
Speed is |v| — the arc-length integrand. And ∫|v| dt is the total distance, exactly as in C5.

ACCELERATION IS NOT THE DERIVATIVE OF SPEED. A particle on a circle has constant speed and constant nonzero acceleration: the acceleration is perpendicular to the motion, so it turns without hurrying.

lessons.title: Beyond Geometric
takeaways: The geometric ceiling was one test for one family. Every other test is a different way of getting a ceiling over the pile.
nth-term test: if the terms do not fade to zero, it diverges. It can NEVER prove convergence.
The harmonic series is the standing counterexample: terms fade to zero, and it diverges anyway.

lessons.title: Comparison and the p-Series
takeaways: Σ1/nᵖ converges exactly when p > 1. The harmonic series sits ON the boundary, on the wrong side.
To prove convergence, sit UNDER something convergent. To prove divergence, sit OVER something divergent.
A comparison pointing the wrong way proves nothing at all — and you never need to know the actual sum.

lessons.title: Alternating Series and the Error Bound
takeaways: Alternating signs can rescue a series whose terms fade too slowly to be summed on their own.
The partial sums bounce and close in, so the limit is trapped BETWEEN consecutive partial sums.
Hence the error is smaller than the FIRST OMITTED TERM — provably, and for free.

lessons.title: Building a Function Out of Powers
takeaways: A Taylor polynomial matches f's value, slope, curvature and beyond — one derivative per term.
The 1/n! is forced: it cancels the n! that differentiating xⁿ produces, so each term fixes exactly one derivative.
eˣ and sin x converge everywhere. 1/(1 − x) does not — and that is the next lesson.

lessons.title: Where the Polynomial Gives Up
takeaways: Inside the radius, more terms always help. OUTSIDE it, more terms make things worse — the boundary is hard, not soft.
The ratio test, pointed at a power series, hands you the radius directly.
Factorials in the denominator crush the terms and give an infinite radius. Without them, the radius is finite.

lessons.title: New Series for Nothing
takeaways: Inside the radius, differentiate and integrate term by term. The radius survives; only the endpoints can change.
Integrating the geometric series gives −ln(1 − x). Substituting −x² and integrating gives arctan x.
Nobody computed those derivatives. The geometric series did all the work — which is why it is worth knowing by heart.
